I believe students should develop their own summer project designs because they can generate highly creative projects, may experience greater enjoyment while pursuing personalized designs, and will encounter reduced stress throughout the summer.

Students can generate highly creative projects during summer by investigating experiments or examining someone’s life. A student can explore scientific experiments to implement as projects that could prove enlightening for the class or for themselves. Additionally, they can discuss a notable figure or someone in their family and clarify why they selected that individual. Students can devise original projects and present them to the class while explaining how the concepts emerged and how their creations might assist themselves or others.

Students may experience greater enjoyment while creating their own projects. They will likely feel more motivated to pursue personally designed projects rather than adhere to a routine assignment provided by a teacher. Students can produce highly inventive outcomes when allowed to explore freely. They may take pleasure in tasks that do not conform to a prescribed checklist. Students can also collaborate on projects with their peers.

Finally, students may encounter diminished pressure regarding project completion. They can pursue work without agonizing over perfection or strict adherence to guidelines. Students can establish their own criteria and demonstrate to classmates how they formulated them, enabling others to attempt similar approaches in the future.

In conclusion, these are my reasons for believing students should design their own summer projects.

I believe learners should plan their own summer projects, since this approach sparks fresh ideas, makes the work more enjoyable, and lowers pressure during the break.

When students choose their topics, they often produce imaginative results. They might study science experiments and present something surprising to the class, or they might explore the life of a well-known figure or a family member and explain why the story matters. Learners can also invent new solutions or tools and describe where their ideas came from and how their creations could help people.

Allowing learners to shape their own projects makes the process more engaging. It feels more exciting to follow personal interests than to complete a task that every classmate receives. When given room to explore, students can think in unexpected ways and focus on the work itself rather than ticking off requirements. They may also decide to team up with friends, which can make progress feel lighter and more rewarding.

Finally, designing their own assignments helps reduce worry. Without strict guidelines, learners do not feel forced to make everything perfect or match a fixed list. They can set their own goals and later share these methods with classmates, offering others a simple way to try something similar.

These are the reasons why I feel students should create their own summer projects.

However, lacking an afterschool homework program would mean that students genuinely needing grade improvement would still have opportunities to succeed and conclude their current grade strongly, preparing them for the upcoming year.

I support the idea of creating an afterschool homework club. Many students struggle to complete assignments alone, and having teachers present to guide them could make a real difference by lowering failure rates. In addition, some learners do not have computers or other devices at home, so staying after class gives them access to the tools they need to keep up with their work.

On the other hand, not offering such a club might push students to learn how to manage difficulty on their own, since life does not always provide immediate help. Still, I believe the benefits of a supervised club outweigh this concern. It also allows students to interact with classmates and observe different approaches to solving problems, which can strengthen their own study habits.

There are possible downsides to consider. Some students might copy answers from others or treat the club as a chance to chat rather than work. To reduce this risk, rules could be set so that learners only look at each other’s work after they have tried independently. At the same time, many students will remain focused and use the time responsibly without disrupting others.

Overall, I think an afterschool homework club should be offered. There are stronger reasons to support it than to avoid it, and it can help many students build better study routines and improve their grades. Those who care about their progress are likely to take it seriously. Even so, students who need extra help would still have a structured opportunity to catch up and finish the school year with stronger results.

Success depends greatly on the way you choose to see the world, and research suggests that your outlook shapes much of what happens to you. A positive mindset matters because it travels with you everywhere, opening paths that might otherwise stay closed. When you carry optimism, you do not just feel better; you also act in ways that lead to stronger results.

To begin with, a hopeful approach helps people reach further than they expect. For instance, looking for solutions rather than dwelling on problems makes it easier to land a job, complete assignments, and earn a place in higher education. Tasks that feel heavy become lighter when you believe progress is possible.

In addition, positive energy changes how a day unfolds. Obstacles still appear, yet they are less likely to stop you, because trust in your own effort keeps you moving. This steady belief often turns goals that once looked distant into practical achievements.

Moreover, a constructive attitude signals respect to others. In classrooms, offices, or casual meetings, people notice calm and courtesy, and they remember it. As a result, doors open, including chances for work and growth that depend on trust and reputation.

At the same time, first impressions matter greatly, especially when meeting employers or new teammates. The way you present yourself can decide whether you are seen as capable and reliable. A negative manner may close opportunities quickly, while a thoughtful and bright presence invites further interest.

In the end, life responds to the attitude you choose, and only you can guide it. Evidence shows that outlook influences achievement, not by magic, but through actions, respect, and the way people see us. Staying positive is not simply a mood; it is a practical key to succeeding in work, study, and everyday steps forward.

Allowing schools to deliver lessons remotely so that learners can study from home through online platforms or video calls may appear useful, yet I believe this option does not truly help students. Several clear problems show why learning away from school often fails to support real progress.

To begin with, remote study makes it easy for learners to lose concentration. Without a classroom setting, phones and other gadgets quickly draw attention away from lessons. Moreover, family members or younger siblings at home can interrupt study time, making it harder to keep up with coursework. When distractions pile up, assignments lag and deadlines are missed, which can lead to failure and wasted effort. For instance, my cousin was allowed to take one subject online after arriving in the United States with his brothers and sisters. Because of constant noise and interruptions at home, he could not focus, and his results dropped until he eventually failed the course.

In addition, many students find it difficult and dull to learn entirely at their own speed. Without a teacher present to explain points and answer questions, lessons become confusing and frustrating. Furthermore, studying alone removes the chance for lively discussion, and many learners feel inactive and bored. As a result, they may skip important parts of the material or simply stop watching and go to sleep. I once knew a friend who faced exactly this problem. He found online lessons hard to follow and felt sleepy even during short sessions. Drinking strong coffee did not help, and he often turned off his computer to rest, which steadily harmed his school performance.

Finally, remote learning can cause tiredness because it leaves no space for proper rest. Some students finish jobs or chores after school before logging on to study, so they are already worn out. Personally, I walk a long distance home after classes, complete homework, and take a shower, which leaves me exhausted by the time my online lesson begins. Learning while feeling drained slows progress and reduces the quality of study.

In conclusion, distance learning brings more drawbacks than benefits for students. Poor focus, boredom, and fatigue together weaken academic results, showing that studying from home is not an effective choice for many learners.

Each group learn something new from each other.

"Everyday we all learn new things in life".

Second, working in groups help the people improve because they will understand better. For example, asking their partners if they have a question or didn't understand really well. "We could do more if we all help each others".

In one of my English classes, the teacher divided us into groups of four and provided a set of questions. After discussing our answers, it became clear that every group reached different conclusions. This comparison showed us how much we could learn from one another.

Daily life itself proves that people constantly acquire new skills through shared experiences.

Secondly, teamwork improves comprehension because it gives people the chance to clarify confusion. When a task is unclear, asking a partner for guidance can make the work easier to complete. During a history lesson, our teacher assigned an activity that had to be finished by the end of the period. I did not fully understand the instructions, but after a classmate explained them again, I was able to contribute ideas and support my group.

When people help one another, they can accomplish far more.

Some argue that working alone leads to better focus. They claim that solitude avoids distractions and speeds up progress. A friend often prefers to work independently, saying that groups easily shift to casual conversation, lose focus, and achieve very little. However, this view misses an important point: when difficulties arise, having someone to turn to prevents stagnation. Without support, a person may struggle to move forward, whereas collaboration offers immediate feedback and solutions.

In conclusion, teamwork brings many advantages, including stronger understanding, new friendships, and greater self-awareness. Sharing responsibilities reduces pressure and ensures that challenges are addressed more effectively. Although opinions may differ, I remain convinced that working in groups is more beneficial than working alone.

At times, improvement simply requires the help of others.

People should rely on their own judgment to avoid being led in the wrong direction by so-called experts. Because individuals understand themselves best, they are usually in the best position to choose what fits their needs and desires, both in mind and body. When someone selects a gift or an item for another person that turns out to be completely unsuitable, it often shows that the recipient’s true preferences were not considered from the start.

Making personal choices also allows people to learn from their errors and poor estimates. For instance, many shoppers order clothes online without checking sizes in person, only to realize later that they should have tried items on or taken proper measurements first. Similarly, customers sometimes focus on attractive images and ignore product details, then receive something that looks different, is smaller than expected, or lacks important parts. These experiences teach them to read descriptions carefully and to think twice before buying.

Another reason to decide for oneself is that not all experts can handle individual situations well. A lawyer might charge a large fee yet still lose a case, or a doctor could insist that nothing is wrong while prescribing costly medication that is already available at home. In some cases, therapists may suggest treatments or drugs that are unnecessary, partly because certain professionals feel free to act as they wish, even when their approach is questionable.

In the end, some of these experts either lack proper skill or aim to profit from people’s trust. While mistakes are a normal part of learning, it is safer to depend on one’s own reasoning than to follow advice that may be unhelpful or misleading. Choosing independently helps people avoid poor guidance and grow from their own experiences.

I agree that music, drama, and art should remain optional rather than compulsory. Since students differ in their talents and plans, forcing them into subjects they dislike or do not need can lead to poor results and wasted effort. These lessons should be choices, not obligations.

First, allowing learners to decide whether to study these areas respects their individual goals. Many young people aim for careers that have nothing to do with performing or creating visual work. Requiring such courses does not make students more capable or better prepared for further study. For those who feel no interest, lessons of this kind quickly become dull and add little to their overall progress.

Another important point is that making these subjects compulsory can be unjust. Failing in an area that does not match a student’s strengths may delay graduation and create unnecessary stress. It seems wrong to block someone’s next steps simply because they struggled in a class that plays no real part in their future.

In summary, music, drama, and art are best left as electives. They are not central to success, nor do they help most learners secure work later. Keeping them optional allows schools to focus on what truly matters without putting students at risk over subjects that are far from essential.

Homework is often difficult, and it can be hard to manage without support. Some students think an afterschool homework club would be helpful and even enjoyable, especially for those who cannot finish assignments or do not understand the work. At the same time, many others have busy afternoons and find it hard to fit extra time at school into their routines.

For some students, staying after classes is not practical. They may need to train for sports, rehearse for music or dance, or look after family tasks, which leaves little room for extra study sessions. A homework club could suit those who have free afternoons and would like a quiet place to complete daily tasks. However, it does not solve the problem for students whose schedules are already full.

I believe that afterschool homework clubs are not the best option. I often have practices that take up my afternoon, so I must try hard to finish homework at home and hand it in the next day. Teachers may also struggle to stay late because they have personal responsibilities, such as caring for children or pets. Because of this, asking staff to run these clubs after hours seems unrealistic.

Another issue is transport. Many students cannot get home easily if their parents are still working or are unavailable. It is unlikely that schools could supervise large numbers of children after hours or provide food if someone gets hungry. These details make afterschool clubs harder to manage than they might first appear.

A better solution would be to offer a homework period during the final class of the day. Students could use that time to finish assignments, and teachers could also use it to correct work or prepare lessons. This approach would reduce pressure on afternoons while still giving everyone a chance to keep up with school tasks.

Another possibility is a morning session during the first block, allowing students who missed the previous night’s work to catch up before classes begin. Even so, placing this time at the end of the day seems most useful, since it gives both students and teachers a calmer moment before leaving. In this way, homework gets done, stress is lowered, and afternoons remain free for other activities.

Putting younger and older students together could bring helpful results for both sides. This combination allows students to share useful learning habits, offer advice about what lies ahead in high school, and exchange ideas for handling pressure. These benefits make the pairing worth trying in many school settings.

One advantage is that students can discover new ways to study and solve problems. Older learners often have routines that help them understand difficult material, and they can explain these steps to younger peers. When younger students ask questions about homework or topics they find hard, older students can guide them through answers and show practical shortcuts. As a result, younger learners gain confidence, while older students improve their ability to explain ideas clearly.

Another benefit is that older students can prepare younger ones for high school life. They can explain how much homework to expect and which subjects might feel challenging or interesting. By talking about clubs, sports, and class choices, older students help younger ones picture their future school experience. At the same time, younger students can share their own interests, which helps both sides plan better for upcoming changes. This kind of guidance makes the move to high school feel less confusing.

Finally, older students can teach useful ways to handle stress and use time well. They can share test strategies, explain how they study, and suggest steps for staying calm before exams. They might also describe how they organize their workspaces and set daily routines to finish tasks without rushing. Learning these habits early helps younger students build skills that support both schoolwork and personal balance.

In short, pairing younger and older students is helpful because it encourages better learning methods, offers practical advice about high school, and shares ways to manage stress. These experiences create a positive environment where both groups grow and feel more prepared for future challenges.

Once they begin checking their devices, attention moves away from teachers and assignments, and using a phone during lessons can start to feel normal even when it is not appropriate.

Another reason is that phone use limits the kind of learning that helps students understand and remember. Writing notes by hand often improves memory and leads to stronger test results, while practical classroom activities encourage teamwork and deeper thinking. If devices are present, these valuable experiences may shrink as students rely more on screens and less on active participation.

Finally, mobile phones should be treated as a privilege that requires careful judgment. Allowing them during class makes it difficult for learners to recognize the right moments to use them, and strict rules can often be ignored or bypassed. This reduces respect for classroom boundaries and weakens the learning environment.

Keeping classrooms free of personal devices can help students stay focused and gain more from their education.

Many online resources make study enjoyable while strengthening knowledge in ways that feel natural to children.

Beyond homes, technology supports almost every part of life. Security cameras, heating controls, fridges, Wi‑Fi and smart doorbells protect households and add comfort. Outside, vehicles, traffic lights and navigation systems keep cities moving and help people reach their goals. When information is needed, the internet allows research to happen anywhere, saving time and opening access to knowledge that once required libraries. Winston Churchill once remarked that success means moving from one setback to another without losing heart, and I share his view. Failure plays a powerful part in reaching success. It is less about falling short and more about gathering lessons, gaining experience, and refusing to quit. By reshaping plans and improving our approach, we often achieve results that exceed our original hopes. This is why failure matters so much on the road to achievement.

Learning from past errors shows clearly how failure supports progress. History offers many examples in which societies and nations have turned missteps into stronger systems. After World War I, the League of Nations was created to secure peace but did not succeed. From that experience came the United Nations, which now helps keep global stability and stands as a major success. This shift demonstrates how setbacks can guide us toward better solutions, and many similar cases show the strong link between failure and progress.

Persistence is equally important, because quitting rarely leads anywhere. Pelé, for instance, became one of the greatest footballers despite being told he lacked talent and would never make it as a player. Early in his first World Cup, he suffered a serious knee injury and was told he could not play again in the tournament. Instead of accepting this, he trained daily and returned for a later match, proving his ability and helping his team. His refusal to give up shows how determination turns difficulty into progress and reveals the role failure plays in building success.

Trying again is perhaps the strongest connection between failure and achievement. Once we see what went wrong and learn from it, we are ready to attempt our goal with greater skill. Space exploration provides a clear example: many early missions failed, with rockets lost because of technical faults. Each failure allowed engineers to improve designs and methods, and eventually satellites and people reached orbit and traveled farther. These advances were possible only because repeated setbacks were studied and corrected.

Some argue that success can come on the first try, that failure teaches nothing useful, and that repeated disappointment kills motivation. I disagree. Not everything is achieved immediately, and even small setbacks often teach valuable lessons. As for losing heart, that choice remains ours; we can decide to keep believing in ourselves. For these reasons, failure cannot be separated from success. It guides us, builds our experience, and helps us grow. When we combine learning, persistence, and renewed effort, setbacks become steps forward, confirming Churchill’s belief that success grows from the willingness to continue without losing enthusiasm.

School should be a place where learners feel at ease, yet not all schools offer the same experience. In my view, studying from home brings both strengths and limits. One clear advantage is that students can avoid interruptions from classmates who do not take lessons seriously. Without these distractions, it becomes easier to finish tasks on time. In regular schools, some pupils lose focus because of others and may have to repeat subjects, which often feels embarrassing. At home, repeating a topic carries less social pressure and allows progress at a calmer pace.

Another benefit is the chance for one-to-one attention. Teachers in large classes cannot always support every learner, while home study can offer more direct guidance. At the same time, distance from school can be difficult for students who would rather be there but cannot, perhaps because of health issues or public life. Staying indoors all day may feel limiting, and young people also gain from mixing with others and sharing everyday experiences.

Finishing courses can happen more quickly when studying at home, and many options are available, though some elements are missing. Public schools often provide free meals and resources without extra cost, whereas home study brings expenses such as internet, equipment and food. Still, these investments can be worthwhile because they lead to real learning and later opportunities.

In the end, receiving a good education from home can prepare students for what comes next. Whether a person attends a traditional school, a private one or studies remotely, each path can bring valuable benefits when used well.

A year ago I believed that business was the path I wanted to follow, yet it proved to be far more difficult than I expected. I could not perform well in those classes, eventually failed, and felt intense pressure without knowing what step to take next. I understood that this field did not suit me, but I feared it was too late to switch. After speaking with my counselor, I learned that changing direction was still possible. I then chose a different field and now feel confident that it fits me better. I cannot promise I will never reconsider, because I sometimes struggle to make firm choices. Over time, I have seen that this uncertainty is common, and my classmates often share the same experience. Although some argue that young students should commit early so they can select helpful high school courses, early commitment is generally a poor idea. Young people risk picking unsuitable fields and often lack clarity about what they truly want to study.

Some claim that deciding early allows students to tailor their high school classes and strengthen skills for the right profession. The issue is that many do not realize the downside of this approach. I frequently hear peers say, “This class is really hard for me, but I cannot change it because it helps my future career.” Such comments reveal stress and unhappiness rather than purpose.

A better approach is to let students explore new directions. The path they start on may not match their strengths or interests, and indecision is natural when facing so many options. There are many reasons to avoid locking in a career too soon, but two stand out.

First, young people may choose fields that do not fit them. Many children admire their parents and aim to follow the same studies, or they face pressure to pursue degrees chosen by their families. Later, they discover that the path does not suit them, leading to frustration and anxiety. Some even consider leaving school altogether, believing the difficulty reflects their ability rather than a poor match. If students were asked how they feel about their current field, many would likely say it is not right for them.

Second, young students often lack certainty about their goals. With so many possibilities, settling on one is difficult. Learners may develop talents that guide them toward other areas, even after doing well in an earlier choice. Changing direction may involve mistakes, but it also brings valuable lessons. Students may decide to pursue two or more fields, take varied courses, and move closer to their aims. Exploring options ultimately helps them make stronger decisions.

In conclusion, early career commitment tends to be unwise because students risk selecting unsuitable paths and often lack clarity about their interests. Impulsive choices or prolonged indecision can both cause problems. The most helpful strategy is to give learners space and support to discover what they truly want to study, so they can approach their future with greater confidence.

Ralph Waldo Emerson, who wrote, "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment," offers a view I agree with because doing things yourself can lead to better outcomes. His advice to be yourself can help you improve by trying new things, and there are many reasons to be your own person.

First, being yourself can lead to a great life and open new opportunities. By this I mean that holding to your own ideals can point you toward a strong future. For example, setting rules for yourself or devoting time to what you want to do can be an excellent way to begin. Someone once told me that if you fight for your dreams and truly want them, you will achieve them through your own effort. Then you can take pride in doing something you never imagined you could do.

Second, when you get things done on your own, you can set a strong example for many children in the world. Believe it or not, being an example for others is one of the greatest accomplishments because they may want to do or be as you are. Also, trying something new each day can help you improve. As the quote says, "Hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard." Something useful to remember is that everyone learns new things through mistakes. Making a mistake is not a big problem; it means you are trying to do better and are learning how to improve.

Third, and last but not least, friendships connect closely to this idea. One important question here is how you can be sure your friends are genuine. Yes, this can be a challenge, which is why being yourself is the greatest accomplishment: friends can pull you down with drugs, alcohol, and bad choices. This does not mean you cannot have friends; it means you must choose them carefully because hypocrisy exists. People may want to see you fall without a future or a great life. Hypocrisy is among the most dangerous things in the world because it can influence how people want to be or what they want to do.

In conclusion, acting for yourself can make you better and open opportunities you never imagined. Try doing something you love or enjoy as a good way to start being yourself. Choose what is good for you and remember always to fight for your dreams.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote that staying true to yourself in a world that keeps pushing you to become something else is the greatest achievement. I share this view because acting in line with who you are tends to bring better outcomes. When we choose to be ourselves, we create room to grow by exploring new possibilities, and there are many reasons why owning our own path matters.

First, living honestly can lead to a stronger life and unlock opportunities we might not see otherwise. By shaping our own values and dedicating time to what we care about, we set a clear direction. Someone once told me that if you truly fight for your dreams, results follow from your own effort. Over time, you can feel proud of reaching goals that once felt out of reach.

Second, completing tasks by yourself sets a powerful example for others, especially young people. Being someone others admire may be the highest form of success, because they wish to follow your steps. Working steadily and trying something new each day helps us improve. As another saying goes, hard work beats talent when talent does not work hard. Mistakes, rather than being failures, show that we are trying to do better and learn along the way.

Finally, although it may sound unexpected, friendship is closely linked to this idea. An important question is how to know which friends are genuine. This is why being yourself is such a major achievement: it protects us from people who might lead us toward harmful choices like drugs or careless behavior. This does not mean avoiding friendships; it means choosing them carefully, since hypocrisy exists and some people may wish to see us lose our future. Hypocrisy can push others to change their aims in ways that are not truly theirs.

In summary, trusting yourself can improve your life and open doors you never expected. Begin by doing what you love, decide what truly fits you, and keep fighting for the future you want.

My friend switched to homeschooling after being bullied so often that she felt ready to quit. Her counselor suggested online classes because her grades were strong and wanted her to finish school with solid prospects. Many schools now provide distance learning so students can study from home through online platforms or video calls. I believe homeschooling offers real advantages for those facing difficulties at school, for students planning to drop out, and for anyone looking for a simpler, faster path to graduation.

The strongest reason is that it helps learners who face serious problems in traditional settings, such as constant arguments, harassment, conflicts with teachers, or the feeling that time is being wasted. Studying online can keep them away from trouble while allowing them to focus on learning. It does more than remove the issue; it supports steady progress and successful completion of school. When things become hard, talking to a counselor or family members about remote options can open a practical way forward.

It also benefits those who consider leaving school completely, often because of money problems. Some young people choose to work to help their households, while others face difficult personal circumstances that make staying in regular classes hard. Online study lets them continue learning and increases their chances of finding better work later. They often feel encouraged knowing that leaving a physical classroom does not have to mean giving up on a diploma. I once saw a student looking upset as he asked where to leave his laptop because he planned to quit. After learning that remote learning was possible, he felt hopeful again.

Finally, homeschooling is simpler and faster. Learners can study when it suits them, pause when necessary, and continue at their own pace. Compared with traditional school, it creates less pressure, and studies show that students learning from home report far less stress than those in regular classrooms. With fewer deadlines weighing on them, they can enjoy more freedom, wake up when they choose, and balance study with personal time. This flexibility makes the process feel manageable and calmer.

Some may argue that remote learning leaves students without immediate help, yet one-on-one teaching means questions are answered directly and attention stays focused. Without the distractions of a crowded room, progress often improves. Overall, online classes offer valuable support for those facing school problems, those tempted to leave education early, and those seeking a quicker, easier route to finishing their studies.

The British naturalist and statesman John Lubbock claimed that character is shaped by personal choice. I share this view because individuals ought to decide for themselves rather than depend on others to chart their course.

Even though friends, family, and society guide us from childhood, character should remain our own creation. People differ, and we are not meant to copy those around us simply because it is common. Choosing our own path helps us become stronger individuals who trust their abilities. Each independent decision builds self-belief and encourages us to lean on ourselves more frequently.

Although guidance can clarify right from wrong, we still need to select the person we aim to become, since those close to us may give poor examples without us realizing it. During upbringing, caregivers might be kind or harmful. It is our task to use good judgment and determine what is morally correct. When someone nearby behaves badly, we should avoid imitating them and instead act according to our own sense of right and wrong, using reason rather than habit.

Some argue that influence is useful when we feel lost, yet forming our own character matters because trying and sometimes failing teaches us to grow. If we merely follow the crowd, we remain dependent, much like someone fed by spoon. Without making our own attempts, we never learn to manage alone. Letting others decide keeps us weak and reliant, whereas personal choices build independence. In this way, self-direction not only helps us mature but also strengthens our minds.

In daily life, people often let others shape who they are, yet it is better to rely on oneself. Personal decisions foster independence, shield us from harmful examples, promote growth, and sharpen thinking. These points show why we should grow by choosing our own paths instead of following others without thought. We each hold the power to become who we wish to be. After all, we are nobody except ourselves, and this truth makes personal choice in character all the more important.

The Bahamas stands out as one of the most delightful destinations on earth. It is a place I long to explore, mainly because of its spectacular scenery, from bright ocean waters filled with vivid fish to rolling hills and gentle, breezy weather that carries the scent of flavorful local dishes. There are countless ways to spend time there, whether hiking, tasting food at lively events, dancing, or swimming. Not every location offers this mix of activities, weather, and tastes.

It is true that the Bahamas is costly, yet the experience justifies the expense. While some prefer spending their money on other popular cities such as Paris, Germany, or Italy, I would focus on discovering Bahamian culture. After learning about local traditions, I would spend days hiking to enjoy wide views and colorful plants. A trip like this could help me relax and teach me more about customs and even the way people speak.

Travel often brings new abilities. Visitors return home having learned to cook, climb, ski, or cycle. For me, improving my cycling skills matters most, and the Bahamas suits this goal well. Its wide, safe streets allow me to ride without worrying about traffic, possibly preparing me to join a cycling team.

I sometimes imagine what daily life would be like there. Although living in the Bahamas is expensive, some people manage by earning good salaries or growing up with wealth. Life near the beach can be risky because of storms and other natural dangers, so I would choose to live farther inland. The islands’ rich plants and wildlife remain a strong reason to visit.

In the end, the Bahamas offers extraordinary beauty, countless activities, and deep cultural experiences, which is exactly why I want to see it for myself.

A group can also be helpful for students who are having issues turning their work in on time, since they can receive support from others and be more productive.

To conclude, no student should be in the position of having a big project without enough time and without the opportunity to work with a group. Many companies assign jobs to be done by more than one person because they know that a team works more efficiently than one person, and teachers should do the same in their classes to help students raise their grades and be more productive in turning work in. Working with a group should be allowed during classes to improve students' qualities of cooperation and to provide different points of view for doing their best in each subject.

Students who work alone avoid disagreements about choices and do not need to deal with unfamiliar classmates, yet most learners favor teamwork because it lets them split tasks, exchange thoughts, and support one another. Group work helps students finish assignments more effectively. Based on experience and evidence, I believe that collaborating with others is more helpful for learners.

First, students normally face several assignments during each grading period, and the pressure increases when a major project counts for a large part of the grade. In a team, the workload can be shared, making it easier to manage. Each person brings different strengths, so difficult parts of an assignment can be handled by someone who finds them less challenging. This approach usually leads to better results and reduces stress.

Second, teamwork teaches cooperation, which is valued in many workplaces. Companies often assign tasks to groups because different knowledge and skills improve outcomes. The idea of working as a team is common in offices to increase efficiency. Schools can offer similar experiences so that students learn how to cooperate and understand each other’s ideas. This prepares them for future jobs where joint effort is expected.

Allowing group work can also boost students’ confidence. When learners discuss topics together, they find clearer ways to approach assignments and feel more certain about their choices. Schools that offer after-hours access help those who cannot meet at someone’s home, so every member can contribute. For students who struggle to finish on time, group support encourages steadier progress and greater productivity.

In conclusion, students should not be forced to handle large projects on their own without the chance to collaborate. Since many workplaces rely on teams to achieve stronger results, teachers should use the same method to help students raise their grades and work more effectively. Group work during class strengthens cooperation and brings together different viewpoints, helping learners do their best in every subject.

How long has it been since you last raised your eyes from your screen to notice the sky? Each morning, many of us reach for our devices before we even get out of bed. We move through daily life attached to technology, as if it were part of us. While gadgets keep changing and improving, it is less clear whether we are growing as people. We hand over personal details to the online world and constantly measure our lives against others. It is no surprise that so many feel low, since we focus on what others appear to have while overlooking the value of our own. People witness the same events, yet each draws a different meaning from them.

Wasting time is one of the biggest problems. Individuals stare fixedly at their private displays, following trends without question. They chase after what is fresh, highly rated, shocking, or glamorous. Attention turns inward, toward phones and brands that shout status, caring mainly about likes and influence. Online, many build artificial versions of their lives, while real conversations turn harsh behind screens that hide their faces. Fear of being left out pushes people to seek the newest, largest, and priciest items, as if cost equals worth. These habits grow from technology, and hours spent staring at displays take a toll. Posture suffers, with rounded shoulders and strained backs becoming common. I have experienced this myself, and if the pattern continues, more people will carry these physical signs while those who stay upright take the lead. It is hard to stand strong when the body is bent.

At the same time, technology brings clear benefits. It helps us find information for schoolwork, meet new people, and discover opportunities such as jobs or homes. The tools themselves are not harmful; the trouble lies in how they are overused or misused. Technology can support us and harm us in equal measure, and this double effect is something we often fail to notice.

Whenever you get stuck or something goes wrong, you always have support from the people you know well to help you. By not giving up on what you are trying to reach, you can feel confident about yourself and remain confident through life.

Churchill’s words matter in American life because they remind people that failure is not final. At present, many individuals rise after setbacks and continue toward their aims, yet others stop trying once things go wrong. It is useful to examine both responses, since Churchill’s message encourages persistence instead of surrender.

One reason to keep going is that mistakes teach important lessons. Failure does not mean everything is lost. When plans fall apart or results are poor, we learn what needs to change next time. Recognizing this helps us stay focused on our aims and move toward success. Fighting for what we believe in usually leads to progress rather than regret.

Another reason is that persistence brings us closer to our highest goals. When we truly want something, effort is required. Those who fail and decide to quit often feel they have wasted time, but setbacks are normal and cannot be avoided. By continuing to push forward, we build the strength and pride that come from knowing we did not surrender.

On the other hand, giving up often leads to failure. Some people expect to reach goals, enter good schools, or land strong jobs without ever stumbling, and they quit when reality proves them wrong. Meanwhile, those who achieve demanding goals usually keep working even when difficulties appear. Individuals who claim they are not talented enough overlook the fact that they have already come far. When challenges grow, friends and family can offer ideas and encouragement to help us cope.

In the end, any goal is worth steady effort. A clear aim becomes possible when we work for it and refuse to stop halfway. When obstacles appear, support from people we trust can guide us through. By refusing to quit, we grow more confident and better prepared for the road ahead.

Life offers countless chances to shape a better version of yourself. Engaging in unfamiliar activities can develop both mind and body, even when confidence feels low at first. I believe that stepping into tasks beyond current abilities helps people progress, and this view is worth explaining.

Working through questions that feel confusing at first tends to sharpen problem-solving abilities, showing that persistence can turn obstacles into progress. There is every reason to believe that hard tasks can be understood with steady effort.

Some argue that people face fixed limits and cannot move forward when they feel stuck. This idea misses the point, since the real barrier is often a lack of encouragement or motivation rather than ability itself. Low self-belief or poor support can slow progress, yet most individuals are capable of advancing when these factors improve. Growth may vary, but it generally remains possible.

In short, I share Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view that avoiding challenges beyond your comfort zone stops personal growth. From my own experience, tackling what I have not yet mastered has consistently helped me develop into a stronger and more capable person.

Work takes up much of a person’s life, and individuals can choose from many paths that catch their interest. The jobs people select often reflect something about who they are, and many treat this choice with seriousness, wanting to understand it deeply. Deciding on a direction while still in school is a good step, since it helps young people see what a job truly involves, gives them regular enjoyment in daily tasks, and removes uncertainty later in adulthood.

Choosing a path early allows students to see what a profession is really like. Some learners have little sense of what becoming a doctor requires and may not understand the basics or the everyday reality of the role. To learn how to care for patients, they need hands-on contact with real situations. By stepping into a field while still young, they gather useful knowledge and insight. Alongside direct experience, students can also investigate jobs they feel drawn to. For example, someone curious about dentistry can research the steps needed to enter it. Starting early opens access to many resources that help turn interest into ability.

A further benefit is that an early commitment gives students something enjoyable to do each day. Many young people have little to occupy them once classes end, and those who remain inactive often grow bored or dissatisfied. Joining organized programs that introduce career options can change this pattern. When students take part in work-related activities, they discover how to spend their free time in meaningful ways. They may also uncover hobbies they had not considered before, and these activities can bring steady happiness.

Another reason to begin early is that it helps students connect with something that matters to them personally. Having a clear purpose makes daily effort feel worthwhile and encourages steady progress.

Finally, making a choice early reduces adult worries about work. Many teenagers are unsure what they want to do later, and this uncertainty can make job searches difficult and stressful. Those who spend time learning about a path while still in school usually know what suits them and can move forward with greater ease. As graduation approaches, pressure to find employment can be strong, yet students who have already explored a field feel less anxious. They avoid much of the strain linked to sudden decisions and unclear plans. For those who still feel lost, researching options and attending career events can provide useful direction.

Some argue that young people lack enough knowledge to choose so soon, and that this may cause problems later. Yet the opposite is often true: engaging with careers through fairs or practical experience builds the understanding needed for success. When students commit early, they become better informed, discover enjoyable routines, and face fewer difficulties when seeking work in the years ahead.

Hearing the words of Ralph Waldo Emerson may bring to mind his claim that staying true to oneself in a world eager to reshape us counts as a major achievement. Even if this view on individuality feels doubtful at first, there are reasons to take it seriously. People need room to choose their own paths and to act and think without constant pressure from outside forces.

Of course, trying to satisfy family and friends or blending into a shared identity can encourage decent behavior and useful habits. Being part of a group often brings a sense of belonging, while shared values and interests can make us feel connected and proud, much like loyalty to a nation. These collective traits help people recognize one another and feel steady in their place in society.

Still, it is important to step back and examine the group when its thinking contains serious flaws. Dogma, for instance, can take the form of beliefs or opinions treated as unquestionable truth, whether they come from a community or from figures in authority. At times it is also wise to doubt the guidance of friends and relatives, since they can unintentionally point us in the wrong direction, even while we continue to trust them in most areas of life.

Ultimately, being yourself means sorting through outside influences and forming a distinct set of qualities that separate you from others. It involves claiming the right to shape your own character and choices rather than letting the crowd decide who you become.

Being in school is better rather than being at home alone just studying.

Studying from home through online video lessons is not an approach that should be widely encouraged, because it cannot offer the same quality of learning that schools provide. If this method becomes common, students will miss the chance to form strong bonds with classmates and teachers. Moreover, without the structure of a school environment, many may fail to treat their studies with the seriousness they require, since teachers, counselors, and school rules normally push them to stay focused.

First, learning at home is different from being in a classroom, where homework, tests, and exams usually carry greater weight. In school, students can raise questions immediately and receive clear answers and practical examples that help them understand topics properly. By contrast, online learners may struggle to have every doubt resolved, and they lose access to after-school support, chances to retake assessments, or study centers where peers help one another. Without this direct guidance, grades often drop because problems remain unsolved.

Second, if video lessons replace real classrooms, students will have fewer opportunities to develop communication skills and meaningful relationships. At school, learners inspire one another and build trust that turns classmates into friends or even family. This encourages them to see school as a second home where academic and personal support are available. Online study, however, can lead to boredom and isolation, and it limits the lunch breaks and informal talks that relieve stress. Considering that many young people already face anxiety or depression, school offers a space to shift attention away from personal difficulties and to receive advice from counselors, teachers, and friends.

Finally, students who tend to avoid responsibility are less likely to stay focused while studying from home. Without a teacher nearby to remind them to pay attention or finish tasks, they may skip assignments and lose the habit of meeting deadlines. Group work in schools also teaches valuable lessons, as teammates motivate one another and show the value of effort. Alone at home, this influence disappears, and learners may assume they can behave casually without consequences.

In summary, attending classes online is not a favorable option for most students, since it reduces learning quality, weakens social and communication skills, and allows coursework to be treated with less seriousness than it demands.

While learners may dislike longer hours, they would likely value a shorter week. This plan clearly brings both gains and drawbacks.

Many students would support a four-day timetable. Cutting the school week to four days would give pupils more space to complete homework, spend time with family, and plan trips or activities. An additional free day allows young people to manage personal tasks that are harder to fit into a normal week. Even so, this arrangement also carries notable problems.

Lengthening the school day by two hours would probably be unpopular. Some students hold part-time jobs after lessons or help at home, and later finishing times could clash with these duties. Changed hours might also make it difficult for young people to find work that fits around school. For many families, a longer day would disturb carefully planned routines.

The idea offers clear highs and lows, yet it remains worth considering. Students would welcome one fewer day in class, but they would reasonably resist much longer days. Schools should therefore explore a four-day week without stretching daily hours. This change would bring real benefits while avoiding the main disadvantages tied to extended school time.

Some say technology is just an extension cord of our bodies; for example, a cell phone goes where we go and is put to use. We use technology every day, yet it can reduce face-to-face contact and become a distraction. Although some say it has a positive effect on our lives, it actually has a negative effect.

Despite its negative effects, technology provides positive effects as well; we use it every day, and it is part of our lives. It helps us in many ways, such as at our jobs, where much of our work involves technology that lets us complete tasks successfully and with greater ease. We use it to communicate—for example, a cell phone lets us reach others—so we can locate people when needed or simply check on their well-being. We use it in school, where computers and cell phones help students with everyday assignments, allow access to the internet when required, and support teachers in their instruction.

Technology also causes distraction. For example, cell phones used daily in schools draw students away from learning and from classmates. When students use these mobile devices without permission, their grades drop and their interest in school fades. These devices are not only a distraction but an addiction. Another example is driving while using a cell phone, which can lead to a crash. Some people text, change music, or rely on GPS; even GPS is a distraction because it requires looking down instead of keeping eyes on the road. This shows how distraction can make us lose focus on and pay less attention to our surroundings.

Cell phones can reduce contact with others. While using them, people often keep their heads down and do not look up, especially teenagers and children. Because of these mobile devices, teenagers interact less with parents, peers, and family members. These devices can diminish interaction skills, leaving people unsure how to approach someone in conversation. This shows that, with this technology, we are losing social skills and no longer know how to say hello; it is a loss that strips us away from the world.

Despite claims that technology has positive effects, it actually has a negative effect. Technology is embedded in human life and can no longer be removed. It can distract people and erode interaction, yet it is not inherently bad; it is the way we use it that makes it harmful and addictive. If we used technology only when necessary, the world would be a better place.

Many argue that technology acts like an extra limb, always with us and always in use. Devices such as cell phones travel wherever we go and shape how we spend our time. While we depend on them daily, they can reduce face-to-face contact and pull attention away from what matters. Although some claim that technology improves life, it often brings more harm than good.

At the same time, it is true that technology offers real benefits and is now woven into everyday living. It supports us at work, where tools and systems help us finish tasks correctly and with less effort. It keeps us linked to others, making it possible to check on family and friends or reach them quickly when necessary. In schools, computers and phones assist students with daily lessons and research while also helping teachers present material more clearly.

However, technology frequently becomes a source of distraction. In classrooms, phones interrupt learning and shift focus away from teachers and classmates. When students use devices without permission, their grades tend to drop and their interest in studying fades. This habit can turn into dependency, and the problem extends beyond school. Using a phone while driving divides attention and raises the risk of crashes, whether someone is texting, changing music, or watching a navigation screen. Such examples show how distraction weakens concentration and makes people less aware of their surroundings.

Cell phones also limit personal contact. Users often keep their heads down while walking, a habit common among young people, and this reduces communication with parents, friends, and relatives. Over time, these devices can weaken social abilities, making it harder to start or maintain real conversations. As a result, we risk losing basic interaction skills and becoming isolated from the world around us.

Even though some believe that technology helps more than it hurts, its negative side is hard to ignore. It is now a fixed part of life and cannot simply be removed, yet it can distract us and damage human connection. The problem lies not in technology itself but in how we choose to use it. If we relied on it only when truly needed, life could feel more balanced and meaningful.

School is a very important part in a person's life; however, it takes away most of a student's and teacher's day. In a normal public middle school in Maryland, a student's first class starts at 8:15 in the morning and the last class ends at 3:00 p.m. That means that a student spends 7 hours and 25 minutes in school, which is a long time for a person to be receiving information nonstop. The school board should not extend the school day, because that would take time away from activities that students need or will need in the future, such as: students would have less time to do homework or study, students would have less time to participate in after-school activities like sports, and students would have less time to volunteer in community events.

Students would have less time to do homework or study. Students already spend more than seven hours at school and usually have 6–8 classes that last 45 minutes each. From those 6–8 classes, at least 3 would have assigned homework to the students, which means that the students would need time to complete their homework with accuracy. If the school days were extended, students would have less time to complete their homework, which means that their grades might go down for missing assignments.

Students would have less time to participate in after-school activities such as sports or clubs.

Every healthy person should exercise for at least 1 hour per day, and at school not every student takes physical education (P.E.) as a course, which leads to the thought that students might not be getting the necessary amount of exercise per day. Even if a student did take P.E., a normal class lasts 45 minutes, which is not enough for a healthy person. If the school board were to add one and a half hours to the school day, students would have less time to practice on an after-school team. Clubs are just like sports and are a very big thing in a school; clubs show students opportunities they usually would not get in a school day. If the school board were to extend the school day, students who are part of clubs would probably get less time to spend in those clubs.

Students will have less time to volunteer in community events. Community service is usually a requirement in most curriculums. In past experiences I have had to complete 75 hours of community service; those hours were earned for volunteer work, like helping a teacher with younger students or helping a teacher organize her classroom before the school year, etc. Those acts were usually done after school and usually took around 2 hours. If the school board were to extend the school day, students would have less time to finish their community service and could eventually fail because of not enough volunteering hours.

Overall, it is just more convenient for the school board to not add any more hours to the school day so students can have more time for their other activities like sports, clubs, and community service.

Education plays a major role in people’s lives, yet it already fills most of the day for both students and teachers. In a typical public middle school in Maryland, classes begin at 8:15 a.m. and finish at 3:00 p.m., meaning learners spend more than seven hours receiving lessons without a break. Because of this, the district should avoid lengthening the school day, since doing so would reduce the time students have for activities that matter now and later, including homework and studying, after-school programs such as sports and clubs, and community service.

Lengthening the day would leave students with less time to complete assignments and review material. Pupils already stay at school for over seven hours and attend six to eight classes, each lasting about forty-five minutes, and at least three of these usually require homework. Young people need enough time to finish these tasks carefully; if the day were extended, they would have fewer hours to study, and grades could drop because of rushed or missing work.

Students would also lose chances to take part in after-school activities like sports and clubs. Health guidelines suggest at least one hour of daily exercise, yet not everyone takes physical education, and even when they do, forty-five minutes is not enough. Adding time to the school day would make it harder for students to train with teams or stay active. Clubs, meanwhile, offer experiences that regular lessons cannot provide. If schedules became longer, members would have less freedom to join meetings and projects that help them grow.

Finally, extending the day would create problems for community service, which many programs require. In my own experience, earning around seventy-five volunteer hours often meant helping teachers or working with younger students after classes, usually for about two hours at a time. If the school day grew longer, learners would struggle to find enough time to finish these tasks, and some might fail to meet the required hours.

In the end, it makes more sense for the school board to keep the schedule as it is so that students can balance learning with other valuable parts of their lives.

Almost everyone chooses the beach or a pool when looking for a break, and I often wonder which pastime brings the most joy. In my view, joining a swimming club stands out as the most rewarding option. Swimming feels pleasant because it settles me when I am upset, it lets me share laughs with friends, and it turns exercise into something lively and light.

To begin with, swimming helps me find calm when anger or sadness builds up. Last year, right after school ended and the hallways emptied, I slipped into the pool and simply swam. Happiness came from small things: the soft slap of water against my skin, the steady rhythm of waves meeting tiles, and the bright feeling that followed each return to the surface. Another memory comes from a two-day trip to the sea with classmates. When evening arrived, I disliked the idea of leaving and felt low. I changed, grabbed my camera, and walked along the shore. The waves seemed powerful enough to surround me, while birds called as I took pictures. That day felt both cheerful and soothing, which shows how swimming can calm the mind.

In addition, swimming is enjoyable because it brings people together and helps new friendships grow. There was a time I swam alone and felt fine, but everything changed when my friends joined. They made me laugh, and we challenged each other with tricks and quick races. Once, several of us bumped heads while diving, and we all burst out laughing at the surface. Learning to swim also feels lighter with company. When someone struggles to float, a friend can offer quick tips, and even tricky skills like certain strokes become easier. Practicing alone may work, yet sharing the water simply adds more fun.

Finally, exercise feels brighter and more thrilling when it happens in water. I once attended swimming class each Friday after school. At first it did not excite me, but by the third session I began to look forward to it. Over time, my body grew lighter and my swimming improved, even though I had only hoped to drop a few kilos. The change did not appear all at once; it arrived as I started to enjoy every lesson. As I gave more energy and care to each stroke, progress followed without forcing it.

Swimming makes effort feel light, offers happy moments with friends, and calms strong feelings. Because of this, I believe swimming clubs bring a truly enjoyable experience, and sharing such real stories can encourage others to try them as well.

Personally, I enjoy exercising and lending a hand to my family. Many people, including me, feel better when they are on the move. For some, activity is central to their lives, such as trainers or coaches whose work depends on constant energy. On the other hand, long periods of doing nothing can cause problems. Staying inactive for too long may lead to illness, and it can irritate others who depend on us when teamwork is required. The body generally needs motion to feel well and stay strong.

Still, there are times when staying still makes sense. In places like a cinema, constant movement would disturb others, so calm behavior is expected. If danger occurs outside, it is wiser to step back and avoid trouble rather than act rashly. These moments show that rest or caution can be valuable.

In the end, most situations benefit from staying engaged. By avoiding idleness and working steadily, we achieve more and move closer to our goals, while recognizing that occasional stillness also has its place.

People enter and leave our lives, and few remain through every season. By meeting our goals alone, we prove that we can stand on our own and that our own effort is enough.

At the same time, staying true to who we are fuels progress by building self-belief. Confidence grows when we repeat to ourselves that we are capable, much like any habit that strengthens with practice. With this belief, we take on bigger challenges, whether it is speaking up in class, improving at work, or meeting deadlines with care. Trust in ourselves turns into a driving force that carries us forward.

Once this trust is firm, it also allows us to help others who may be struggling. When someone faces disappointment or stress, our own experience of staying strong can encourage them not to quit. Difficult times shape better days, and choosing not to give up, even when pressure feels heavy, shows the power of inner strength. I have faced my own hard months, yet I refused to let them weaken my resolve or shake my belief in myself.

In the end, Emerson’s idea that being ourselves is a major accomplishment holds true, especially when outside influences try to change us for the worse. By holding onto independence and confidence, we move closer to our goals and gain the ability to lift others along the way. A steady, positive mindset and belief in our own strength can guide us toward the success we hope to see in life.

Early commitment to one job can pull students away from their studies. In high school, courses become more demanding each year, and teachers expect serious effort. Students must manage heavy homework loads and frequent tests while keeping their grades high enough to graduate and enter a good college. Adding a job related to a future career can overload their schedule and lower their performance. Many believe that first impressions cannot be undone. Experiences teach us that behavior, speech, and looks often reveal who we are, and many support this view because these things can be managed and refined.

To begin with, conduct matters greatly when meeting someone new. Actions tend to carry more weight than promises, and the way we behave early on sticks in others’ minds. Acting harshly or carelessly in front of a stranger can lead them to form a lasting negative opinion. Trying to stay thoughtful from the start helps avoid misunderstandings.

Words also shape how we are seen. Using crude language may suggest a lack of respect or skill in communication. Speaking clearly and appropriately, whether with simple or more thoughtful language, helps build trust over time. Even if nerves cause slips or hesitation, effort and calmness can leave a better mark. Some listeners are willing to offer another chance if they sense sincerity.

Furthermore, appearance holds strong influence. Outer presentation, including grooming and attitude, is often noticed before anything else is known. A careless look may lead people to judge character unfairly, while a neat and suitable style can encourage openness. Still, their own impressions also guide how they respond.

At times, opinions can shift. A difficult day does not define a person forever, and others may recognize this and allow room for improvement. Although first impressions are powerful, they are not always final.

In conclusion, many argue that initial judgments are hard to erase, and actions, words, and appearance play key roles in forming them. People learn through experience and tend to remember early encounters. Being mindful of behavior, speech, and presentation remains important whenever new meetings occur.

The school day is already long, and I firmly oppose plans to make it even longer. My concern is not just that I am a student who wants less work; it is that stretching the day will cause problems for students, teachers, and the school as a whole. When young people are forced to stay in one building for too many hours, their behavior often suffers. Tired students struggle to focus, and their results usually drop because effort falls when energy is low. Longer days would also leave less time after classes to complete homework or review for tests, and many learners would simply run out of steam.

This change would also create difficulties for staff and for school life. Teachers have families, and some need to be home for their own children. Keeping everyone at school longer makes that harder to manage. Health appointments add another worry. I, for example, visit my orthodontist each month, usually in the morning, and I already miss several lessons. Recovering the lost work is stressful, and a longer day would make it even harder to find appointment times that do not clash with classes. Illness causes similar trouble: missing one day can mean double the catch-up, and that pressure can build quickly.

The school itself would face extra costs and stress. More hours mean more meals, more paper, and more supplies for bathrooms and planners. Managing students for longer stretches can lead to more arguments and conflicts. If the day ends later, the school run would overlap with younger children’s schedules, creating busier roads and a higher risk of traffic accidents. Early starts combined with longer hours would leave students exhausted, and tired minds cannot absorb lessons well, no matter how hard teachers try to explain them.

As shown, extending the school day affects students, staff, and the whole school environment. It risks lower effort, more tired teachers, and avoidable practical problems. I believe the board should reconsider this plan and listen to the views of those who experience school each day. Many learners share this concern because the change touches everyone. In short, adding extra hours is likely to bring more harm than benefit, so the proposal should be dropped before it creates further difficulties.

Collaborating with others is more useful than handling tasks by myself, and I hold this view for several practical reasons. To begin with, teamwork allows people to support one another so that no one needs to carry the full load alone. Dividing work among members also makes it easier to explore the topic in greater detail. These points explain why I consider group work more valuable, and I will now expand on them.

One clear advantage of teamwork is that peers can offer help when difficulties appear. If someone struggles, other members usually notice and step in with guidance. They explain ideas in different ways and suggest alternative methods until the task becomes clearer. For instance, during a recent math activity, my teacher paired me with a classmate. I could not grasp the concept at first, but she sat with me and demonstrated various approaches. Without her support, I would have remained stuck for much longer.

Another reason why teamwork outperforms individual effort is that responsibilities can be shared. When each person handles a specific section, progress speeds up and stress decreases. No one has to manage every detail, because all participants contribute their parts. In history class last week, three classmates and I divided a project among ourselves. One gathered facts, another collected images, a third selected useful videos, and I organized the references. We completed the work by the end of the lesson and received a strong grade.

Finally, working with others broadens what each person learns. Group members often bring facts or viewpoints that others had not considered, which sparks fresh ideas and deeper understanding. This exchange helps everyone prepare more effectively for tests or quizzes, since the discussion itself reinforces knowledge. This is my last point for choosing teamwork over solitary work.

In summary, groups allow members to learn more, share duties, and receive timely help when concepts are unclear. These strengths give teamwork a clear edge over working alone. I believe this approach is far more helpful, and the reasons above explain why I hold this view.

Cities often discuss whether young people should have set times to return home, and a local council is now weighing such a rule for teenagers. The main concern is safety, especially after dark, because conditions outside have changed and risks feel more present. The council’s interest in a curfew comes from a desire to shield young residents from harm, limit exposure to dangerous situations, and reduce problems tied to poor choices, such as underage drinking or other risky behavior.

If this rule is approved, being outdoors past the set hour would not automatically make a teenager a lawbreaker. Much depends on the reason for being out. Young people who are working, facing an urgent need, or accompanied by a responsible adult would not be seen as violating the rule. At the same time, staying out to socialize or attend gatherings after hours would likely count as breaking it. In short, the situation changes according to purpose, not just the time on a clock.

The larger question is whether curfews protect young lives or simply restrict them. Many teenagers view such rules as unfair limits on their freedom, since they want to spend time with friends and enjoy nighttime activities. However, curfews can also keep them away from trouble they may not expect. Leaving home without adult knowledge at night carries risks that are hard to predict, and assuming nothing will go wrong is not the same as being safe. Young people are encouraged to ask whether staying out late is worth the danger that might follow.

The council’s discussion reflects divided views. Some argue that a clear curfew should become law to prevent harm, while others see it as unnecessary control. Whether a young person on the street after hours is acting illegally will depend on the reasons for being there and who they are with. In the end, the rule tries to balance two aims: keeping teenagers safe and respecting the course of their growing independence.
