Scientist Albert Einstein once said, "Imagination is more important than knowledge." Now imagine yourself as a beginning engineer, sitting at your desk, aggravated because you can't come up with a new invention. All you have around you are textbooks but no image or thought of what your invention may be. If only you could imagine a new invention of some sort then maybe you could build something. But with no imagination, how can you build knowledge? I agree with Einstein's quote. I believe imagination is more important than knowledge.

I agree with Einstein's quote because having imagination is how we've had all our inventions yet. Without imagination how were many of the things we own invented? For example, the telephone. The telephone couldn't have been invented without someone imagining a device where you could communicate without leaving your home. You need imagination in order to make new things. Another example would be the camera. Whoever invented it, had to have imagination in order to think of a device that captures any moment almost in an instant. Even I, as a student, need imagination in order to make new things. For example, when making an essay, such as this one, I need to imagine of a good story hook that goes along with the prompt.

Furthermore, I believe in Einstein quote because without imagination, knowledge is almost useless. For example, when learning a new vocabulary list. You may know all the definitions but you can't put them in your own words or use the words in different instances. Why? Because you can't imagine it. You can't picture it, you just know the definitions. Another example is when reading a book. Knowing how to read isn't even near of what you need to fully comprehend a book. You need to imagine it. Picture the story in your mind in order to fully understand the book's theme, setting and tone.

Lastly, I agree in Einstein's quote because without imagination, all our decisions would be made carelessly. For instance, before you speak or move, most of the time you imagine what the outcome of that action will be. If not, the outcome won't be for the better. Another instance is when in an experiment, you hypothesize what the result of the experiment will be. That takes imagination. When signing a contract, it's needed to imagine the consequences of signing and not signing the contract. In other words, you need to imagine things before you decide to take them on. Knowledge isn't the only thing that will help you when making decisions.

In conclusion, Einstein's quote is correct in my perspective. Knowledge isn't the most important factor to have, imagination is key to everything you do and will do. You can't fully understand most things without imagining them. Can't go on inventing things before imagining them first. Also, you won't be able to make good decisions before imagining the outcome. All in all, imagination is also how you'll enjoy your life. Knowledge is great and all but it can't bring others as much happiness as imagination can. It's how we've been happy for all these years. Imagination is how we have gone so far in this world and how much we've survived.

Albert Einstein claimed that imagination matters more than knowledge. Picture yourself as a new engineer seated at a desk, frustrated because no fresh idea appears. Textbooks surround you, yet no vision of what you might create takes shape. Without the ability to dream up possibilities, how could anything new ever be built? The camera offers another example; its inventor needed to envision a device that freezes moments almost instantly. Even in my own studies, imagination is essential. When I write an essay like this one, I must picture an opening that draws readers in and fits the task.

In experiments, forming a hypothesis relies on picturing what might happen. Signing agreements calls for weighing imagined futures, both good and bad. Deciding wisely demands more than facts; it calls for seeing ahead.

In short, Einstein’s words ring true from my point of view. Knowledge is useful, but imagination drives invention, deepens learning, and guides sound decisions. It also colors life with joy, lifting us further than facts alone. Over time, this ability to dream has carried us forward and helped us endure.

Are vacations a necessity to us and to our success? Why do we need them? While some say that inactivity gives us time to reinvent ourselves. Others believe that it instigates procrastination. Inactivity serves a purpose because it keeps us from giving up and it allows us time for new ideas.

Inactivity serves a purpose because it keeps us from giving up. For example, I was once taking a very long test that lasted around 4 to 5 hours. At first, I was just guessing my way through it because I was very tired and ready to give up. Then, we were given a five minute break so I got up and walked around a bit. After walking for a few minutes, I was energized and ready to finish the test. With my new found energy, I was very content with the test and my score. In fact, students who take mental breaks during long testing periods score 31% higher than the ones who did not take any breaks. In conclusion, inactivity keeps us enthusiastic about our work.

Inactivity serves a purpose because it allows us time for new ideas. For example, one of my friends named Generic_Name once did not go to school for three days. Have you ever had a really important decision you had to make? Did you feel overwhelmed because you didn't know what you should do? Asking for help or advise from people such as friends and family around you can really help alleviate all that stress. Most people encounter big decisions often throughout their lives, so getting advise from numerous people can help you get more input on something, and may end up helping you make a final decision. Seeking multiple opinions can really help someone make a better choice when dealing with decision making.

One way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is that by asking more than one person, they can get more input. Asking numerous people can be a huge help when making an important decision. Not only are people getting different ideas of what they may want to do, they can also get advise from people who may be more experienced than themselves. For example, if someone was debating on which college they should apply to, they may end up asking people such as older siblings or parents for advise because they may have more experience with that matter. By asking multiple people, you can get multiple ideas, each of them being different in their own way. By getting more people's input, you may be able to start to make your own choice about the matter because of the advise you've gotten.

Another way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is by not getting any biased opinions. By asking more than one person for advise on a subject, they can get more than one new idea that isn't one of their own. This way, they can get more than one person's thoughts on the decision, and have different ideas on it. For example, if someone were trying to make a decision on what sport they may want to tryout for at school, they could possibly ask their friends and family about which they should choose. However, they should also ask people like classmates and teachers, as they may have their own ideas, and won't give the person any biased ideas or information. Friends and family can have a great deal of influence on people, so it's important to always get people's thoughts that are on the outside. This will make it to where there's a greater chance of the decision maker not being biased, as they've heard numerous people's thoughts, and can make their own decision off of that.

A final way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is by being more prepared about the choice they're going to make. The decision maker can use all the advise they've gotten from different people to make their own choice, and feel better prepared. They will be more focused as they know what they want to do, and will feel more confident and less overwhelmed. Feeling less overwhelmed can be a big help as the person doesn't have to be so worried, so they won't have any distractions from making the best possible decision. For example, if someone is trying to decide what kind of car they want to get, and they've gotten advise from numerous people, they can make a better choice when picking. They'll know exactly what they want, as they've heard many thoughts from the people around them, and so they can make their final decision.

After getting advise from multiple people around them, the decision maker may be able to make the best choice possible, as they've gotten new thoughts and ideas. Asking for help or for some advise from those around you can help you make the best possible choice because you've gotten a lot of new information and opinions that you wouldn't have gotten if you had only asked one or no one at all for advise. Making an important choice can seem a little bit easier and less stressful after seeking advise from multiple people. Getting help from others around you can help you make the best choice you can.

Life often places difficult choices in front of us, and it is easy to feel stuck when we try to decide alone. Talking to friends, family, or others who care about us can reduce that pressure. Since big moments happen again and again, listening to more than one person usually brings clearer views and helps us move toward a sound decision. Gathering different opinions often leads to better choices.

One reason for this is that several voices offer more information. When we ask more people, we collect a wider range of ideas, and we may also hear from those who have faced similar situations before. For instance, someone choosing which university to attend might speak with older relatives who have already gone through the process. These conversations bring fresh perspectives, making it easier to see options that might have stayed hidden.

Another benefit is that we lower the risk of one-sided thinking. If we only turn to a small circle, we may hear the same preferences repeated. By asking classmates, teachers, or others further from our daily lives, we receive less familiar points of view. For example, a student picking a school sport can learn more by speaking with peers and staff, not only with close family. This mix of input makes it harder for personal bias to take over and allows for a fairer judgment.

Finally, collecting different opinions helps us feel ready. When we bring together what we have heard, we understand the choice more fully and worry less about making mistakes. With clearer goals and greater confidence, we can focus on what truly matters. Someone deciding on a car, for example, can compare many suggestions and settle on one that fits real needs, rather than acting hurriedly or anxiously.

In the end, reaching out to others gives us ideas we might not find alone. Important decisions become less stressful when we let varied voices guide us. Support from people around us does not remove our responsibility, but it makes it easier to choose with care and move forward with trust in ourselves.

Students should be allowed to select their own elective courses instead of being placed into arts classes by default. When learners are forced into subjects they know little about, they are more likely to struggle and lose confidence, which is not a fair approach within any school system. Motivation matters greatly during the school day, and pupils need something they can look forward to in order to stay engaged. While exposure to music, drama, and visual arts remains valuable, it is only fair that young people have a voice in which of these areas they explore.

If students are able to pick a course that interests them, they usually arrive each day with greater energy and willingness to participate. Young people are capable of forming clear preferences and standing by them, and they can achieve success when they care about what they are learning. On the other hand, if counselors assign classes that students dislike, attendance and effort often drop. For this reason, schools should gently guide learners toward electives that match their interests rather than deciding for them.

In short, giving students this choice should raise overall satisfaction and spark fresh ideas that benefit the whole school community. When pupils make decisions that feel meaningful to them, they tend to develop a positive outlook and perform better academically. Such steps may also help them shape clearer plans for the future and build habits that support long-term growth.

In schools, music programs give students the chance to learn instruments and take part in lively activities. Marching bands fill football fields with movement and sound, performing routines that demand hours of practice. Orchestras blend tones so that melodies flow across rooms, moving from gentle classics to bold, energetic pieces. Playing an instrument opens up experiences that are consistently enjoyable, especially when musicians hear themselves create strong sounds, travel for special events, and discover many styles of music.

Instrumental classes explore a wide range of music, and each piece brings something valuable. When a song comes together cleanly, confidence grows, and the trust among classmates rises as well. It feels rewarding to handle music that others cannot yet play, and satisfying to share quality sound as a group. Auditions often decide which ensembles students join, and earning a spot brings real joy. Working toward personal goals shows that progress is possible, and the options available to musicians keep expanding.

Band and orchestra members also gain chances to travel. Because of the focus and effort these classes require, schools plan trips that other groups seldom take. Friendships develop easily in this setting, and schools respond to student enthusiasm by offering more outings. These trips are treated as recognition of hard work, with visits to places that include theme parks, water slides, and carnival attractions. Such locations give everyone a break and a shared sense of fun.

Technology now allows learners and instructors to connect for lessons over the internet. Students weighing the pros and cons of online study often face this choice while balancing classes with jobs or family duties. Because their time is limited, they need to know the drawbacks and benefits before deciding. I support online learning because it offers flexibility, a wide selection of subjects, easier contact with teachers, and faster course options.

First, flexibility is a major strength of studying online. Learners can usually engage with materials at any hour that suits them, provided deadlines are met. Assignments such as essays or research tasks still require effort, yet students decide when to work rather than follow a fixed timetable. This arrangement helps people with jobs, especially those who work afternoons or evenings, because they can study without clashing with their shifts. Such freedom often makes completing a program possible when face-to-face classes would be impractical.

Another benefit is the variety of courses available through distance learning. Many institutions now provide programs on different topics, and a simple search makes them easy to find. Some worry that learning remotely limits contact with teachers, but in practice, online setups often improve access. Shy learners, for instance, can ask questions and receive answers quickly, which helps them stay on track. This level of support can strengthen understanding and confidence.

Finally, online study suits undergraduates and graduates who value convenience and speed. People can plan writing or research tasks around personal routines, which helps when they also work or care for family. In addition, accelerated options let motivated learners finish material faster than in traditional settings, where the pace may slow to accommodate others. This advantage helps students progress without unnecessary delays.

In summary, online learning allows people to manage their studies at their own speed as long as they meet requirements and participate responsibly. It does demand self-discipline and strong time management, since learners spend more time working alone. Beyond subject knowledge, this approach encourages motivation and focus, qualities that benefit careers and personal growth. It also helps teachers and students develop broader perspectives and make thoughtful choices in their educational paths.

Primarily, technology’s objective is to render specific tasks simpler, not to render us unsociable or overweight. Everyone employs social applications on their devices, and this represents a major difficulty because it ranks among the primary causes of people favoring social media over face-to-face dialogue.

Ultimately, these remarkable innovations, these resplendent creations, have captured our attention and distanced us from one another. When attempts are made to alter a being’s intrinsic character, resistance follows, for it has evolved across millennia to its present condition, and now we endeavor to reshape it. What I emphasize is that technology serves as a valuable component of our lives, though it does not enhance our social fabric.

Technology stands among the finest achievements of the twenty-first century, admired by most people. Yet its beauty is worth questioning. When I was younger, adults often warned that technology would damage our social lives. I did not take this seriously then, but now I understand their concern.

The main purpose of technological progress is to simplify tasks, not to turn us into isolated or unhealthy individuals. In my view, technology holds strong potential that we are not fully using. It should make routine jobs smoother, yet we often misuse it by choosing fast food deliveries instead of preparing meals ourselves, which harms our health. Another serious issue is the tendency to build lives around devices. When people lose access to their gadgets, they feel lost. Social applications dominate daily routines and are a key reason why face-to-face conversation is being replaced by screens.

At the same time, technology brings clear advantages alongside its drawbacks. One major benefit is saving time in everyday activities. In the past, people relied on letters that took days to arrive, while today messages reach their destination in minutes. Technology also supports cleaner living through electric cars, homes and planes that avoid fossil fuels. Renewable sources such as solar panels, wind turbines and hydroelectric systems can supply endless energy unless a major disaster occurs. As long as natural conditions remain stable, we can enjoy efficient and low-waste power.

Overall, I see technology as a valuable human achievement despite its harmful side effects. These problems can be reduced if we stop centering our lives around it and treat it as a tool rather than a necessity. From powering a single light bulb in the past, technology now runs vehicles, cities and almost everything we build.

Yet these impressive advances have captured our attention and separated us from one another. Technology is both useful and damaging to social life. Humans are naturally social beings, and anything that blocks this part of our nature leads to trouble. Trying to reshape a nature that has evolved over thousands of years often causes resistance. In short, technology improves many aspects of life, but it does not enhance the social dimension that keeps us human.

Many of us have heard the idea that the greater risk is not in reaching too high and missing, but in aiming too low and hitting the target. Although some may disagree, choosing higher goals tends to be better. This is because lifting our targets enables us to reach larger achievements, encourages more original thinking than rigid or limited plans allow, and opens up meaningful possibilities in many directions.

To begin with, aiming high creates wider possibilities. People often decide what to try before they act. For instance, which choice is likely to offer more job options: applying only for simple tasks because they feel safe, or trying several fields that match one’s skills? The same idea applies to education. A student who is unsure about the future may join the military or attend college. College can expand career chances and lead to a better job than a narrower path would offer.

Moreover, higher goals help people discover their genuine and creative ideas rather than sticking to fixed habits. Those who set low aims often hide or ignore their own thoughts, since they avoid difficult tasks. By contrast, aiming higher pushes people to tackle tougher challenges and consider more options. This process helps the mind grow and supports fresh ways of thinking. Major artists likely would not have produced important works if they had limited themselves. Their notable ideas and creations grew from refusing to place ceilings on their efforts.

In addition, raising our aims increases the chance of reaching larger outcomes. Choosing only the minimum effort for a task rarely leads to the best result, while striving for the maximum usually does. With a low aim, people may stop too soon, even when the task matters. A higher aim encourages persistence until the work is finished. Therefore, trying for more than the easiest option tends to bring better results.

Some may argue that very high aims bring suffering. This can be true, but the solution is not to aim too low; it is to find balance. Just as people are told to eat balanced meals, they should judge their own abilities and choose targets that stretch them without breaking them. Others may say that lower aims reduce effort and stress. While stress may decrease, not all stress is harmful, and some can be useful. I once avoided school and chose to stay home to escape pressure, but this did not make me feel better. Returning to study, despite the stress, helped me improve. Stress can harm, yet it can also push people forward.

In the end, avoiding challenges and choosing the simple path is rarely the best choice. Aiming low may feel safe, but the real danger is forgetting to imagine greater possibilities and losing belief in what we can achieve. The goal is to decide in a way we will not regret, using the short time we have as well as we can. No one needs to be perfect, but everyone should try their best so that, in the end, there is little left to wish for.

People form first views in different ways, and these early reactions often shift once more details become known. Because everyone brings their own habits and feelings to a situation, an immediate impression may adjust after a short time, whether hours or days. These first responses matter since they mark the opening moment of contact, yet they do not have to remain fixed.

A class, for example, may feel dull on the first day, leading to a poor opinion, but by the next lesson it might turn enjoyable, and the view changes. Attitude plays a large role here, as a negative mood can produce harsh early judgments. Unkind first reactions can also reveal something about the person who holds them. In some cases, impressions stay the same because many individuals prefer to keep their original opinion.

At the same time, a positive view can fade if someone later behaves badly. When work seems simple and pleasant at first, and friendships appear likely, a change can occur quickly if a supervisor shows an unfriendly manner; the overall opinion of the job may then turn less favorable. This early moment is important because it guides how we approach people or places, and a good start can help build strong connections.

In the end, first impressions may shift depending on the person and their attitude, but they do not always change, since some people hold to their initial judgment. If impressions never altered, life would be more difficult, because deciding that someone is not worth knowing without learning more about their life would close off many chances.

I support individuality and believe people should choose what they want in their own lives. Many of my friends follow others and copy what the crowd does, but I prefer to listen to myself and act on what feels right, even when I am not sure where it will lead.

At home, my family can be negative and sometimes refuse to let me speak, even when I want to share my thoughts. That is another reason I value individuality: I want to be heard and to make my own decisions. I have met too many people who depend on others, and I do not think that is healthy.

In history class we learned that in the past, people had less freedom to be themselves. It seems to me that many people want attention, so they follow others instead of choosing their own way. Life now feels different because people care too much about what others say about their looks or their actions.

I like who I am. I try to be kind and stay true to myself, and I do what I want because I value people and do not worry about their opinions.

I arrived from Puerto Rico two years ago, and since then my life has changed completely. I have learned to appreciate everything I get, because I now understand the value and sacrifice behind even small things. I still want to improve and grow, even when it is not easy. The language and customs here are very different from what I knew.

I keep going because I believe in myself and finish what I set out to do. Meeting people from other places has been hard at times; some are kind, and others are not. I enjoy learning new things and seeing new places, but it bothers me that many treat us like outsiders just because Spanish is our first language, even though Puerto Ricans are part of the United States.

School has been one of my biggest challenges. It is difficult to enter a classroom and feel completely alone just because I cannot ask questions or talk with others like they can. A few months after I arrived, I started skipping school and making bad choices because I had no support there or at home.

Today I feel out of place, but I stay for my mother. I want her to have a better life and receive what she deserves, because she always tried to give us the best, no matter how hard life was in Puerto Rico.

Thomas Jefferson asked whether we achieve more by constantly acting or whether stillness also has value. Not everyone accepts this view, and people generally take one of two positions. Some prefer comfort and avoid effort, while others push themselves to create new chances. I agree with the statement because it highlights three useful approaches: striving, using time wisely, and staying connected.

Nevertheless, some disagree. They feel unable to create new options because of their circumstances. For example, many face difficult lives and lack money, which seems to limit their choices. Yet we must accept that nothing worthwhile comes easily. My grandfather once told me how his family lived with very little; his five children often ate only once a day. Despite this, he kept saying that things would change. He never stopped believing, and eventually he found new ways to improve life for them. This reminds me daily that if I want something, I must struggle for it.

In addition, we can reach impressive goals when we make good use of time. People can achieve dreams faster than they expect, obtaining things that once seemed impossible, such as a fine car or a spacious home. These become possible through steady effort. Furthermore, success allows us to change the lives of others because we gain the means to help them. Those who refuse to give up usually manage to accomplish a great deal.

Lastly, staying connected matters greatly. It means refusing to remain in one place and instead seeking new paths. When I thought about how to reach my dreams quickly, I realized that looking for alternatives leads to results. This reflection shows that progress requires movement; starting from nothing will bring nothing.

Overall, the message is that opportunities grow when we move forward rather than stand still. Those who avoid effort rarely discover what they could achieve, which is unfortunate. By working hard, exploring possibilities without wasting time, and keeping in touch with others, life becomes simpler and more rewarding. In this way, even large goals can be met, and the effort turns into lasting satisfaction.

Some people argue that learners should bring phones to class so they can search for information and finish tasks quickly. However, phones should stay out of the classroom because they often disturb lessons and lead students to chat instead of paying attention.

To begin with, phones can create problems during class. When a teacher is explaining something, a student might listen to music, which distracts classmates and stops them from working. Watching videos or playing games also interrupts learning. If a teacher does not allow music but a student insists on using headphones, this can cause arguments. When someone keeps using a phone in lessons, it happens again and again, and the school may eventually ask that student to leave.

Second, learners may focus on chatting while the teacher is speaking. In this situation, they ignore what is being taught and lose the chance to study properly. Instead of following the lesson, they spend time sending messages and sharing jokes or unsuitable pictures with friends. This behavior gives a poor impression and can make classmates feel uncomfortable or disrespected. As a result, some students lose confidence and start avoiding school because they feel embarrassed or afraid.

Third, phones make cheating easier during exams. If a test is being taken, a student with a phone can look for answers and get better marks unfairly. This shows a lack of trust in their own abilities and encourages them to study less, depending on dishonest methods that harm their real progress.

Fourth, frequent phone use reduces participation in class activities. When learners keep looking at their screens, they waste valuable time and miss opportunities to answer questions or join discussions. Staring at devices for long periods is also bad for health, as it affects eyesight and mental focus. Spending too much time on movies or music limits the ability to pay attention to people and tasks around them.

In short, students should not use phones in class because they cause disruption and lead learners to chat instead of concentrating on their lessons.

Some schools provide distance learning so that students can join lessons from home through online platforms or video calls, while others avoid this option because they see it as a weak way to study. I agree with the second view for several reasons.

First, studying from home limits the help students can receive when they face difficulties. In a classroom, teachers and classmates can respond quickly, but at home a learner may struggle alone and lose valuable time. Second, proper learning usually requires the structure that schools provide. Schools give clear routines, reliable materials, and guidance that help students build what they actually need to know. Finally, even though home study is possible, attending lessons in person remains the most effective path. Direct contact with teachers and a set schedule make it easier to stay on track and understand topics deeply.

Some schools still offer distance learning because it fits certain students. For instance, people who move to a new country may need to work while they study, or parents who care for young children may find it hard to attend in person. In these cases, online classes can open a door to progress and allow motivated learners to reach their aims. However, for many students this setup brings more problems than benefits.

At home, distractions are common. Electronic devices, family members, and daily chores can interrupt focus and reduce the quality of study. Moreover, video calls cannot replace real interaction. When questions arise, a screen cannot answer the way a teacher can, and doubts may remain unresolved. For this reason, going to school and working steadily each day still offers the clearest route to strong learning.

Our future depends on the effort we put in now, and choosing a reliable way to study helps us avoid later regret. Experienced people often remind students that persistence matters. With determination, it is possible to succeed, but choosing the right setting for learning makes that journey far more certain.

I do not support the idea of my school moving to a four-day week by adding two extra hours to each school day. Although this schedule may help organisations save energy, it would create serious problems for students. Longer days would increase stress, reduce the time available for homework, and make daily life harder for those with responsibilities outside school.

First, extending the school day would disadvantage students who need to work or care for family members after class. For example, I have a job that starts at four o’clock, and if school finished two hours later I would have to give it up. This change would affect many others in the same situation, making it difficult for students to balance school with work or other duties.

Second, two additional hours would make lessons much longer and more tiring. As the day wears on, students would struggle to concentrate and absorb what teachers are explaining. When classes end late, there is little energy or time left for homework. Staying up too late to complete assignments would lead to fatigue the next day, and over time this could harm students’ results.

Some people argue that attendance would also suffer because students would skip school more often if they felt worn out. Since regular attendance plays a key role in keeping up with lessons and passing the year, this is another strong reason to avoid the change.

In conclusion, even though the school week would be shorter, the longer days would not be easy for students to manage. Tiredness, missed work and weaker class focus would create problems that outweigh any possible benefits. For these reasons, I believe my school should not adopt this model.

The first time when i met him was in my math class; he did not even want to talk to me or be my partner, and when i asked him about problems that i did not understand he ignored me and did not answer. To conclude, if i would have to take a position on this issue i would disagree; the reason why i would disagree is that in my circle of friends there are two of them who did not give me a good impression, and if you look at us today we are good friends, which is why you do not have to say that the first impression is literally impossible to change.

I do not agree with the idea that first impressions cannot be altered, since individuals are capable of change. In my view, people often say this because the person they meet or speak with does not seem interested in them at that moment.

A first meeting does not always reveal the best side of someone, yet this does not mean it is fixed. We should not label or judge others only by how they appear initially, because people can adjust and behave differently over time. One reason not to treat first impressions as unchangeable is that external conditions can affect them. If someone is having a difficult day, they may feel uneasy and struggle to communicate, which can create a misleading impression.

For example, I can mention my closest friend. The first time we were in math class, he refused to work with me and ignored my questions. He made it clear he did not want to talk or cooperate.

In conclusion, I would argue that first impressions are not impossible to reshape. Among my friends, two people left me with a poor initial feeling, yet today we share a strong friendship. This shows that early judgments can be wrong and that people can grow beyond them.

Failure shapes the path to success in powerful ways. When people make mistakes, they learn what not to do next time and slowly improve. Imagine a person aiming to be a professional soccer player. Clubs notice him, he earns awards, and he is never told to leave a team. Then one day his coach mentions a tryout the following week and asks him to prepare. A strict plan is given for diet and training that must be followed each day. There are moments when unhealthy choices feel easier, yet he pushes through and stays focused. On the day of the tryout he feels fully ready. Warm-ups go well and the drills look sharp. During practice he stands out as one of the strongest players. When the day ends, the coaches gather everyone and read the names of those accepted. His name is not on the list, and the failure hits hard.

What happens next depends on attitude. He can walk away and choose another direction, or he can lift his head and try again. Failure shows how patient someone is and whether they are ready to keep risking disappointment in order to reach their aim. The book The Pursuit of Happyness offers a clear example. The main character creates a device and hopes to sell it, but buyers keep refusing. He is a father with a young child, living in a small rented room, and he soon loses his home because he cannot pay. For weeks he has no place to stay, yet he continues to carry his machine and look for chances. Rejection does not stop him. Eventually someone agrees to buy the device and is impressed enough to tell others. More people follow, and his life begins to change. By refusing to quit, he turns struggle into progress. Difficult moments, therefore, are often the key to lasting achievement.

I once tried to write something that could help people who are bullied, and it shows how quickly people’s attitudes can change once they really know us. I did many things to fit in with others, yet not everyone is kind. There are still people who choose to bully or mistreat others simply because they never bother to meet them; they judge without knowing anything. This is why I often feel alone, since too many individuals speak badly about others. I dislike how people gossip, and it worries me that those who are threatened by bullying often stay silent, afraid to speak up because they think it will only make things worse.

I try not to let words bother me, since people can say what they want and it is their issue. However, when someone is upset or hurt, they sometimes come looking for help when they are already in trouble. When I feel angry or sad, I usually play soccer, because it helps me push my problems out of my mind. If I could do something useful, I would create chances for everyone who wants to play soccer to join, so they can forget their worries too. This is why sports exist, to let people enjoy themselves without fighting. Another option could be going with friends to watch movies, soccer, basketball, or volleyball. There are many ways to understand others. In my view, most problems can be solved, but we often forget to show respect. If we offered it more often, everything would feel very different.

What we want is to feel safe in places free from gangs, since they only push people into deeper hardship. We should involve families in stopping those who harm others. Many people study hard to improve their lives and help their families leave bad situations behind. With more education, it becomes easier to earn money honestly, and even finishing high school can lead to a job that at least provides stability.

People can feel safer if they protect what they own, and if someone tries to take it, they can go to the police and explain what happened so they may recover their losses. We should not look frightened, because fear can encourage others to act against us. We are clever, but we must use that wisdom in every part of life, since being smart in one area does not mean people will treat us kindly if we provoke them.

Everyone can be pleasant, but anger changes people and can make them frightening. To avoid trouble, it helps to invite others to play sports, spend time with friends, or enjoy places like the beach so anger cools down and friendships can grow. At the same time, we should never reveal our weakest spots, because in a disagreement our friends might already know how to hurt us most. This is why I believe no one should show their greatest weakness, and it is the reason behind what I tried to write.

I have a personal ability that lets me show ideas visually: drawing. I first used it simply for enjoyment, especially when I needed to shift my thoughts somewhere else, and I improved it by joining art classes.

Waldo Emerson praised standing alone, yet I do not agree with him because life often requires us to rely on others. Being independent is not only about acting alone; it is also about organizing our time and choosing when to join with people. In this essay I will discuss how cooperation helps us in three areas: work, society, and decision-making. These points may show that individuality alone does not let us become everything we wish.

In jobs, there are many moments when we must set personal preferences aside. Sometimes we do not like a colleague because of the way he or she acts, but it is useful to try working together. If we break the barrier between ourselves and that person, progress becomes easier, and we may need his or her help later on. Another problem is doing work that does not match our dreams. This does not mean that we should give up on our goals; instead, it reminds us that staying in a job we dislike is a common part of life while we look for change. Most companies reach their goals by acting as teams, and joining with others at work often brings better results than acting alone.

Some people prefer to be alone for long periods and seem asocial because they feel at ease that way. Others avoid others because they like doing things by themselves and being the center of attention; they can be called individualists. Still, they are not all the same, and their habits can come from past experiences. Living with society can be harder than it appears, especially around such people. However, many of them do change when they ask for help or when someone close supports them, showing that contact with others can lead to growth.

We all make choices, yet some of these choices push us in wrong directions or change who we are. Wanting to be different is not enough; it takes a firm decision. We can let the world guide us, or we can decide what we truly want to do. Many people accept a life managed by others because it seems safer or simpler. A president may prefer to act alone, yet he knows he needs to work with members of congress because one person cannot do everything. We can act in the same way by deciding to cooperate or not, and by setting our own goals instead of letting pressure shape us.

In conclusion, we all have the freedom to choose our path. As I have explained through work, society, and choices, cooperation often helps us solve conflicts and move forward. These ideas show that Emerson is mistaken when he suggests that we should always let the world push us. Instead, we can change and become what we aim to be by balancing independence with working together.

John Lubbock, a British naturalist and politician, once stated that character is what we decide to create for ourselves. This idea carries weight, yet it also meets reality, where earlier experiences help form who we turn out to be. If we accept that we guide our character, then we also accept that our daily choices matter most. Even so, hardship does not have to repeat itself. For instance, growing up with abusive parents does not force us to treat others the same way; instead, it can strengthen us and add depth to our character.

We play a role in shaping how people see us, though others may confuse character with personality. When someone is called unkind or selfish, this may reflect a passing mood rather than a fixed trait. Ultimately, each person builds their own character and lives with the results. Accepting ourselves matters more than seeking approval, because in the end we travel through life with only ourselves. True understanding comes when others look beyond first impressions and learn where we have been. A strong character can lift us and leave a lasting mark, leading people to wonder how we became so resilient or self-reliant.

We cannot simply claim to know our character after a single action. Imagine losing a family member to illness and spending days in sadness and denial. Over time, we can still choose to honor what they taught us by standing firm and making each moment count. There will be setbacks and tears, yet continuing to move forward quietly builds strength we may not notice at first. In every life there are moments of doubt, when quitting feels easier than trying. Once we see what we can actually achieve, fear shrinks. Our minds may whisper that we are not capable, but we do not have to listen. Character thrives when it pushes past these barriers, and only we can remove them.

Because of this, we should follow what feels right and let our values guide us. Life should not be shaped by what others call impossible. By choosing to stand apart, we let our character stand out as well. Life is not a list of perfect options; it is a path we shape with decisions that feel true to us. The idea that character is what we choose to make fits this view. Treat life as an opportunity, and let every step you take reinforce the person you wish to be.

Few people look forward to staying at school longer when they could be enjoying their free time. Joining an after-school homework club can spoil plans for activities that matter, and it often creates more stress than it solves. Students should avoid these clubs because they reduce time with family, interfere with sports, and limit opportunities to enjoy hobbies.

To begin with, staying for extra lessons can damage family routines. When a club runs late, simple plans such as eating out become hard to keep. Imagine someone who is ready to leave school, only to learn that a parent had arranged a meal at a favorite restaurant. Missing events like this shows how homework sessions can quietly steal valuable moments that families rarely get back.

In addition, sports commitments become harder to manage. A student who trains regularly may arrive late to practice or feel too tired to perform well. For example, someone who plays basketball might have to choose between staying for extra help and getting to the court on time. Coaches usually do not accept excuses, and repeated lateness can lead to warnings or even removal from the team. As a result, something meant to improve schoolwork can instead harm activities that build discipline and future goals.

Finally, hobbies and personal interests also suffer. Free time during the week is often the only chance to enjoy pastimes such as gaming, streaming, or practicing creative skills. When students leave school late, they return home exhausted and face a rush of unfinished tasks, leaving little energy for fun. Over time, this can affect progress in these activities and weaken the support of people who follow their work.

In the end, after-school homework clubs add extra hours to the school day without solving the real problem. Balancing study with family, sport, and hobbies is difficult when time is limited. Students should complete schoolwork when it best suits them and keep their afternoons free for the people and activities that matter most.

A positive mindset is one of the surest paths to doing well in life. People usually show either a helpful or a harmful way of thinking, and the difference can change many outcomes. When you treat others calmly and with respect, even during disagreements, solutions become easier to find. For example, if you and your supervisor disagree about pay, speaking calmly can lead to compromise, while reacting harshly might cost you your job. A positive outlook also helps during difficult or uninteresting moments. On a rough family trip, choosing to stay cheerful can lift everyone’s mood and turn the day around.

Several situations make it easier to keep a positive mindset, such as sleeping well, enjoying sunny weather, receiving a gift, eating a favorite meal, or spending time with friends and family. Pleasant experiences like traveling or sharing good food often bring out the best in how we act and feel.

On the other hand, a negative mindset can push people toward poor choices. Those who are often irritable or upset are hard to get along with and may struggle to build strong friendships. For instance, arriving at school stressed and reacting badly to a teacher’s comment can lead to arguments and discipline. If someone meets anger with anger, conflicts may grow and create bigger problems.

Negative moods often appear when people are tired, overwhelmed with tasks, stuck indoors because of bad weather, treated poorly by others, upset with someone, or disappointed by an unexpected situation such as bad food or missed plans.

In the end, a positive attitude supports us at work, in school, and during family gatherings. The next time you feel upset or face a difficult day, choosing a constructive outlook is often the most effective way forward.

Dear Principal, changing the cafeteria menu to healthier choices is a positive step. Introducing fresh, nutritious options that many students have not tried before can improve daily meals. As a student, I support this idea because it would give everyone access to better food during the school day.

A new menu could lift students’ spirits, especially those who grow tired of eating the same meals each week. At the same time, some classmates enjoy familiar dishes and may feel uneasy about sudden changes. In this case, it would be wise to speak with the cafeteria manager and review which meals are most popular. Together, you could decide to keep the favorites while replacing the least chosen items with healthier alternatives. This balanced plan allows students to keep meals they like and still try something new.

Students may feel happier when their preferred foods remain available and fresh choices are added. Offering a different menu could also set our school apart and encourage other schools to follow. Many students in different districts face the same problem with unappealing cafeteria food. If schools in other states notice our approach, the change could help more than just our class. Healthier meals might also reduce the amount of money parents spend when students refuse to eat at school and ask for outside food instead. Some families cannot afford these extra costs. Additionally, students would be less likely to skip class to buy meals elsewhere, which improves safety and spares parents the worry of not knowing where their children are.

Trying new foods is something many students enjoy, myself included. The cafeteria currently serves items that are not always healthy or appealing, so a shift is needed. Some students also have allergies and avoid cafeteria meals, which leaves them hungry or unwell during the day. Adding healthier, varied options would allow everyone to eat safely at school instead of risking trips outside the building. This change would help students stay focused in class and prevent problems for parents and the school’s reputation.

In conclusion, asking the cafeteria manager for a list of favorite and least-liked foods would help create a menu that most students accept. Keeping popular dishes while replacing unpopular ones allows both comfort and progress. Healthier meals can improve students’ well-being, help families save money, and reduce the dangers of skipping class. This plan has clear benefits, and even those who doubt it at first are likely to adjust. Other schools may follow our example, creating better habits beyond our own building. I offer this opinion in the hope that you will consider what is best for all students. Thank you.

I do not support the idea of school districts offering programs that let students finish high school in three years instead of four. Compressing the same learning into a shorter period leaves too little time to study thoroughly, and the workload becomes very heavy. Students would likely have to attend classes during evenings and summers, which can lead to exhaustion. Without regular breaks, their ability to concentrate may decline, and they could miss important elective courses that help develop skills and interests. Forcing learners into such a schedule may create stress rather than real progress.

Although completing school earlier might seem useful because it allows students to move on faster, this advantage is often misleading. The pressure to study intensively can reduce the quality of learning and leave students less prepared, not better prepared, for what comes next. Working hard during holidays and after normal hours does not always lead to stronger results, especially if rest and personal development are ignored.

I believe it is better to allow four years to finish high school. This longer period gives students more time to grow, explore different subjects, and decide which path suits them best. With a steadier pace, they can focus more deeply, learn with less pressure, and still have time for personal activities. Having this extra time helps them build stronger foundations before entering university or the workforce.

In the end, four years in high school can offer more lasting benefits than three. It allows students to gain broader knowledge, think carefully about their future careers, and prepare in ways that are difficult when time is rushed. A calmer and more complete approach to learning is likely to support their success and well-being in the long run.

In my opinion, students taking classes from home by online or video conferencing do not benefit from attending classes remotely.

First, students face more distractions at home, such as video games and other options; many work while taking classes, so as more students enroll in distance learning, schools need to consider other alternatives. Learning in school allows students to focus more specifically, since having a teacher present helps them learn more effectively when classes are conducted in person.

Second, I think distance learning, which permits attending classes from home, is not a good option. For example, in my house I have three brothers and one sister, and I find that learning at home creates distractions.

In conclusion, distance learning is not a good idea because it is more effective to take video conferences online in the morning than in the evening, when students have more energy; yet I do not think this is a good option, as students do not gain significant benefits from attending classes from home. Therefore, students learn more when they go to school. Parents think the same way, because taking classes in school is more effective than learning at a distance.

I believe that studying through online or video calls from home does not help students as much as attending school in person. In my view, learning at home brings more problems than advantages, and it cannot replace what happens in a real classroom.

First, there are many distractions at home, such as games, phones, and other people. When students try to study while sharing space with family or entertainment, their attention breaks easily. In school, a teacher is present and can guide them step by step, which helps students stay focused and understand better. Face-to-face lessons also allow students to ask questions immediately and take part in activities that are hard to organize online.

Second, home environments are often too noisy for studying. For example, in my house there are three brothers and a sister, so it is difficult to find a quiet place to concentrate. When several people move around, talk, or use devices, it becomes almost impossible to follow a lesson with the seriousness it requires.

Finally, learning through screens is less effective for memory and effort. Many students feel more energetic in the morning, but online classes may be scheduled at inconvenient times, forcing them to study when they are tired. Watching videos and listening to explanations from a distance does not help students remember as well as real interaction and practice do.

In conclusion, students learn more when they go to school rather than studying from home. Parents would likely agree that attending classes in person is a stronger and more reliable way to gain knowledge than distance learning.

I agree with the idea that success means moving from one setback to another while keeping our excitement alive. No one achieves perfect results all the time, and learning how to continue after disappointment is often what brings progress.  

Last year, I took an English exam hoping for an A or at least a B. I studied hard and felt ready, but the result was a fail. At first, I felt upset, yet my teacher offered me another chance. I used that opportunity and earned an A–, which made me realize that falling short does not have to stop us. What matters is staying determined and trying again with the same energy.  

Another example involves my aunt, who wanted to travel to El Salvador to visit family. When she first checked ticket prices, they were too high, so she waited. Months later, prices rose even more, but she still chose to buy. While completing the purchase, she learned her ID had expired, so she had to pause and renew it. After waiting several more months, the new ID still had not arrived. Despite feeling disappointed, she refused to give up on the trip and kept her excitement alive.  

Some people argue that this view of success is not realistic because repeated failure can feel discouraging. They may label those who lose early as weak or incapable. In my view, such reactions often come from losing motivation rather than from failure itself. Without enthusiasm, it becomes easier to stop trying.  

In conclusion, being successful does not mean avoiding mistakes. My exam experience and my aunt’s situation show that setbacks can teach strength and patience. As long as we hold on to our drive, failure becomes a step forward rather than an ending.

In some countries, young people are expected to choose a path before starting high school. While some learners prefer to decide early, others would rather not think about jobs while they are still in school.

On one hand, deciding early can help because youth is a time when many choices begin to take shape. Young people who consider their future early often feel more prepared to move forward and may wish to repay their parents’ support later on. As parents grow older, having a clear goal can allow students to plan steps that lead to steady progress and greater security for their families.

On the other hand, many people aim to improve their lives and offer better conditions to those they care for. This is why understanding which field suits them matters, since different jobs open different doors. Some learners are drawn to challenging areas such as technology, teaching, technical work, or public service, yet each option can lead to growth when it matches personal strengths and interests.

However, not every student is ready to make such choices while studying. Some feel too young and believe that school should be a time for building friendships and relationships rather than settling on a profession. When direction is missing, risks such as poor decisions, substance use, or conflicts can increase. In my view, thinking ahead about a career during school years is valuable because it encourages responsibility and can guide young people toward meaningful goals that benefit not only themselves but also their relatives.

In conclusion, I support the idea of choosing a path before finishing basic education. Early reflection makes it easier to discover genuine interests and build useful skills, so that by the time studies end, learners already have a clear sense of direction and a stronger chance of creating a stable and rewarding life.

There is frequent discussion today about whether schools should lengthen the school day to save energy and resources, especially as some workplaces move to a four-day week with ten-hour days. Some argue that adding two hours to each school day achieves the same goal, while others believe it simply increases costs for electricity, lighting, computers, smart boards, and other equipment. Water usage is another concern, since students sometimes forget to turn off taps. Despite these worries, I believe schools should adopt the longer day because it can promote better care for energy and resources, and it gives students and teachers more time to contribute to a healthier planet.

One reason to support a longer school day is that it can lead to greater energy savings in the long run. Schools can teach students how to use electricity wisely, both in classrooms and at home, and show them simple ways to lower consumption and reduce bills. When young people understand which habits make the biggest difference, they are more likely to carry them into daily life.

Another benefit is that extra time can help save important resources such as water, paper, and plastic. Because many students use restrooms several times a day, clear reminders can encourage them to avoid waste. Schools could display posters or run small campaigns that explain why saving water matters, and they might also reduce unnecessary printing and packaging. The money saved could then be used to improve school facilities while helping students develop more careful habits.

Finally, a longer day provides more opportunities for meaningful projects. Teachers and students could create campaigns that explain how everyday choices affect the climate, or design online pages that share tips with families and the wider community. These activities turn learning into action and help spread responsible behavior beyond school walls.

As shown, adding two hours to the school day can strengthen awareness about energy and resource use while giving everyone more time to make a positive impact. When people understand the need for change, they can help create a better future.

Studying from home is a good idea because it helps students save time and manage their lives more smoothly. People with jobs often have schedules they cannot change, and trying to attend traditional classes after work can reduce their ability to focus. Learning online allows them to rest, eat, and prepare so they can pay better attention during lessons. It also creates space for other activities, such as sports or meeting friends, which can improve overall balance.

Health and travel issues are another reason to support online study. When a student is seriously ill, going to school can spread sickness to others, and it is not easy for everyone. Some students do not own cars or cannot afford parking, and bad weather can make driving risky. Studying from home removes these obstacles and lets learners continue their education without added physical or financial stress.

Family responsibilities also benefit from online classes. Some students care for children or have disabilities that make travel difficult. Parents can more easily look after their children while still joining lessons, and those with health problems can rest when needed without falling behind. This flexibility reduces worry about missing important material and helps students stay on track even when life is demanding.

In the end, technology makes daily life simpler and more efficient by saving time and offering reliable ways to complete tasks. When students are busy with work, health, or family needs, online classes can provide an option that fits their real circumstances and helps them move forward with less pressure.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said that staying true to yourself in a world that keeps pushing you to become someone else is the greatest achievement. Even though some people question this idea, I support it because society often pressures individuals to shift their views, values, and cultural identity. To remain genuine, a person must refuse to surrender, learn to value themselves, and honor where they come from.

First, the world constantly invites change, yet we should not abandon who we are. It matters to stay faithful to your own nature even when others do not approve, since comfort with yourself is more important than pleasing everyone else. When you refuse to bend just to fit in, you protect the core of your identity.

Second, loving and respecting yourself plays a key role. Being proud of who you are does not mean ignoring mistakes; it means accepting them as part of growth. Errors may be hard to face, but they should not force you to become someone different. Instead, they teach you to improve. The qualities, character, and personality you carry make you distinct, and they deserve appreciation rather than doubt.

Third, remembering your roots is essential, especially for those living far from their homeland. It is easy to feel pressed to act like someone else in order to belong, but giving in only weakens your sense of self. Holding on to your background allows you to prove that you can succeed without erasing what made you who you are.

In the end, do not wait for permission to be yourself. Keep standing firm for what fits you, care for and respect yourself, and carry your origins with pride. These choices shape your uniqueness and turn the struggle to remain authentic into your finest achievement.

We enter the world crying, pushed by instinct and sometimes by a doctor’s tap until our lungs announce our arrival. From that moment we begin to shape sounds that are ours alone, just as our fingerprints form patterns unlike anyone else’s, even for twins who look almost the same. Slowly we build a sense of self. Early on, our minds learn to signal hunger, discomfort or the need for comfort, and we discover how to make sense of what our bodies require.

As toddlers we watch others to understand how to stand, speak and manage simple tasks like holding a bottle or a spoon. We do not invent these skills alone; we collect them from the people and spaces around us. Later, between childhood and early adolescence, we long to belong and notice the many roles society offers: artists, athletes, scientists, caregivers and more. This exposure pulls us toward certain ambitions and shapes how we see ourselves.

When the teenage years arrive, a personal voice begins to emerge. We make choices without someone guiding each step, even if parents stand nearby with warnings drawn from their own stumbles. Mistakes feel heavy, yet they teach us what we can endure and what we should avoid. Adulthood then removes the safety net of home life and asks us to build our identity in earnest. Work, relationships and daily duties reveal whether we are careful or careless, patient or quick to snap, open to others or closed off.

I believe we are born to learn within a rough and uneven world, and our attitude grows from what we survive, not from what we are handed. Some face deep hardship yet keep hope, while others with every comfort feel defeated. Labels do not arrive with our first breath. Character rises instead from our mindset: if we accept weakness, negativity follows; if we choose strength and purpose, our actions earn respect. In the end, we are not assigned a role by fate or power; we build who we become through the choices we make each day.

One voice alone cannot solve big issues, but when many people talk and weigh options, more ideas and facts come forward. Instead of teaching children to follow, we should show them how to lead, because building these skills early creates lasting change. Leaders keep learning, starting small and gathering knowledge over time, yet even then they continue to ask questions and seek more information.

We can connect these habits and resources to family, work, and daily life. Self-reliance is not just for students. When we combine independence with the willingness to seek advice and learn, we improve our jobs and lifestyles. At the same time, we teach others, making these abilities stronger and more useful. Self-reliance can be compared to leadership: standing up for what we believe is right for ourselves and our future. We prefer to be correct, but by listening to other people’s views and asking questions, we open up new choices for ourselves and for those around us. We do not have to look far to see why this matters. Military affairs and global decisions affect us all, and many problems that people ignore actually need to be solved.

The military is both a job and a lifelong path that depends on personal choices. The men and women who serve the country face difficult calls. Before taking action, they must prepare their minds and skills, which is where self-reliance becomes important. A commander can give orders, yet lives depend on each person’s ability to decide wisely. This is why training at base and boot camp focuses on judgment and readiness, helping prevent mistakes. During that time, asking questions and collecting information is vital because it improves how people work and what they can achieve. These skills matter not only in the military but also in everyday life when big choices involve children or careers.

No matter a person’s age, race, or background, seeking this kind of growth is valuable now and later. These abilities can carry us far, and one day we may pass them to our own children when teaching them about money, work, and responsibility. Right now, we need to pay attention to what is happening in our government and help create change. We do not want another stock market crash, so using our voices and skills to support others, not just ourselves, matters greatly. Our society and community improve when we step by step ask for advice, offer new ideas, and stay willing to question what we see.

Our jobs come from employers, and employers depend on money that flows from the government. When the government shuts down, many people lose pay, and business owners can lose their companies and homes. This reminds us to look at what truly matters instead of focusing on small wants, such as buying a new car. Showing others clear steps, asking for guidance, and sharing fresh ideas make a real difference. There is no harm in asking, because we are here to learn each day. We are human and not perfect, so we should never stop seeking answers or sharing what we think. In closing, let us keep asking questions and looking for advice, for our own sake and for the sake of everyone around us.

Technology has changed how we connect with others, and whether this shift helps or harms us depends largely on the person using it. For some, reduced face-to-face contact offers real advantages. Spending time alone no longer has to mean feeling empty, because devices provide easy ways to stay occupied. Reading, shopping, gaming, streaming music, or watching shows can lift moods and pass time in harmless, even pleasant ways. In this sense, technology acts as a safe companion that can shield people from darker feelings that might otherwise lead to poor choices.

At the same time, no benefit comes without a cost. As my grandfather used to say, good cannot exist without bad. The same tools that entertain and inform also make it simpler to ignore everyday life. Family gatherings and personal conversations lose importance for some people, including me at times. I used to favor time with cousins and childhood friends over long talks at home, but now it is common to meet people who barely look up from their screens while speaking. To me, that behavior feels disrespectful and can push others away.

It is true that technology has made many tasks faster and easier. We can communicate across long distances, follow world events, and handle chores like shopping or ordering food without leaving home. Yet this convenience has a downside. It encourages laziness and makes it tempting to avoid real interaction. Why go on a date, start a conversation, or solve a problem in person when a phone or computer seems ready to do it all? Over time, this habit can leave people isolated, surrounded by devices instead of other humans.

In the end, technology is a powerful good when used with care. It should serve our needs without taking over our lives, helping us stay connected without replacing the human contact that truly matters.

The only action you must take is to distance yourself from them and grant yourself the opportunity to encounter those who share your outlook, who can make you feel as though you belong. These individuals will elevate your spirits because you are demonstrating to them that you can surround yourself with people who enable you to lead a more satisfying life and achieve greater success. For example, I behave respectfully toward everyone, with my family and with my friends. I will tell you something about my friends: they are remarkable, and I cherish them and they cherish me. I know this can be very difficult. Lacking inner peace can affect you in various ways. I think that to feel tranquil you must engage in activities that genuinely appeal to you or discover something you can pursue consistently without tedium and without becoming irritated easily, because a single difficulty should not provoke frustration for an extended period. I can tell you that harboring such resentment is unfavorable. I am 20 now and I suspect that sentiment may remain with me indefinitely, but I am attempting not to dwell on it. When I do recall it, I remind myself that I love my brother and we are intimate; he is someone who listens to me, and when I converse with him about events in my life I feel serenity within myself.

A strong bond with those around you can assist you in sustaining a positive demeanor because if you encounter individuals who are consistently constructive or consistently discuss matters that will benefit your life, they can shape your future. However, in your life you will encounter numerous people, perhaps admirable or perhaps harmful. Some will be kind and invite you to venture out frequently or urge you to amuse yourself, and you may assume these individuals are beneficial for your prosperity. Let me clarify that sometimes the admirable people are those who offer you not entertainment but opportunities that can genuinely improve your life without jeopardizing your future. I know sometimes you may feel that those who intend to assist you are unreliable, but you would be mistaken. This illustrates why I emphasize that to attain a prosperous future you must associate with people who will support your advancement.

I think we can all agree that after these three elements—treating everyone respectfully, preserving inner tranquility, and establishing a strong connection with those nearby—our perspective on the importance of maintaining a constructive demeanor becomes clear. We must exhibit a favorable disposition toward everyone regardless of our circumstances.

Technology has limits when it replaces human contact, yet its presence in daily life brings both benefits and drawbacks. Today, technology surrounds us, and without it we would lose many chances to learn and grow. People rely on it for countless purposes, and it often makes tasks simpler. In my view, technology tends to affect our lives in a positive way, and several examples support this.

In human life, technology often creates advantages. For many people, it is part of their job, allowing them to find answers without asking others and to earn a living. In schools, teachers and students depend on it regularly. Most assignments are completed on computers and submitted online, while questions are answered through quick internet searches. In the United States, schools use technology for about half of class activities, preferring it over books to gather information. Similarly, doctors use advanced devices to perform operations and save more lives than in the past, placing greater trust in reliable tools than in printed manuals. Technology also helps factories by taking over difficult tasks, such as packing, which reduces human effort.

People can use technology wisely or unwisely. Over time, many have learned to apply it in helpful ways, such as secretaries, teachers, and doctors who use it to communicate or protect valuable information. Some parents in Latin countries treat devices as modern babysitters, using phones or tablets to keep children occupied while they handle other duties. However, not everyone uses technology responsibly. Some misuse it to deceive others, stalking social media, kidnapping people, or stealing bank accounts. There are cases where older people trick children through online games or messages, and some individuals become hackers who steal without concern for their victims. These examples show that greater access to technology does not guarantee good choices.

Technology can reshape how people live and think. It can increase a sense of safety by offering better ways to protect homes. It also allows those who enjoy public expression to build careers as content creators, sharing their interests even without knowing their audience personally. Older generations now think differently because they can send messages or make video calls instead of writing letters. Limits in face-to-face contact become less serious when we can communicate easily across distances, such as while playing online games with friends in other countries. In these ways, technology turns communication limits into practical advantages.

In conclusion, losing human contact can sometimes be harmful, for example at work or in close relationships where personal conversation matters. Yet in schools, checking answers through technology or discussing ideas online can be useful. Overall, both human contact and technology have positive and negative sides. People often prefer devices because they are quick, even if results are not always accurate. Despite the benefits of technology, we still need more meaningful human communication than digital contact alone.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once observed that growth only happens when we attempt things that stretch beyond what we already know well. He is correct, because to claim mastery is to perform a task steadily, without repeated failure. Progress depends on setting personal aims, and even small steps matter; they build the path toward larger achievements. Not all skills arrive quickly, and some demand years of attention, yet with steady belief in ourselves we can reach high levels of ability.

When you can manage a bicycle, you can choose to learn a motorcycle; when you bake cupcakes, you can move toward baking whole cakes; when you can stay afloat, you can teach yourself proper swimming. These everyday challenges sharpen talents you already own. By polishing them, you create space for greater work and broader impact. Until you test your limits, planned goals remain out of reach, but consistent effort can carry you past familiar ground.

Difficulty in one small task does not mean it cannot be mastered. You must repeat and adjust until it is within your control, or else growth stops. The choice now rests with you: to develop as a person or remain unchanged, to move forward toward meaningful aims or settle for what is already known.
