I believe that when people have their first impression of something, they can change; changing is a good way to show everyone that you are not the same person you used to be, and that each impression others give you can become a way to try and avoid repeating the same mistake. People may say it is impossible to forget what we did in the past, but when we try each day, we can improve. No one is perfect, but we can improve at changing our attitude and at not trusting people we believe are not the kind we should trust.

I think first impressions can shift, and each person moves in their own direction, so no one reacts in exactly the same way. Some people never adjust because the matter simply does not matter to them, while others reshape their views after experiences push them to rethink.

There are those who stay the same because they pay little attention to outside opinions. They follow their routines and ignore gossip. Yet if someone leaves a strong negative mark, they may pause and examine what went wrong. Real change usually arrives when it feels necessary, and it rarely happens overnight. Mistakes can repeat themselves until a person chooses to act differently.

Relationships often trigger these shifts, especially when trust breaks down. Jealousy, toxicity, or harmful habits can appear between people. Some young people suffer deeply after feeling betrayed, without seeing how heavy the moment is for the other side. Staying in a relationship should not be about impressing others or making them envious, and although change is difficult, it can help bonds grow stronger.

I once believed that I could not change after my first impression of myself. When people said my attitude let them down, I felt disappointed and began to think badly about my abilities. I clung to habits that suited me even if they bothered others. Eventually I decided that I had to become someone different, no matter how hard it felt, and that it was possible with or without help.

I still believe that first views can change. Showing that we are not the same as before is a way to prove growth. Each new reaction can push us to try harder and avoid old mistakes. The past may not vanish quickly, but daily effort helps us move forward. No one is flawless, yet we can learn to adjust our behavior and to be careful about whom we choose to trust.

I believe that allowing students to study from home can bring real benefits, mainly because it helps them feel more prepared and attentive. At school, some learners hold back because they fear being judged by others, and as a result they do not show what they are truly capable of. Learning from home can reduce this pressure and let students focus on their own progress.

When a student is alone at home, there is no one watching every move, which can encourage independence. If something is unclear during an online lesson, the student has to look for solutions, learn how to manage time, and build confidence. This kind of environment also makes daily life more practical. For instance, if hunger or tiredness appear during long study hours, it is simple to take a short break, prepare food, and return to work without losing momentum. Questions can be sent to teachers by message, and answers can be studied at a calm pace.

Studying at home can be especially helpful for those who feel uncomfortable in large groups or need one-to-one explanations. It also offers flexibility for people who struggle with early mornings, since lessons can be followed later in the day. In more serious cases, such as students who are pregnant or have just given birth, remote learning can make continuing education possible. A friend of mine went through this experience and showed how difficult it was to balance health, a newborn, and school expectations. Being able to study from home would have made that period less stressful for her and for her child.

However, there are important challenges. Not every family can afford internet or devices, and some students may lose motivation if they stay at home for too long. Others might work to support their household and end up skipping classes or losing concentration. These difficulties show that studying remotely is not a perfect solution for everyone, but it can still help when students combine work and study in a balanced way. For example, alternating work days with study days can allow progress without forcing impossible choices.

During the school year, videos and online meetings can explain subjects clearly and repeat content as needed. Possible advantages include fewer distractions, more time to review material, and the freedom to study in a calm personal space. In addition, students do not have to worry about cold weather, strict dress codes, or unwanted social situations, and they may avoid certain emotional pressures. If schools offer online options with proper support, learners can protect their well-being and make steady progress. In my view, giving students the chance to study from home, when possible, is a valuable step that deserves careful consideration.

Many societies now expect students to choose a career path before starting high school, and classes are arranged to lead them toward that goal. I do not believe this is wise, because learners at this stage are too young, often inattentive, and not ready to make such important choices.

First, teenagers usually lack enough knowledge about different jobs to decide on one clearly. High school students have had little contact with real workplaces, so asking them to pick a lifelong direction can lead to confusion and poor planning.

Second, beginning this process feels premature. It makes more sense to use the early high school years to explore many subjects and develop basic skills. Only when students reach later years, such as junior or senior year, should they choose specific courses that match a clearer sense of their interests and abilities.

Third, young people can be careless, and their wishes often change. Life events or new interests may make earlier choices seem unsuitable. If a student selects classes in ninth grade based on limited information, those credits may lose value later, forcing them to restart their planning. For instance, a friend of mine took a technology course as a freshman, expecting high earnings, but after learning more he switched to construction trades to study building techniques instead.

Finally, making rushed decisions in youth increases the risk of mistakes. Better outcomes come from staying focused, taking school seriously, and acting responsibly. With time, students gain experience and learn what they truly value.

As shown above, early career commitments often create more problems than solutions. A stronger approach is to concentrate on general studies first, earn strong grades, and wait until senior year or college to choose courses that genuinely guide a person toward a fitting career.

I agree with the idea that unless we attempt things beyond our current abilities, we will not truly grow. At seventeen, I have noticed that staying in comfortable routines often leads to stagnation. When we aim only for what feels easy, we lose the chance to develop into stronger versions of ourselves.

Choosing comfort may feel safe, but it wastes time that could be spent improving our skills and sharing what we know with others. Pushing ourselves further helps us gain knowledge and confidence, and it allows us to support people who struggle without asking for help. Growth is not just about personal success; it is also about lifting others when we can.

Some may argue that they have already reached a point where extra effort is unnecessary. They might believe they have mastered the challenges they face and have nothing left to learn. I think this view is limiting. People always have room to learn, whether as students, workers, or family members. Settling for “good enough” prevents us from discovering what we could become.

It is not wrong to rest or feel proud of progress, but refusing to step beyond our limits can stop us from reaching our potential. Small, steady efforts to learn and improve each day can make a big difference over time. Talking with others, asking questions, and offering help do not weaken us; they strengthen us.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote that unless we try to do something beyond what we have already mastered, we will never grow. This statement holds true. By choosing courage over comfort, we can grow into people who inspire others and contribute to a better community.

Have you ever spotted something on the sidewalk and picked it up as if it were yours?  

That choice is a lie, and it matters because we cannot know whether the money or toy we found belongs to someone who will soon return for it. When owners come back, the object is simply gone, carried away by a stranger who decided to keep what cost someone else time and thought. When I was young, I often saw things dropped. I would lift them and hand them back or point out what had happened. Most people’s first urge is to take what lies unclaimed, yet this is unwise; we rarely know to whom it belongs or where it has been. Keeping what is not ours is taking from another, even if the act feels small.  

Many say to leave an item where it was found because people usually remember what they have and expect it to wait for them. Few abandon their things without noticing or caring. Schools repeat this lesson; at my primary school, signs everywhere reminded us not to take what was not ours, and most children paid attention, though some still ignored it. They grab things not from need but from impulse, without thinking of the owner.  

Needing something means we truly depend on it and would struggle without it, yet if something is truly necessary, we can usually buy it from a nearby shop. Wanting something is different; we simply desire it for show or amusement, even though we are not lacking and can live without it. Taking in this case is a choice, not a necessity, and it shows little care for others.  

If you find something, do not take it.  
If you see someone drop something, return it.  
Notice what you do.  
Do not follow the crowd.  
Be useful.  
Be gentle.  

This lesson matters because fewer people practice it today, and some parents no longer guide their children closely, leaving schools to show what is right and wrong. When someone drops an object, handing it back is simple. If you lose your favourite toy or phone and later discover it was taken by a passer-by, you feel angry and sad because something you valued is gone. But if a stranger brings it back, you feel thankful and relieved, knowing they chose honesty over convenience. An owner may not even realize what slipped away until they need it, and a small act of kindness can spare them that worry.  

Years ago, I left my tablet behind, and someone kept it without concern. I did not see who took it, and my happiness vanished when I understood what had happened. I relied on my mother’s phone until my father could replace it. That moment showed me that taking what we do not own is neither clever nor harmless. Many people ignore this until it happens to them, then wonder why. The answer is simple: they once did what they now suffer from, allowing someone else to repeat the same loss.  

Items like phones hold great value, often costing over a thousand dollars, and their absence creates real difficulty. A damaged or missing phone can mean missed calls, lost help, or long waits in unsafe places. If someone took my phone, I would feel anger and sorrow, not only because it is costly, but because it connects me to others and keeps me safe. These reasons make it important to teach children that walking away with what they find is neither smart nor kind, and that returning it can change someone’s day from broken to whole.

Thomas Jefferson once said that remarkable achievements become possible when we stay active. His words suggest that progress depends on steady effort, whether for personal growth or for the benefit of others. This raises the question of whether we achieve more by keeping busy or whether stepping back also has value. While rest can restore strength, remaining engaged in meaningful tasks often leads to greater results and helps build a responsible society.

Each day, millions of people get up and devote themselves to work, giving their best to earn a living and improve their skills. Even those who lack formal jobs can still contribute by staying involved in their communities or focusing on self-improvement. Volunteering, helping neighbors, or learning new abilities are all ways to remain active. Everyone needs time to recharge, yet too much idleness can weaken motivation and delay important goals.

Working consistently is worthwhile when the effort is purposeful. People labor hard for many reasons, such as securing their future, paying necessary expenses, or caring for loved ones. Others are driven by a love of their craft or the desire to offer something valuable to society. These different motives show that staying busy is closely tied to personal dreams and a sense of responsibility. This is why taking action usually brings better outcomes than doing nothing.

From a social perspective, activity is closely linked to survival and dignity. Adults must meet basic needs like food, housing, and bills, which often requires steady work. At the same time, staying active beyond formal jobs can strengthen communities through support and cooperation. When people choose to give their time and energy, they often grow as individuals and help society function more smoothly.

Human progress depends on this willingness to act. Ambition and purpose push people to contribute and improve their circumstances. Although short pauses can be helpful, frequent reflection may encourage us to favor effort over passivity. In the end, Jefferson’s statement invites us to examine our choices. Rest is useful, but turning goals into reality remains possible only when we decide to keep moving forward.

Four-day School

Debate between benefits and disadvantages. Resume any ongoing school activities on a regular five-day week and change that to only four days.

To adopt a four-day school week is an option that must be implemented not only for many workers but also by each high school and higher education institution after seeing these reasons.

This involves losing ten hours per week, but those missing hours can be recouped by extending the school day by two hours and increasing time for each class per day. This is an option to improve attention and time devoted to each class and complete any project or assignment assigned by your teacher. With the extra two hours, we can spend more time with friends and teachers for support in any class where someone is struggling.

Additionally, we could adopt an option for the fourth day: using the extra two hours for time in the library, which could be valuable for students who enjoy reading, or for those who prefer extra time for sports or other after-school activities.

The fifth day of the week can be used for medical appointments or health matters. The common excuse for missing regular school hours is a note from parents explaining absence from certain class periods. Handling such situations outside regular school time will reduce student absences during class periods.

We must also remember teachers who are parents and need one extra day for family time and carrying out regular activities with their children if they have them.

Do not overlook seniors who face demanding situations as they decide their future; they need time to keep all options open among universities and colleges for the next step, higher education, and possibly weekend employment. The same applies to freshmen, who are transitioning from middle school and require adjustment to heightened high school activities beyond their former routine.

Additional options for a free Friday or Monday can include community service, with parental permission and adult supervision. Students who wish to participate can help with neighborhood or river cleanups or other community service tasks. Schools could also develop programs that involve major companies assisting students in finding jobs on this new free day, with possible part-time work continuing into weekends.

Consider:

Only a four-day school week, eliminating the fifth school day (not briefly attending five days but using full time across four days).

Three free days per week (using this extra time for family or friend gatherings, or any plans you and your parents choose).

No waking early on Friday or Monday mornings (depending on which day the school selects as the free day); use the time to rest and fulfill responsibilities.

This arrangement may not suit students with part-time jobs, because extending the school day by two hours could reduce their work schedule. Nevertheless, those in this position could use the fifth school day—which would be free—for full-time work across three days.

Always remember: balancing two different activities per day can be difficult and tiring. Attending school and then working is exhausting when there is no time to rest. However, with only four school days, even with the two-hour extension, you will have time after school to rest, complete projects or homework, and use the other three days for any job you find suitable.

Recognizing disadvantages also means acknowledging solutions and benefits for each concern about this plan, because advantages outweigh disadvantages for more than 90 percent of students.

After presenting all points regarding benefits, disadvantages, and solutions, the case for a four-day school week stands. I willingly conclude that everyone needs three free days from school and only four days of classes. Even if individual student situations differ—staying home, following family routines, helping with household tasks, working, or studying—and if we all agree with this proposal, together we will have the strength to advocate for this new right for high school and college students. With shared resolve, together for a new right.

Changing from a five-day schedule to a four-day school week is a reform that deserves serious attention in secondary and higher education. Although it removes ten hours of weekly class time, this loss can be recovered by lengthening each school day by two hours. With longer periods, students can concentrate more deeply, finish assignments during class, and receive timely help. The extra time also creates space for teachers and classmates to support anyone who is falling behind.

The additional hours on the four school days can be used in flexible ways. Some students may choose to study in the library, while others may prefer sports or clubs after class. This freedom allows different interests to be pursued without the rush that often marks the end of a regular school day. Meanwhile, the fifth day, now free, can be reserved for medical appointments or health needs. Absences would then happen outside lesson hours, reducing interruptions and helping students keep up with their studies.

Teachers, who are often parents as well, would also gain a full day for family responsibilities and daily routines with their children. For older students, the change offers more time to handle difficult decisions about university, college applications, and part-time work. Younger students, moving from middle school routines to high school expectations, could use this day to adjust gradually to new academic and social demands.

A free Friday or Monday could also be dedicated to community service, with parental permission and adult supervision. Projects such as cleaning public areas or supporting local organizations would promote responsibility and connection with the community. Schools might also partner with companies to guide students toward job opportunities, using the extra day to build career skills.

Of course, the model has drawbacks. Extending the school day reduces the hours available for part-time work during the week. However, the fifth day remains completely free, allowing students to pursue full-time employment over the weekend. It is true that combining school and work can be tiring, but four slightly longer days still leave time to rest, complete homework, and manage other tasks before using the remaining days for work.

Although disadvantages exist, solutions and benefits clearly outweigh them for most students. Having three full days free each week supports rest, family time, and personal planning, while avoiding early mornings on at least one weekday. In the end, moving to a four-day school week can meet a wide range of needs, whether students stay at home, help with family duties, work, or study. If we agree on this goal, we can unite and push for this change as a new right for students, together and with shared purpose.

When motivation disappears, students may give up, fail to earn the credits they need, and risk not finishing school. Without a diploma, entering college becomes difficult, and finding a stable job is much harder. This can lead to serious struggles later in life, which is why letting students pick their electives is so important.

When students study subjects they are good at, they are more likely to attend regularly, earn better marks, and stay curious about learning. This also increases their chances of gaining credits and opening doors to new opportunities. For instance, a student with strong drama skills might become an actor, achieve recognition, and build a successful career. Students can also develop more than one ability, and having a wider set of skills makes them more prepared for different situations. This is another reason why finding and using personal strengths in elective classes is valuable.

The future is important for every student, and focusing on electives they enjoy can shape life after school and college. When students build skills they care about, adult life feels less uncertain, even when challenges appear. These abilities help them overcome difficulties and begin chasing their dreams. With a clearer sense of direction, students can create better futures and feel more certain about where they are heading.

Some may argue that students are not always motivated enough to take electives seriously and might treat them lightly. Even so, allowing choice remains a stronger way to encourage effort and growth than forcing uninteresting classes on all learners.

I totally agree that the students should design their projects. For example, I am an ESL student who likes to make my own projects during summer so as not to forget what I already learned during the year; in other words, students need to work on their own projects during their break.

The first reason for this position is that some students who feel more comfortable making their own projects will know how the topic goes because they were the ones who created it. In fact, if schools let students make their own projects, the students will be more comfortable because they will know what the topic is about and it will be easier for them to complete it.

A second reason is that students making their own projects during summer can be more helpful when they return to school, because they are not going to forget what they already learned. The students do not have to stop working on their own projects, because if they stop, they probably become lazy. For example, ESL students, if they do not try to make their own projects, will forget everything.

I think that students need to have their own projects during summer, and that would be good for them. Also, students will not forget everything they already learned during the year, because they are still working on their own projects and understanding them better. I totally agree that the students can do better without teachers during summer; students can be more active and show more of their abilities if they try, and they will succeed. There are many reasons for students to make their own projects during summer.

Some schools ask learners to finish summer assignments so that education continues while classes are not in session, yet it is debated whether these tasks should be planned by teachers or by students. I believe that learners should create their own projects. Students usually understand which areas are difficult for them and what they need to improve, so personal projects can help them keep learning while practicing ideas that matter to them. This ongoing work can build useful skills and help them return to school with stronger habits.

One reason to support student-designed projects is comfort with the topic. When learners develop their own tasks, they already know the direction and purpose, which makes the work feel clearer and easier to manage. If schools allow this freedom, students can choose themes that fit their needs and study them in ways that suit them best.

Another reason is that continuous effort prevents forgetting. When learners stop working completely during the break, they may become less motivated and lose progress. For instance, language students who keep using their skills through personal projects are more likely to remember what they studied and strengthen their abilities. Without this practice, it is easier to lose confidence and forget important points.

In conclusion, I support the idea that students should design their own summer projects. This approach helps learners retain knowledge, stay active, and become more independent. Personal projects encourage responsibility and allow students to show what they can do, making the return to school smoother and more productive.

Author Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote "To be yourself in the world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." Currently your accomplishments, actions, and attitude reflect who you are and how remarkable you are; globally, many individuals believe that acting otherwise is a gesture of humility. For example, in your career, your workplace, or at school, undertaking tasks beyond your obligations signals a generous spirit and demonstrates how vital it is to present yourself as someone striving to create difference. I concur because when you remain authentic, others perceive something exceptional in you and attempt to become someone you admire while learning new skills; perhaps the initial attempt will not be flawless, but you persist in standing out among numerous people. Three reasons validate the significance of being yourself: first, others will emulate you; second, you will motivate everyone; third, your accomplishments can reshape the perspectives of many around you.

First, being yourself is significant because others will imitate you. In situations where you consistently go the extra mile—such as assisting others regardless of obligation—your conduct stands out. For instance, at school you explain to a classmate how to solve any math equation although it is not your role; the teacher bears that responsibility. Such deeds encourage many individuals to mirror your behavior.

Second, being yourself is significant because you will inspire everyone across settings like home, neighborhood, school, university, and even church. For example, if your neighbors observe you maintaining your yard or aiding fellow residents with tasks such as trimming lawns and cooperating, you become a catalyst for motivation, thereby fulfilling your achievement of inspiring others.

Last, being yourself is significant because your accomplishments can alter others’ outlooks. When people witness your progress in life by accomplishing what others merely contemplate, they wonder how you managed it. You can offer guidance and explain your approach, assuring them that they can succeed as well. For example, within families we often encounter varied circumstances: some members hold modest salaries while others operate their own enterprises. If you embody a disposition inclined to assist your relatives, you transmit encouragement, optimism, and similar positive energies.

In conclusion, as the author indicated, we persistently strive as humans to pursue additional efforts in order to achieve notable results and accomplishments in life. More than half of the world engages in this behavior because the majority recognize the advantages of aiding others, and, more crucially, the global community observes a constructive dimension in this principle that Emerson described. Consistently acting beyond expectation can become our finest accomplishment, serving as a model for those near us; indeed, we can become inspiration for countless individuals worldwide.

For example, in school you explain to your friend how to resolve any math equation, but it is not your job in the class—it is the teacher’s responsibility to explain to your friend—and the accomplishment leads many people to be like you.

Second, being yourself is important because you are going to be an inspiration for everyone in many areas, such as in your house, neighborhood, school, college, and even church. For example, if your neighbor sees you clean your yard or house, or help other neighbors by cutting the grass and sharing tasks, you can be motivation for others; that is how you complete your accomplishment of being an inspiration for others.

Last, being yourself is important because your accomplishments can change the mentality of others; when people see your progress in life by doing things others ask themselves, “How did they do it?”, you can leave a message and tell them how you did it, and if you did it, they can do it too. For example, in families we can see different types: some have jobs but with lower salaries, while others have their own companies. If we are the type of person who likes to help our own family, we transmit that as good vibes, hope, and so on.

In conclusion, as the author said, we as humans are constantly trying to do extra things to achieve great results and accomplishments in life, and more than 50 percent of the world does that because the majority of people see the benefits of helping others. Most importantly, the world sees a positive side to this message that the author gave: always doing something else can make our greatest accomplishment an example for others around us, because more than an example, we can be inspiration for many people in the world.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote that remaining true to yourself in a world that keeps pushing you to conform is among the greatest achievements. What we do, how we act, and the attitude we carry often speak louder than words. In many places, people believe that taking on tasks beyond our duties shows humility and care. At work, in school, or in daily life, doing something that is not strictly our responsibility can reveal a generous spirit and a desire to stand out by making a difference. I agree with this idea because staying true to ourselves allows others to notice something special and perhaps inspires them to grow. Even when the first attempt is imperfect, persistence in being different among many people matters. There are three main reasons why being ourselves is valuable: others may follow our example, we can become sources of inspiration, and our achievements can shift how people think.

To begin with, being ourselves encourages others to act in similar ways. When someone consistently goes further than expected and helps even when it is not required, people take notice. For instance, at school, choosing to explain a difficult math problem to a classmate, although teaching is the teacher’s role, can lead others to adopt the same helpful attitude.

Moreover, staying true to ourselves inspires people in many areas, such as at home, in the neighborhood, at school, at college, and even in religious communities. When neighbors see someone tidying a yard, cutting grass, or assisting others, it often motivates them to behave in the same caring way. This ripple effect turns personal effort into a broader example of responsibility and kindness.

Finally, our actions can change how others view their own possibilities. When people observe steady progress in someone’s life, they begin to ask how it was achieved. Sharing how we overcame challenges can encourage them to believe they can do the same. In families, for example, one person who helps relatives despite limited income can spread hope and positive energy, influencing others to value support over self-interest.

In conclusion, as Emerson suggested, humans constantly strive to do more in order to achieve meaningful results. Since most people recognize the benefits of helping others, these efforts often reveal a brighter side of life. Doing something beyond ourselves can become our proudest achievement and serve as a guiding example, because true influence lies in inspiring others to grow through our actions.

Setting up a homework club is one useful step toward raising student performance. This kind of club matters because it can lift grades, leave more personal time after class, reduce tiredness, and give students a reliable place to ask for help from both teachers and classmates.

To begin with, a homework club encourages better results by creating a focused space for work. When teachers and peers are present to explain ideas, students finish tasks more efficiently and feel more confident about tests. For instance, someone who is stuck on an assignment can stay after school, get guidance, and leave with a clearer understanding instead of worrying about low marks.

In addition, students gain extra free time once the main work is done at school. With fewer tasks waiting for them at home, they can relax, see friends, or spend time with family. A club like this would appeal to many learners because it turns stressful evenings into chances to rest or enjoy hobbies, while still offering support from others who face similar challenges.

A homework club also helps students feel less worn out. Knowing that help is available during the school day reduces anxiety about falling behind, which often leads to better sleep and more energy for the next morning. Since young people already manage many pressures outside class, having this kind of steady support can make daily life feel more manageable.

Moreover, regular sessions allow students to learn new skills and strengthen what they already know. Even when progress feels slow, working alongside others reminds students that effort can lead to real improvement. This steady encouragement helps them keep trying instead of giving up.

In the end, creating a homework club is a practical choice that raises achievement, increases personal time, lowers tiredness, and gives students a sense of gratitude for a system that genuinely supports them.

People need to rely on their own instincts and thoughts when making choices. I agree that individuals should trust themselves first, since believing in one’s own abilities is the starting point for earning trust from others.

To begin with, personal decisions should come from one’s own mind rather than from outside voices. When people generate ideas themselves, they do not depend heavily on suggestions from others. This independence also applies to creative work, such as writing, where copying from others prevents real growth. By valuing their own thinking, people can develop stronger judgment and clearer goals.

Secondly, following one’s instincts helps people manage difficulties without always waiting for rescue. When problems arise, confidence in one’s own judgment allows a person to act quickly instead of searching endlessly for guidance. This self-trust often leads to more careful and responsible choices.

Moreover, self-belief shapes how others see us. For instance, giving a class presentation shows this clearly. If a student does not trust their ability, the teacher may also hesitate to trust them, and this can affect grades. Constantly seeking approval during the talk only weakens both performance and impression.

In conclusion, people should make choices based on their own instincts and ideas before looking for outside help. Trusting oneself is important because others struggle to believe in us if we do not believe in ourselves first. Ultimately, listening to one’s inner voice helps build personal value and stronger independence in life.

Some schools create programs that bring younger and older students together. These projects exist so both sides can see what responsibility means and learn how to support one another. Older students discover what it means to guide others, while younger students get a clear idea of what they will face as they grow up. At the same time, older students can learn from the energy and honesty of the younger ones.

Older students are able to share their mistakes because everyone has made different errors in judgment. By explaining what went wrong, they can steer younger students toward better choices. Older students can also talk about real-life situations and show how to act with care and respect.

This is helpful in schools where some younger students are still learning English or feel unsure about daily tasks. There are many forms of these programs. For example, an older student may step in during a disagreement and remind others to choose peaceful solutions, since nobody is perfect and everyone makes mistakes. The main difference is that older students carry more responsibility, while younger students have less, though they still have roles to play. Because of this, we need older students to teach what is safe and sensible. They cannot force anyone, but they can explain why certain actions are harmful and what is better for everyone. Both sides can protect each other and strengthen respect. By doing so, they encourage harmony between age groups and help the whole school feel safer and more connected.

I disagree with the idea that success is built on moving from one failure to the next. Winston Churchill claimed that success comes from facing repeated failure without losing enthusiasm, but in my view this overstates how necessary failure is. Everyone makes mistakes, yet reaching goals depends mainly on steady effort and refusing to quit, not on treating setbacks as required steps.

It is true that nearly everyone experiences failure at some point, whether in personal life, school, or work. Some may let others down or fall short of their aims, and while a few seem to avoid big mistakes, most of us stumble along the way. I have seen this in my own family; for example, my cousin focused on her studies and earned a scholarship, but this does not mean she never struggled or felt unsure. Mistakes happen, but they are not a fixed path to achievement.

To reach important goals, people usually need hard work and patience. After a failure, it helps to stay calm and look for the next chance instead of feeling defeated. Life offers many possibilities, and when one plan does not succeed, it is often wiser to adjust and try something new. Giving up too quickly stops progress, while persistence and flexibility keep it moving.

Enthusiasm also plays a key role, but it should not be mistaken for a rule that failure must come first. Caring deeply about something gives people strength to continue even when results come slowly. Those who lack this interest tend to settle for whatever happens, without pushing for better outcomes. When I was younger, strong study habits helped me, but moving to a new country forced me to rebuild my skills through steady effort rather than repeated failure.

In the end, I believe success does not require a long chain of failures. Hard work, refusal to quit, and genuine interest matter far more. Difficult moments may appear, but they do not define the journey. By holding on to enthusiasm and working steadily, people can reach their goals without accepting failure as a condition for success. Life is challenging for everyone, yet consistent effort remains the clearest way forward.

Technology changes how people live and connect, and I agree that it is not among the best things humans have made. Many argue that devices separate families or simply dislike how tools reshape daily life. These reactions show awareness of the damage technology can do. There are several ways it weakens human contact and personal wellbeing. People grow attached to screens, spend too much time buying things online, and lose real conversations with others.

Many individuals are drawn to their phones or games, and this habit is harmful because it turns attention inward. When someone nearby needs help, a person absorbed by a screen may ignore them or respond harshly, showing that the device or game matters more than a human need. This applies to both adults and children, who may forget how to be kind and supportive toward others.

Shopping online can feel empowering, especially for women who value independence in choosing their own clothes. However, some develop a strong urge to buy again and again. While occasional purchases are harmless, constant shopping becomes a habit that replaces balance with excess.

In my view, a person who avoids talking with others often lacks inspiration for life and for the future. When someone never tries activities that encourage growth or bring purpose, they risk blending into the background rather than standing out through positive action.

In conclusion, we must offer guidance to those trapped by their devices, because this attachment harms their present and their future. This is why I believe technology is not the finest creation humans have produced.

Communicating with the group often leads to clearer understanding and helps students pass their classes. Group work is also a chance to meet classmates who might otherwise remain strangers. Albert Einstein once said that imagination matters more than knowledge, and I fully support his view. Imagining possibilities can lift our mood, support others, and guide us toward work we truly enjoy. The following points explain why this is true.

Instead of focusing on embarrassment, we can invite her to imagine that she is a princess receiving attention from guests. By seeing the situation differently, she may calm down and feel proud rather than upset. This shows how creative thinking can turn stress into strength.

Finally, some adults claim that imagination has little value when searching for a good job, yet the opposite is often true. A lack of imagination can lead to poor results, whether in designing homes or writing stories. On the other hand, strong imaginative skills enable us to create appealing work that others appreciate. Over time, this can lead to steady employment and even success that matches or exceeds many traditional careers.

In conclusion, I still agree with Einstein. Imagination can increase happiness, improve the way we help others, and open doors to meaningful work. It is a powerful quality that shapes both daily life and long-term achievement.

I find science experiments to be among the most enjoyable activities. One reason is that they feel different from many other school tasks. In subjects like math or language arts, we often end up solving sets of problems or writing essays. Science work, on the other hand, can involve hands-on discovery. I remember a time when our class examined the inside of a frog. It might sound unpleasant, and honestly the smell was not pleasant either, but what caught my attention was how few organs frogs have compared to humans. Perhaps some were removed, but there simply were not many inside.

I also noticed that their insides had different colors. I recall seeing blue and pink areas, while human organs are almost always red. The frog’s body looked a little dry because my teacher said it had been frozen, although this made it easier to cut. Since our teacher allowed us to explore wherever we wanted, my group tried to look at everything. There was a part I found disgusting, like the flies inside the frog’s stomach, but that did not make me want to stop.

After we finished observing, the teacher explained the names and purposes of each part. One classmate thought it was amusing to poke the frog’s eye. I still do not understand what he was thinking, but the eye was not completely frozen, so liquid came out and he got wet. Fortunately it did not reach me, though it did land on my partner, and the teacher sent him to wash up.

Because of this, the teacher decided to end the experiment, but it had been very enjoyable. Another recent activity involved working in the dark as part of our unit on light. The task was simple: spray a liquid in front of a flashlight to see how light travels. At first I was disappointed because I saw nothing, but after a few seconds the waves appeared faintly for a brief moment. Although the project was short and the explanation took too long, I still found it interesting.

These examples show that science experiments are not always dull. You might not like them at first, but giving them a chance can change your mind. In my opinion, such activities are the best part of school because they teach through direct experience and make classes more engaging.

This feeling can stay with a person long after the moment passes, making it one of the strongest lifts we can offer each other without effort or cost.

Receiving kindness also invites us to pass it along. When someone treats us gently, we are reminded that we can do the same for others. Returning this light does not require grand plans; listening closely, offering a smile, or helping with ordinary tasks can show care. These actions tell people they are not alone and encourage the same spirit to continue through families and communities.

In families, such gestures hold special power. Shared kindness builds trust and softens difficult days, reminding everyone that they belong to one another. Whether it is through patience, help, or simple presence, small choices create steadier bonds. If we ask ourselves to notice and act on these chances, kindness becomes less rare and more natural, shaping how we live together.

American jazz musician Duke Ellington claimed that a problem is a chance to do your best. He meant that facing trouble gives you the option to repair it before it grows worse. I do not agree with him, because some situations cannot be corrected, and trying your hardest may only make them more difficult. When effort does not succeed, conditions can actually become worse than they were at the start.

Imagine a broken sink that you do not know how to repair, so you ask a plumber for help. After he leaves to work somewhere else, water begins to spray from the pipes again. Because you watched him earlier, you decide to try fixing it yourself. Your attempt causes the leak to spread, flooding part of the house. Now you must call the plumber again and pay more money, even though asking him to guide you at the right moment might have avoided the damage.

Similar problems appear when children lose pets and adults quickly bring new animals into the home. For many young people, this change does not help; they may stop eating, lose sleep, or refuse to speak for a long time. When my dog Lucky died, my brother and I hardly ate or talked, and my father’s attempt to find another dog did not work, because we both understood it could never be the same.

In school, there are moments when a classmate looks upset and you try to cheer him by making plans for a project. Asking him to check with his father about meeting after school may seem harmless, but it can become harmful if his father has recently died. This happened when a student began crying and explained that his father had passed away in a car accident the night before. One careless remark made his sadness much stronger than it had been minutes earlier.

For these reasons, I disagree with Ellington’s idea. Attempts to do your best can sometimes deepen trouble, whether by fixing a sink incorrectly, replacing a lost pet too quickly, or speaking without understanding someone else’s pain.

It is often said that first impressions are nearly impossible to change, and I agree with this view for three main reasons.

To begin with, when we meet someone, the way they behave quickly shapes how we feel about them, whether that feeling is trust or dislike. Moreover, there is a strong chance we may never see that person again, so the single encounter becomes the only basis for our judgment. Even if we do meet them repeatedly, early behaviour tends to fix our attitude toward them, making later impressions hard to shift. For these reasons, our initial views often stay the same.

The liking or disliking we feel usually comes from how a person acts during that first meeting. For instance, I once met someone for the first time and did not know what to expect. After speaking with him, I did not like his tone or his manner, so my impression of him was poor. Because we never met again, that opinion never changed. This shows that once we form an idea about someone, we rarely rethink it.

In the end, altering how people see us is difficult, and first impressions usually remain fixed.

Although it may appear that "unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow" is actually accurate. But possessing something that you master does not mean that attempting something new will cause you to fail. However, abandoning it is what would prevent you from ever growing; for example, altering your lifestyle by eating properly and attending the gym is not going to be effortless, yet you still intend to attempt it. The reason is that we wish to test ourselves in a new environment that we never imagined we would encounter. Another rationale is that attempting something new indicates that we are seeking something we would appreciate or enjoy.

For instance, we instruct ourselves on how to cook, but we recognize that we previously did not know how to cook; nevertheless, that does not mean we will refuse to attempt it. That is why we experiment with new experiences, because we aim to test ourselves in a circumstance that we never realized we could resolve or abandon. Another motive is that we value experimenting with new experiences because we are curious whether we can become proficient in them; another illustration would be raising a child, questioning whether we possess everything necessary while instructing them regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate. Emerson once claimed that we cannot grow unless we attempt things that stretch past what we already know. This idea sounds sensible, yet it often meets a tired world that has little patience for thoughtful advice. I agree with him, at least in most ways, even if I feel my physical growth is nearly finished. The real question is whether staying inside familiar skills actually moves us forward.

In my seventeen years, trying new activities has shaped me into the person I am now. If we prefer the same dull routine, boredom will catch up sooner or later. Some might answer that steady repetition brought them success, and it is true that certain fields demand it. Athletes repeat actions to improve, and dancers rehearse the same steps until the performance is ready. Even so, others discover success through unfamiliar paths, although talent alone does not guarantee it.

In the end, trying something beyond our skills changes us in small but real ways. It can lift us or challenge us, but either result teaches something. Some people grow into wisdom with time, while others remain hasty and unchanged. Emerson was right to remind us that growth waits beyond what we have already learned. The city council is discussing a plan to set a 10 pm curfew on weekdays and a midnight curfew on weekends for teenagers. I fully support this measure because curfews help keep young people out of difficulty and guide them toward safer choices. When clear limits are in place, teenagers are less likely to face harm and more likely to focus on what truly matters.

One key reason for agreeing with these curfews is that staying out very late can expose young people to risky situations. At night, some individuals in public spaces may behave unpredictably or engage in harmful activities, and teenagers can easily become targets or witnesses. Returning home earlier reduces their chances of being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Another important point is that evenings at home strengthen family bonds. When teenagers spend more time with their families, they can concentrate on schoolwork, share concerns, and discuss positive goals. This supportive environment helps them grow into more responsible adults.

A further reason to respect these rules is that following laws teaches accountability. Ignoring curfews can lead to police involvement, fines, or records that create problems later in education or work. By obeying the curfew, young people show maturity and avoid unnecessary trouble.

In conclusion, the proposed curfews offer a practical way to protect teenagers and encourage better habits. Limiting late hours keeps them safer, supports family life, and helps them understand the value of following rules for a more stable future.

Taking part in a program at your own school makes sense when you choose something you truly enjoy. This is my first point: doing an activity you care about helps you stay interested and feel sure of yourself. Too many people ignore their own talents or let doubts hold them back. When someone finds an activity or sport that fits them, they can build real skill over time and aim for goals that matter to them. Life moves quickly, and schools should encourage students to explore what they value instead of just sitting still.

My second point is that staying active keeps us moving forward. Spending the day doing nothing does not lead anywhere useful. Sports and after-school activities can shape a stronger body and teach useful habits. For some, these activities even turn into serious opportunities, possibly at a professional level. Even if that does not happen, regular effort helps people grow and care for their health. Choosing to stay busy in a positive way makes daily life feel more purposeful and rewarding.

My third point is that staring at screens all day is a poor habit. Electronics can distract us from practice and from real relationships. Staying inside and scrolling through devices often leads to tiredness, poor focus in class, and less rest at night. Spending time outdoors, meeting friends, or handling responsibilities is a better use of time. Going outside and doing things helps avoid boredom and makes life feel fuller and more balanced.

These are the reasons I support joining a school activity that fits a student’s interests. Taking on something meaningful helps people work hard, stay healthy, and avoid wasting time on distractions. Life is not always simple, but trying new things can make it better and even inspire others. By aiming high and acting with purpose, we can shape a life worth remembering, and we show others what is possible when we choose to do more than just follow.

Life without setbacks would not lead to lasting achievement. Although failure can feel like a lack of success, it often guides us toward better results. In many cases, stumbling along the way actually supports our progress and brings us closer to our aims.

I support Ralph Waldo’s view because failure reveals our weaknesses. When everything goes smoothly, we may not notice the errors we are making or learn how to correct them. By experiencing disappointment, we gain a clearer sense of the effort required to reach our targets. Understanding what went wrong helps us prepare for future challenges and raises our chances of doing better next time.

At the same time, I see why someone might question this idea. Constant setbacks can slow progress and reduce the number of goals we complete. If we never enjoy steady success, we may lose confidence or miss opportunities to build on our strengths. It is true that achieving positive outcomes brings motivation and shows us what effective effort looks like.

Overall, I believe that success and failure work best together, but failure plays a stronger role in our growth. Because life is full of surprises, learning how to respond to difficulties is essential. This is why I lean toward Ralph Waldo’s opinion: facing the unexpected often teaches us more than constant victory does.

I feel certain that something inside me lifts when I notice how strange some people’s actions have become. It is often said that the way we act is the strongest way to shape others because it builds trust, proves that we care, and leaves a clear, uplifting mark on those around us.

For instance, if I suffer a bad injury and cannot walk, true friends quickly sense that I am serious and step in to help. Teachers work the same way. Their steady, encouraging manner pushes students to believe in them and ask for help when it is needed. Even if some young people doubt that teachers see their efforts, adults usually keep faith in them, hoping that belief will push students to work harder for the future. In families, good behavior travels in both directions. I have seen my own relatives grow kinder because someone chose to act with patience and honesty. Trust grows when people help, stay steady in character, and treat relationships with care.

Friends act in similar ways by standing close when stress arrives. They calm me when anger or sadness takes over. Teachers also guide students toward success, even when results are not perfect. They push for effort and offer help so that progress becomes possible, such as preparing me for quizzes and exams. When friends, teachers, and family members see this wish to help, they respond with the same support for us and for others.

Finally, our actions can leave a strong, bright effect on society. Respect and affection often follow when someone behaves with goodness. Among friends, love shown openly tends to return, so we should keep offering care rather than anger. In families, a positive manner works like a bridge to softer hearts and better moods. His answer shows how love, healing, and courage can reshape how people feel and act.

School systems are debating whether to shorten summer vacation because they worry students forget much of what they learn after a long pause. While it is true that memory can fade, cutting this break would create other problems that outweigh this concern.

Long months of classes can be tiring, and summer gives students a chance to step away from schedules and pressure. During this time, families often travel, visit relatives, or simply rest. These experiences help young people return to school with clearer minds and new energy. Summer also allows students to deal with academic setbacks, such as retaking failed courses to recover credits, without mixing this work with regular lessons.

Outside of school requirements, this period supports personal interests. Athletes have more time to train and play, while readers can spend hours with books they could not touch during the year. Those who enjoy exploring can visit new places and later share these stories through journals or photos. All of these activities build skills and confidence that classrooms cannot always provide.

Reducing summer would mean more days spent in classrooms and less time for such growth. Without a proper rest, stress would likely rise, and many students would feel burned out before the year even ends. The joy of meeting friends and relaxing would shrink, and families would find it harder to plan meaningful trips.

For these reasons, the break should remain as it is. After so many months of study, students need time to recover, explore and develop in different ways. Keeping summer vacation protects not only their well-being, but also their ability to perform better when school starts again.

Churchill’s view that success depends on moving through failure without losing drive carries weight, yet I believe it matters only for people who truly want to reshape their lives. First, every mistake can become a lesson. Second, setbacks reveal who people really are. Most importantly, avoiding repeated errors protects both progress and spirit.

Because we are human, errors are certain, and each one can teach us something useful. Those who study their missteps gain insight that later helps others facing similar struggles. Since more obstacles will appear over time, learning must become a steady habit so that each new difficulty does not cause a collapse.

Failures also uncover true character. When plans fall apart, some companions step back, while unexpected people offer support. A loyal friend or partner often stays close during early defeat rather than waiting for easier times. This honesty helps us see whose presence is worth keeping.

Above all, repeating the same error weakens motivation and delays improvement. After several rounds of the same problem, energy fades and hope shrinks. Facing one setback is hard enough, but meeting many without change makes progress nearly impossible. Accepting that life holds more tests helps us prepare rather than fear them.

In sum, failures belong to everyone, but their value lies in leaving them behind with clear lessons and fresh determination. Changing direction is always possible, yet the desire to grow and the readiness to act remain the true keys to turning failure into success.

It is often claimed that first impressions are hard to erase. Some believe they can shape these impressions whenever they wish, yet this is not entirely true. Such impressions form in a flash, leaving little room to pause or present ourselves differently. They arrive faster than a second, and while some can be adjusted later, others resist change no matter the effort. I agree with this view, because impressions are effects, feelings or images that remain after an encounter.

Certain impressions leave a strong mark on our lives. Suppose someone once had no choice but to create an unwanted impression. Imagine a student in a classroom who feels unwell and produces a loud noise that everyone hears. His first reaction may be to stay calm, but he cannot manage it. Knowing that all ears turned toward him, he feels embarrassed, his face grows hot and his body tenses, and this response is hard to control.

The feeling tied to a first impression is often rare and intense. If embarrassing moments happen daily, the awkward sensation may become familiar, yet when they occur unexpectedly, shame, confusion or discomfort usually follow. By contrast, when such events are routine, happiness can take their place. In my case, when family members ask awkward questions or create funny scenes, I often end up smiling, because these situations repeat and feel normal.

People who face many first impressions learn to adjust. Repeated exposure to embarrassment or awkwardness can train a person to respond calmly. From my own experience, I have moved from shame to ease. When my mother asks if I have a partner, or when friends wonder about the girl I like, I now answer without blushing or overthinking. These moments feel ordinary because past experiences have reshaped my reactions.

I hope that in time, whenever an embarrassing situation triggers an uneasy first impression, my habit of calmness will take over. I want the moment to remain manageable, so it does not disturb me or grow into something far worse than it needs to be.

Some argue that young learners should not lock themselves into a career path too soon because they lack time to explore options. However, deciding on a direction while still young can be valuable, since early commitment allows students to build deeper knowledge and avoid spending years testing possibilities that do not fit their strengths or interests.

When students understand their goals before high school, they can use their school years more wisely. They can choose useful subjects, join related activities, and gain practical experience that matches their aims. Over time, this focus helps them grow more confident and skilled compared to peers who delay planning until later. It also means that by graduation, they have a clearer sense of what steps to take next, whether that involves further study, training, or work.

Critics point out that younger students are not yet mature enough to make such choices, and that leaving room for change is important. Nevertheless, having an early sense of direction does not remove flexibility; rather, it provides a helpful guide while still allowing adjustments along the way.

In conclusion, committing to a career at a young age can support steady progress and greater understanding over time, giving students an advantage as they move into adulthood.

It will not be the same to impress someone with an ex—we are the attitude, the way we talk, walk, and even eat, and no one can change that. When we make a first impression on people, even if we know they will try to copy or change it, it will be impossible because everyone knows the impression; it is not something we can change. Even if we change it, it is not going to be the same. For example, Generic_Name tried to impress Generic_Name with her food; Generic_Name loved it and went to make the same food. Generic_Name lied about her personality and family to try to impress her friends in school, and they believed her, so an impression can sometimes be a lie but is impossible to change.

We need to understand that a first impression is something that is impossible to change, and we need to believe in ourselves and not try to change or copy other people’s first impressions. It will be painful to try again, even though we know it will not be the same.

I agree with the idea that first impressions are almost impossible to change, even when we try hard to correct them. Once we create an initial judgment in someone’s mind, it tends to stay, and later efforts usually fall short.

A first impression can come from our attitude, emotions, or behavior, and these things stick with people. Whether it is how we speak, move, or express ourselves, these details leave a mark that is hard to erase. For example, someone who has liked another person since childhood may find it difficult to reshape that earlier image, even if someone new enters the picture. The original impression still lingers and influences how that person is seen.

When we meet others, they often remember what they first noticed, and trying to replace that memory rarely works. Even if someone copies or imitates a behavior, the effect is not the same. Imagine a person trying to recreate a dish that impressed a friend. Even with the same recipe, the taste will differ because small details and personal touches cannot be fully copied. In the same way, impressions carry unique qualities that cannot be reproduced exactly.

First impressions also connect to feelings, and feelings are not easily rewritten. Sometimes people present a version of themselves that is not entirely honest, perhaps to fit in or gain approval. Others may believe this image at first, but once it is set, changing it becomes difficult. Even if the truth comes later, the original impression continues to shape how they are viewed.

We should accept that first impressions are hard to change and focus on being genuine rather than trying to rewrite what others think. Attempting to force a new image or imitate someone else’s impression usually leads to disappointment, because what came first still holds the strongest power.

I support the school board’s plan to lengthen the school day by one and a half hours because it would create more learning time in every class and help both students and teachers. Instead, we could finish tasks properly and use the extra time to review anything we missed.

This change would also benefit teachers by giving them enough space to complete their lessons without hurrying. They could explain topics fully, check class understanding, and address questions instead of leaving material for the next day. As a result, classrooms would run more smoothly and fewer topics would need to be postponed.

Longer lessons would allow us to learn more deeply, especially in subjects that are difficult. If students struggle, teachers would have the chance to go over steps carefully and provide extra practice. This kind of support could help us gain confidence and raise our grades, since we would be better prepared for tests and assignments.

Teachers would also gain more time for planning and other professional tasks, which can improve the quality of lessons. Meanwhile, students could complete unfinished work during the school day instead of taking it home or falling behind. Without these extra hours, there is a real risk that lessons would stay incomplete and some learners would lag while others move ahead.

For these reasons, extending the school day makes sense. It offers clearer benefits for students who want to improve and for teachers who want to teach thoroughly, creating a stronger and more balanced school day for everyone.

Laws: the consumption of drugs and alcohol, the carrying of guns, and driving; the consumption of drugs is unlawful in many states, and you need permission to buy it, while alcohol is legal but requires you to be twenty-one or older to purchase it; carrying guns is legal but, like drugs and alcohol, requires permission and a minimum age; and to drive you need a license at sixteen or older, which is up to you, but if you choose to get your license at sixteen, you must drive with a copilot who is older than you, because they want to be sure you have the experience to drive alone.

Work: when you have a job you have rules to follow, such as a schedule and duties; you have a specific schedule that tells you when to come to work and when to go home, which helps your job stay organized for employers, because if employers come to work whenever they want it can affect the company, like if you are an accountant and the company needs you in the morning but you decide not to go in the morning and go in the afternoon instead, then skipping your schedule creates a problem with accounts and it is your fault for not following it; duties mean you have specific tasks based on your skills, so you cannot decide to do other things, or you can be fired.

Society: you do not have the freedom to do everything you want outside, like burning a library because you had the idea, or kicking or hitting people just to get attention, because you have an idea to make your friends laugh, and you cannot enter private property to pick a flower you see and like; you cannot make such decisions in your life.

In conclusion, we cannot let people make their own decisions in all things; I am not saying that people cannot have rights to do or be something, but that they cannot do everything they want, and they need guidance from experts and authorities, especially to help minors who do not have the conscience to know what is right or wrong.

People often need advice from experts and authorities when facing important choices because acting only on personal impulse can lead to mistakes and violations of shared rules. Without proper knowledge, individuals may think their actions are right even when they cause harm or break laws. Guidance helps ensure that decisions are safe, fair, and respectful of others.

Rules play a big role in daily life, such as those about drugs, alcohol, weapons, and driving. In many places, drugs are not allowed and can only be obtained with permission. Alcohol is legal, but only for people who are twenty-one or older. Carrying weapons is also permitted in some areas, yet it requires approval and a certain age. Driving follows a similar pattern; a license can usually be obtained at sixteen, but new drivers must first practice with an older companion. This rule exists to confirm that they have enough experience before driving alone.

At work, guidance matters just as much. Employees must follow schedules and complete tasks tied to their skills. When everyone sticks to their timetable, the workplace runs smoothly. If an accountant, for example, chooses to ignore set hours, the whole company may suffer. Duties are clearly assigned, and changing them without approval can lead to serious problems, including losing a job.

In society, personal freedom also has limits. No one can damage public places, harm others, or enter private property just to satisfy a sudden desire. These actions may seem harmless to the person acting, but they affect many others. Respecting boundaries helps communities stay safe and peaceful.

In conclusion, people should not be left to decide everything on their own. This does not mean they have no rights, but rather that they need support from those with experience, especially young people who are still learning right from wrong. Guidance does not remove freedom; it protects it.

I believe that school leaders should consider letting students bring phones and use them during breaks and lunch, as long as the devices remain off during lessons. One practical reason is that students often need to contact their parents once the day ends around three fifty. Having a phone also helps in urgent situations when a quick call home is necessary.

Most young people enjoy owning a phone, yet some may be tempted to message friends or get distracted during teaching time. To prevent this, clear rules can be applied: if phones appear in lessons, teachers can issue consequences such as detention. When expectations are firm, students are more likely to keep devices away while learning.

For these reasons, I support the idea of allowing phones on school grounds for safety and communication, provided they are switched off during class. Used responsibly, phones can offer reassurance without disturbing lessons and can be helpful once the school day has finished.

Ralph Emerson claimed that staying true to yourself while the world pushes you to be someone else is the greatest achievement. This view is mistaken. To reach true success, the world does not need to strip away your freedom; instead, you must guide your own life and shape what you are becoming. Emerson seems to have acted without reflection, because being yourself means making your own choices, following what you truly want, and refusing to let the world steer your path.

First, protect your right to choose. If you allow others to decide for you, you may end up lost and exhausted, regretting a life lived on borrowed terms. When you stay yourself and resist pressure to become something else, you gain results that matter, since those choices come from your own reasons and understanding. By contrast, people who surrender their will to outside voices often grow tired of life and wonder how they ended up so far from themselves.

Second, real achievement comes from doing what you love rather than accepting what the world demands. If you aim for something meaningful, pick paths that fit your interests. When you enjoy what you do, work stops feeling like a burden, and you can keep going without burning out. To make this possible, you must refuse to let the world treat you however it wishes.

Staying yourself and choosing your own direction is the clearest step you can take. You alone understand your strengths, your faults, and the difference between right and wrong for you. By trusting your own judgment, you learn what goals fit you and what choices bring value. Allowing the world to decide invites regret, while taking charge helps you avoid a future shaped by someone else’s preferences.

In short, do not let the world rewrite your life. If you hand over your choices, true satisfaction will always stay out of reach. Hold to your own nature, follow the activities that feel right to you, and treat your career or hobbies as personal expressions rather than chores. Giving others control may look harmless at first, but it often leads to boredom and loss. If you want to achieve something real, never let the world change who you are.

Modern tools let us finish many activities without meeting others face to face. We can borrow books, buy goods, and enjoy games all without talking to someone. Cutting daily contact with people because of these tools harms our lives, and the reason is clear: we lean on technology so heavily that we feel powerless without it.

These tools bring real damage to how we live. In school, lessons are shown online, yet this does not teach students how to carry out tasks themselves. Screens remove the personal link between teacher and learner. When I was young in my country, we had no such devices. Our teacher wrote on the board and explained work step by step, and if we still struggled, he explained again. That kind of care created trust and understanding. At lunch, my friends and I sat in the cafeteria and shared stories about our day. Now, during breaks, everyone stares at a screen, and real conversation has faded. This loss of contact hurts people’s well-being.

At a larger level, technology fuels conflict between nations that hold powerful weapons. It also keeps people indoors, where they watch films, read, and play without leaving home. They grow numb to what happens outside, even when others suffer, because these habits weaken feelings and strength. We rely on devices for every small need. In the past, I walked to the library for a book; today, many prefer to order online and remain on the sofa. We become less active, and meals that once meant sharing time and words are now eaten alone while phones glow on the table.

In jobs, tools can help, yet they often pull attention away. A game or match can tempt workers to stop and watch, leaving tasks unfinished. This leads to stress, job loss, and worries about basic needs. Without so many devices, this pressure would be smaller. Sometimes these inventions harm more than they help.

Accidents also increase because of them. Drivers who type messages miss turns and cause crashes, and innocent people lose loved ones because of a moment of carelessness.

In the end, technology damages human life. It makes us passive, distant, and fragile, and it erases the bonds that once held us together. Depending on it so completely leaves us less human and less able to manage our own lives.
