Saying yes to early planning is sensible, because young people understand what they hope for later in life. When they can decide on a path, they are more likely to pick a career that fits them and prepare for solid universities. By the time they become adults, they already have experience, jobs, and income, which helps them face responsibilities. They can also support their families or partners, just as their parents once guided them with clear examples. Listening and learning early makes it easier to avoid careless mistakes.

In many communities, this readiness allows people to build stable futures. When they decide to start families, they are better prepared for change and can provide a better life. Planning ahead opens more job options, because education brings chances to grow. A person who studies and focuses becomes reliable at work, moves ahead, and may even lead others. Still, this requires effort: good grades, clear goals, and steady focus during school. These habits help secure better jobs and create ways to help friends and family.

Not everyone manages to reach their aims, often because they were not ready when chances appeared. Some miss the moment to value opportunities and later find it harder to begin. Yet starting later is still possible through different work, such as construction, driving, or banking, depending on personal interests. What matters is to keep moving and choose work that feels meaningful.

For example, studying hard prepares a person for adult duties and increases the chance of steady jobs, perhaps in offices. The goal is a better life where personal wishes have room to grow. Parents can help by watching progress and encouraging study, but adults must also guide themselves instead of waiting for others. 

My suggestion is to prepare and study seriously, because this builds a strong start and the skills needed for life’s goals. Learning does not make someone perfect, but it can shape a person who sets a good example for future generations. Children who see effort and responsibility in their parents are more likely to follow it themselves. In the end, believing in yourself, knowing your aims, and working steadily are the clearest ways to protect your future and stay strong.

Tomas Jefferson once declared that one should resolve never to be idle, since it is astonishing how much can be achieved through constant action. His words suggest that individuals must commit to staying active, because only then will they realize the volume of work they are capable of completing. There will always be two kinds of people: those who support this idea and those who question it. Some argue that it is not essential to push forward all the time, believing that effort should come only when the moment feels right or when a goal truly demands it.

Nevertheless, I strongly agree with Jefferson’s statement. Continuous effort allows us to obtain remarkable outcomes, exactly as he implied when he described the impressive results of steady action. The phrase “determine never to be idle” can be understood as a refusal to let laziness take control. Around us, many individuals look for reasons to step back, often influenced by negativity that convinces them their ambitions are out of reach. Such attitudes easily lead to passivity and abandoned dreams.

At the same time, it is true that not every task requires urgent attention, yet choosing to act consistently still brings us closer to what we desire. Progress tends to build quietly through regular decisions rather than sudden bursts of work. This is why Jefferson’s message remains meaningful: it reminds us that motion creates opportunity.

In conclusion, I fully support his view. By refusing to stay idle, we can witness the results of our labor and shape the future we hope to achieve. All it takes is steady effort and the will to keep moving toward the success we imagine for ourselves.

We keep yearbooks so that important moments do not slip away, and they help us stay organized even when some students do not enjoy them. For me, they make it easier to remember homework, tasks for tomorrow, and plans for the coming week. We no longer have them now that we are in eighth grade, but younger students still use them to show their families the sports they played, the subjects they studied, and the friends they spent time with. A yearbook can also help relatives meet classmates one day.

I agree that we should continue making them so families can see what school life looks like and so memories remain clear. When friends move away, these pages help us care for them and hold onto our connection. I support yearbooks and feel comfortable with them, even if we receive them only once a year and the wait feels long. I also think it is fair to pay for our own copy, and I value the photographs they contain. Yearbooks look good, and I miss them a lot; I want them back in our routine.

Although some people believe online learning is helpful and have reasons for this view, taking classes on the internet brings both benefits and drawbacks. Studying from home allows you to avoid traveling to a building, waking up early, and facing people you would rather not meet. You can choose when and what to eat instead of relying on school meals, and you have more freedom to set your own routines. In addition, completing tests online can feel simpler because you can search for information and check answers while you work, which is not allowed in a regular classroom.

In traditional schools, you must wake up early, get ready, catch the bus, and arrive at class on time. Once there, you sit in a small room and follow many rules. If you arrive late repeatedly, you can earn detentions and eventually be placed in isolation, where you lose your phone and must stay quiet without speaking to others. Skipping class can lead to further consequences, such as being found by staff and having parents contacted through calls or emails. Most parents become upset when they realize their child avoided school without permission.

Disrespecting teachers may result in security being called to handle the situation. Fighting with another student causes even greater trouble, involving security, the principal, police, and parents, while the other family might press charges. Such incidents can harm your record and reduce your chances of being accepted by colleges, which look for students with better behavior. Using or selling drugs at school brings serious problems with the school, the police, and parents, and can lead to removal from the school, legal penalties, and separation from friends you see every day. Losing these connections can be painful.

Because schools contain many pressures and strict rules that not everyone enjoys, trying online classes may be a useful experiment. It is not just about eating what you want or sleeping later, but about avoiding unnecessary difficulties that can influence your future. For these reasons, choosing online learning seems like the better option.

Studying independently often brings greater advantages because learners gain full knowledge of the task. When people work in teams, responsibilities are usually split, so individuals may only complete one section and miss the rest. By handling everything alone, a person engages with all parts of the task and understands the complete subject.

Working together does have its strengths. Tasks can be finished more quickly and with less effort because each person handles one piece. Group work also allows students to support one another; if someone struggles, a peer can explain the topic, helping everyone to grasp it. Many students prefer this approach because it feels easier, although it sometimes leads to some members doing less while others do more.

Even so, I believe that working alone is better for me. When I complete all steps by myself, I search for information, solve exercises and explain my ideas fully. This process helps me understand different types of tasks more deeply. However, learning both methods is important, since future situations may require either teamwork or independent effort.

In my view, starting with individual work is often the best choice. For teachers, this approach offers a clearer picture of how each student thinks and performs. It reveals their abilities and helps teachers guide them more effectively. Although both options have value, working alone seems to offer the strongest benefits while still preparing students for any kind of task they may face.

Many individuals believe that first impressions remain fixed, yet I disagree because people often behave differently at first compared to how they truly are. When I first met my girlfriend, I thought she was always cheerful, but as time passed I noticed she was not as happy as she seemed, and my view of her shifted.

Most of us adjust our behavior when meeting someone important. For example, during a job interview, a person may smile and appear full of energy to be accepted, even if they feel tired or worried. Later, as days go by, colleagues notice the real attitude and the early impression changes.

It is common to create a different image during first encounters so that others will respond positively. At a new school, students may pretend to be relaxed or share opinions they think others will like in order to fit in. As weeks pass, classmates discover the true personality, and their early judgment changes as well.

In my view, first impressions can change because they do not always reflect the real person. At work or in personal life, people eventually see who we really are and learn to accept us for it. Therefore, when meeting someone, it is better to act naturally, since sincerity will shape the impression others keep over time.

As young people grow, they develop views on matters that concern them, including how others see them. It is not true that first impressions cannot be altered. People are capable of change, especially when their expressions or behavior have not been kind in the past.

It is possible to shift how others feel about us once we realize that they have formed an unfair opinion. Being known as a considerate and respectful person is rewarding, and acting in a friendlier way often helps create that image. It feels good when others hold positive thoughts about us, and making that happen is within reach. Sometimes faces look serious or upset even when we do not mean to appear that way, and adjusting how we present ourselves can change what people believe.

We do not have to display our troubles in front of others, because sharing sadness rarely brings help. Staying pleasant in company and speaking or doing good things can encourage a brighter expression. Personality plays a strong role in shaping first impressions, since it is among the first qualities people notice.

Some argue that impressions can shift only if people decide to see us as friendly, yet others point out that impressions can also improve when those who misunderstood us get to know us better. There are practical reasons to change as well. For example, workplaces often require friendly attitudes and warm expressions, and adapting can make it easier to work well with others. People are generally more willing to stay close to someone who shows a positive manner.

Leaving a good impression during job applications matters, because treating others with kindness is important in any role. In the end, it is not impossible to reshape how others see us. By showing who we really are, we can replace mistaken ideas with fairer ones.

I do not share the view that changing how others see us is simple. Many argue that it is demanding and time-consuming because it requires understanding how behavior and perception work, and not everyone finds this clear. As a result, the process can feel confusing, and initial judgments often miss the point, since not everyone wants to be seen in the same way.

Moreover, reshaping an impression is far from easy when people already have busy lives. Between work, household tasks and family responsibilities, there is little energy left to manage how others view them. This is why many claim that first impressions are hard to correct, as daily pressures make consistent change almost impossible.

In addition, adjusting how we are seen needs patience and certainty about our aims. It also requires sustained effort, and without enough time, progress becomes unlikely. Although opinions vary on whether impressions can truly shift, the common experience is that they resist quick fixes and demand persistent work.

In conclusion, I disagree with the idea that impressions are easy to manage. They require attention over a long period, and for people already pressed by life, this can feel endless. Since many also stress how difficult this work really is, it is clear that changing perceptions is a slow and challenging task.

I believe that switching to a four-day school week is not a good idea for students. While it may look like a way to gain an extra day of rest and freedom, the trade-off is actually hard to accept. That additional day could be used to sleep longer, review subjects, spend time with family, or grow personal skills. However, this benefit disappears when the remaining school days become longer.

If schools keep students for about seven hours each day and then add two more hours to fit the timetable into four days, the day becomes very tiring. Most learners already wake up around five thirty or six in the morning to prepare for school. Staying in class for nine hours can cause exhaustion and reduce concentration. This makes learning less effective and makes the day feel too heavy.

Moreover, those two extra hours in school take away time that could be used for rest, personal study, or family life. Instead of enjoying a balanced routine, students would spend more time in classrooms and have less energy for activities that matter to them. I value the stability and free time that a five-day schedule provides, and I do not want to lose it for a longer, more demanding day. We should carefully consider what truly supports students’ health and progress before making such a change.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson because he believes that avoiding action prevents growth, and without progress we cannot achieve meaningful change. Although it sounds difficult to follow his idea when people feel afraid or unsure, agreeing with Emerson does not mean everyone must think the same way. Instead, it allows different opinions to exist while still recognizing what matters most. When we accept important ideas, we can move forward together without forcing everyone to feel or act identically.

Agreement does not require total approval from every person. Some will support an idea while others hesitate, and this difference can still help us learn. For example, not everyone enjoys spicy food, yet people can still respect each other’s choices. When a person accepts an idea, they may not change their own preferences, but they can understand why others value it. Experience shows that people who keep trying and listening tend to grow more than those who choose to stay inactive. Staying down stops progress, while effort, even with difficulty, helps us improve.

Emerson likely expects others to accept his viewpoint, but he also understands that disagreement can lead to growth. When people accept or question his ideas, both sides gain experience and learn from each other. If he has strong beliefs, he should express them, yet he should not expect agreement without discussion. Sharing ideas and allowing others to respond creates better understanding. When we explain our views clearly, others can decide how to agree or disagree, and this process often leads to helpful outcomes for everyone.

Finally, if people refuse to act or engage, it becomes harder to agree or grow. Taking action, even in small ways, shows that agreement can lead to support and progress. If we help one another and accept useful ideas, we create opportunities to improve both individually and as a group. This kind of effort can make a positive difference for many people.

I believe that a positive attitude is the key to success in life. When we choose to see the future with hope, we open ourselves to better chances and greater achievements. This mindset affects everything, from personal growth to work and family, and it starts within us.

Having a positive attitude raises the level of success we can reach, both personally and professionally. When we treat others with optimism, life often responds in the same way. A smile or a kind expression can lift someone who is having a difficult day, helping them to see beyond their problems for a moment. In this way, our attitude encourages others to move forward and improve their own lives. At the same time, it brings us satisfaction, because seeing people smile reminds us that we can make a difference, even briefly.

At work, a positive attitude creates better results and more opportunities. When we support our team and treat colleagues with respect, relationships improve and the workplace becomes healthier. This kind of environment makes it easier to do good work and to be considered for growth and new responsibilities. A positive tone in our words and actions also prevents negativity from spreading, allowing success to grow naturally.

At home, the same attitude strengthens family life. Good relationships with family members bring peace and confidence, and they help us become better people. For example, in my own life, strong family bonds helped me cope after losing my father. That support showed me how a positive approach can help us survive hard times and keep moving forward.

In conclusion, a positive attitude leads to success because it never leaves us alone. It improves our professional and personal lives by shaping how we treat others and how we face challenges. Even when times are difficult, we should not let our attitude change, because others are not responsible for our problems. If we remain positive, we create better connections and better results. Over time, this choice becomes the strongest key to success in every area of life.

Allowing learners to study from home through online or video meetings can bring clear advantages, especially when they can manage their time well. Studying remotely removes the need to travel by foot or bus, so students gain more hours to focus on learning or to balance work and study. Without the noise and unrelated conversations that often happen in school hallways, many find it easier to pay attention and feel calmer while working.

Another benefit is flexibility. Some learners have jobs or other duties that make fixed schedules difficult. When weather is bad or personal energy is low, attending class from home lets them keep going without losing progress. This can encourage responsibility, though the outcome still depends on each student’s habits and the type of course they take. The key point is that remote study offers many useful possibilities for different situations.

Working at home can also reduce stress for certain students. They can pause when necessary, eat without rushing, and use their mental energy in ways that suit them best. Parents may also follow their progress more closely and see whether tasks are completed properly. For many, online homework feels simpler to organize and finish.

In my view, learning from home by way of online or video classes is often the better choice, although it still relies on the subject and on the learner’s own attitude. Some may become less active without a school routine. Even so, there are enough strong reasons to say that students can gain real benefits from being able to attend classes from home.

Do you wonder if selecting a career at a young age is a beneficial notion?

In my view, it is an excellent notion to choose a career at a young age, because in some societies, students are expected to identify a career by the time they enter high school. There are many courses selected to guide them toward choosing a specific career. For example, first it benefits them to begin early with an awareness of which career fields they desire for their future after graduating high school. Second, it would influence which type of diploma they prefer, whether the advanced diploma or the standard diploma; the advanced diploma requires passing nine SOLs and all required classes, while the standard requires six SOLs and all classes. When you enter high school, your counselor would direct you toward the diploma and career you prefer for the future. Third, while in high school, students receive foundational classes they must pass in ninth and tenth grade to advance more efficiently, acquiring experiences and knowledge about their goals and preparing for the final two years.

If you favor the same career chosen upon entering high school or decide to change to a different field, teachers and counselors offer valuable support to help students succeed by outlining the advantages of the selected study area, estimating potential earnings, and encouraging success after high school completion. Finally, in eleventh and twelfth grade, students encounter more demanding classes to fulfill graduation requirements; eleventh grade is generally more challenging because it necessitates passing two specific classes to advance, whereas twelfth grade primarily involves completing courses assigned by counselors to match the chosen diploma, whether advanced or standard, for the selected career.

In conclusion, initiating this process at a young age is a valuable approach to begin contemplating future aspirations, assessing whether a chosen career offers meaningful benefits, and recognizing how high school prepares students for post-graduation plans, whether pursuing higher education or entering the workforce. Students gain knowledge about careers where they can succeed and clarify preferences to turn aspirations into reality.

There are numerous careers to pursue in life, which is why I believe beginning at a young age, when students enter high school, allows teachers and counselors to best guide them toward one career that aligns with their interests, fostering future study, success in college, and improved prospects for their families; thus, selecting a career early is a strong idea.

Choosing a career path early often raises questions. In my view, deciding on a direction during youth is very helpful. In many communities, students are encouraged to name a field of interest when they begin high school. Schools then shape their class choices so that each subject supports that aim.

Starting early allows students to picture possible jobs before graduation. As a result, they can see which studies match their goals. Another factor is the type of diploma they will earn. An advanced diploma usually calls for passing more exams and taking extra courses, while a standard diploma needs fewer requirements. When students enter high school, counselors explain these options so young people can choose what fits their plans.

The first two years focus on basic subjects that build confidence and useful skills. This foundation makes later steps feel clearer and more manageable. If students later decide to keep their original choice or switch to a new field, teachers and counselors offer valuable support. They show how each path can lead to stable work and a realistic income, helping students imagine a successful future.

In later grades, coursework becomes more demanding. Grade eleven often feels harder because it includes key exams needed to move forward. In grade twelve, schedules are shaped by the diploma selected and the career goal in mind.

To conclude, thinking about work choices early is a wise step. High school gives students time to test their interests, learn about their options, and prepare for what comes after graduation, whether that means further study or training. Young people gain knowledge, set clear aims, and turn dreams into plans. With many possible careers available, starting this process in youth, guided by teachers and counselors, helps students commit to a path they truly care about and build a stronger future for themselves and their families.

When I first arrived in the United States, I could not speak English, so outings to school or play became puzzles I had to solve with my hands and eyes. Whenever I wanted to join a soccer game or visit the playground, I pointed out the window or sketched quick pictures. Words failed me, so I relied on gestures and images to reveal what I meant. This method felt like the only option until I began learning the language.

I agree that showing rather than telling is often the strongest way to influence people. Examples guide understanding when words cannot reach across barriers. Children watch adults carefully and mirror their behavior, believing that grown-ups know what is right. If parents hope for polite, thoughtful children, they must first model those habits themselves. In a library, for instance, a child who sees adults talking loudly may decide that noise is acceptable, while calm behavior teaches respect for shared spaces. Actions, more than lectures, shape how people choose to act.

At the same time, some argue that examples are no longer the only key to influence because technology offers new tools. Devices and programs now help us bridge gaps that once required drawings or gestures. Translation apps, online dictionaries and video tutorials allow us to explain ideas clearly even without a shared language. A traveler can look up a museum and show the name on a screen instead of sketching a building, and students can search for meanings instantly rather than waiting for someone to demonstrate.

Still, whether we use screens or signals, the heart of influence remains similar. People continue to learn by observing others and by sharing clear, concrete illustrations of what they mean. Examples may take different forms today, yet they remain a dependable bridge between minds, helping us understand each other and choose better ways to live together.

Aesop, the ancient Greek storyteller, once claimed that no kind deed is ever wasted, however modest it may seem. This view reminds us that even simple gestures can leave meaningful traces in the lives of others.

To begin with, offering basic help, such as sharing food with someone in need, can lift a person’s spirit. When we take notice and respond to another’s hardship, we show that their situation matters, and this recognition often encourages hope and trust.

Furthermore, acts that demonstrate responsibility can also create influence. Caring for a task or looking after someone else’s needs proves reliability, and this steady support helps build environments where people feel safer and more valued.

In addition, assisting others in practical ways, such as helping someone protect important work, can bring immediate relief and confidence. When we step in to prevent loss or stress, we strengthen not only the moment but also the person’s belief that they are not alone.

Ultimately, the size of the gesture is less important than the intention behind it. Whether the action feels small or significant, its value lies in the care we show and the difference we make for others, which is what truly counts.

Curfews are meant to guide teenagers away from trouble, yet many feel these rules step too far into their private lives. While the goal is to protect young people, being told when to return home often feels like an unwanted intrusion. Communities set limits such as sending youths home by 10 pm on weekdays or midnight on weekends, believing these hours reduce risky behavior. However, not everyone accepts that these choices are helpful, especially when they feel their freedom is being restricted.

I believe curfews come from a wish to keep teenagers safe rather than to control them unnecessarily. Even so, once a curfew becomes law, staying out past the allowed time is treated as an offense, which forces young people to follow rules they may not support. This creates tension, because authority is asking for respect while making decisions that many disagree with. Curfews may be planned with good intentions, but they do not always lead to the results that adults expect, since problems do not simply disappear after dark.

It feels unfair that others can decide how people should spend their time, especially when individuals are capable of making their own choices. Some may accept these limits, but feelings often change depending on the situation. In the end, protecting young people is important, yet this protection should not ignore their need for personal freedom and trust.

I do not agree with this idea because a positive mindset cannot fix every difficulty in life, and many situations make staying optimistic very hard.

When someone moves to a new country alone and without support, it is difficult to feel positive. Not understanding the language limits everyday communication, and being undocumented removes many opportunities available to citizens. Hiding from authorities and struggling to find stable work because of legal status can leave people feeling trapped rather than hopeful.

Losing a close family member and being unable to visit them because of distance or immigration rules also hurts deeply. In such moments, forcing a positive attitude does not feel natural or helpful, which shows that optimism is not always useful.

Immigrants often face discrimination from people who think life here is easy. These people ignore the dangers and sacrifices involved in moving to a new place. Judgments based on skin color or the belief that immigrants only want money can be painful. When others treat newcomers harshly without understanding their wish to build a better life, keeping a positive outlook becomes even harder.

Of course, there are reasons to feel hopeful, such as family, friends, a good job, or finishing school. These successes can bring happiness. However, there are also times when problems take over. Economic hardship, for example, can make it difficult to rely on friends, especially if they offer empty promises or pretend to help while actually refusing. Realizing this can lead to frustration instead of motivation.

In the end, people can try to stay positive, but difficult circumstances, such as separation from family because of immigration, often create strong negative feelings that positivity cannot simply erase.

Most people tend to repeat what they already know instead of reaching for what they are truly ready to achieve. The problem is that many choose what feels safest, believing that sticking to familiar habits is best, even when those habits do not support future growth. I disagree with this approach. First, trying new paths can improve the years ahead. Second, fear of change should not limit action. Third, remaining fixed in one identity prevents people from understanding both the world and themselves.

Attempting different activities can shape a better future. When someone keeps doing only what is known, progress slows. In my family, my sister once wasted time following the same routine until our mother helped her see the need to think ahead. After she chose to act differently, she became a doctor, showing how change can lead to meaningful results.

Fear should not stop people from acting in new ways. My father once hesitated to start a company because the work seemed too unfamiliar. When I encouraged him to try something different, he took the risk, and today the business is stable and supports our family. This proves that avoiding change can limit what families achieve over time.

Staying exactly the same also narrows what a person can learn. My mother often said it is important to be yourself, but I explained that doing so all the time can block goals. A self that prefers easy tasks will struggle to reach valuable aims. Only by moving beyond old habits can people recognize their own potential and the opportunities around them.

In conclusion, repeating familiar actions will not create growth. People should think about the future, act without fear, and allow themselves to change. Only then can they build lives that go beyond what they have already known.

Learning from what others have lived through matters because similar situations can reach us, and knowing what to expect helps us face them without fear. When someone meets the same difficulty we do, it is wise to ask what occurred and how they handled it, and whether support from others made a difference. This makes it easier to choose safer, clearer steps when trouble appears.

Another useful habit is to talk with older relatives, such as grandmothers, about the hardships they faced and the choices they made. Understanding what they could not do, and why certain solutions worked, gives us a map for later problems. It is better to ask before hardship strikes, so we can prepare ourselves and protect people close to us.

There is only so much we can manage once trouble arrives, which is why asking early gives us tools to respond alone or with the people we care about. Still, not every challenge can be met in the same way, and knowing our limits keeps us from making things worse.

We cannot truly help others if we stay quiet or guess instead of asking what they are going through and how we might lighten their load. Some pains run so deep that quick fixes do not exist, and pretending otherwise risks leaving people alone with heavy burdens.

Not everyone has family to lean on, often because they never allowed others near their struggles. Trying to fix everything alone may seem strong, yet there are moments when help is not optional but necessary. Accepting that we sometimes need others can save lives, because real danger grows when pride stands in the way of reaching out.

Each person has the same twenty-four hours every day. The question is how we fill that time and whether we achieve anything meaningful. People often plan to act but then lose energy, or they try to handle several desires at once and end up stuck.

As a student, I sometimes face homework and other tasks after class. I may want to relax, eat, or finish a project, and it becomes a battle inside me to choose the right order. If I deal with the important task first, the rest of the day opens up for what I truly want, giving the day a clear purpose.

I hold the view that concentrating on one thing at a time helps me achieve more. Being inactive usually means wasting time and moving farther from my goals. Most worthwhile activities follow a process, and avoiding that process only delays results. Although people can choose to do nothing, I find it hard to believe that anyone can truly avoid idleness all the time, because everyone faces moments when doing nothing feels easier.

Doing things we enjoy tends to bring faster results. Even during slower moments, we can look for solutions and plan how to reach our aims. When we finally reach those aims, we can look back and see how much we have done. Life offers the freedom to decide between acting and simply letting time pass, and choosing action usually leads to a fuller and more satisfying day.

When people look for guidance, they often turn to several individuals at once, hoping to find a reliable answer. They do this because poor advice can make it harder to choose wisely, especially when someone is dealing with stress, sadness, or big changes in life. In such moments, it is easy to lose control, feel overwhelmed, and struggle to see a clear next step. This pressure sometimes leads people to collect many opinions, thinking that more voices will bring a better result.

However, gathering too many viewpoints can also create confusion. With so many suggestions, it becomes difficult to decide which path is truly helpful. While it is natural to ask different people, the real challenge is sorting through those ideas without losing clarity. I believe it is acceptable to seek advice, but we must also use our own judgment. Without thinking carefully, we cannot move forward. Each opinion should be examined to see what it really means and whether it fits our situation. We need to ask whether following a certain suggestion could cause problems later, and then turn to someone we truly trust for further discussion. If that person agrees, we can feel more confident about acting.

In practice, the process works best when we limit the number of opinions we collect. Listening to two or three people, then pausing to reflect, often leads to a stronger decision. Everyone ultimately makes their own choice, and it helps to find a trustworthy adult who genuinely wants to help. Their experience can guide us, but we still need to think through their words before acting.

For example, I once had to organize a birthday party and choose outfits for everyone in a very short time. Worried and unsure, I asked friends, cousins, family, and teachers for ideas. At first, the flood of replies only made me feel stuck. Then I spoke with an older cousin, who explained what to do step by step. By managing my time and focusing on her advice, I arranged the party and picked the outfits within a week, and everything went well. This showed me that making better choices often means narrowing the input rather than expanding it.

If we cannot find clarity, we should at least take time to think for ourselves and seek help from someone we know well, rather than relying on strangers who may not have our best interests in mind. I also learned, through earlier mistakes, that ignoring adult guidance can waste time and create problems. While it is good to follow our feelings, we must also recognize that some choices look right at first but lead to trouble later. Listening to parents and other caring adults can protect us from these risks.

In the end, strong choices come from using our minds, trusting ourselves, and turning to honest, experienced people for support. Believing in our ability to decide, while also valuing the guidance of adults and the strength we draw from faith, helps us move forward with more confidence and fewer regrets.

We often notice the idea that having money, many friends, and strong international contacts can make life smooth and independent. Some believe that being rich and helpful to others removes the need to rely on anyone else, offering security for both family and career. While these things can bring comfort, the way we let them shape our choices matters more than simply having them.

Influence can also come from friends who encourage quick or risky decisions, such as acting without thinking or breaking the law. Many follow others only because they appear popular at school or in the neighborhood. If we do not pause to ask why we are acting a certain way, we may end up doing things we do not truly want. Some people face serious consequences, including time in prison, simply because they followed the crowd instead of thinking for themselves.

I believe influence should be used for positive purposes, such as earning money honestly, building strong friendships, and helping others without causing harm. A true friend will not ask you to do something wrong, knowing it could bring trouble with the police, school, or family. When someone distances themselves from bad choices, it is often because they care about your future rather than pushing you toward danger. Real friends stand by you when you need support, not just when it is convenient.

Influence is about the example we set for others and what we encourage them to do. The best way to lead is by acting with respect and kindness so that others trust and follow you for the right reasons. Choosing harmful behavior only brings legal trouble and damages relationships with those closest to you. Making thoughtful decisions helps avoid many problems and creates a more stable life.

Bad influence does not attract genuine friendship, because most people avoid those who bring risk or conflict into their lives. If we want to be respected, we must be willing to shape our behavior in a positive direction. People usually judge character by the choices we make, and repeated wrong actions can lead others to doubt us. If others truly value you, they will not insist on reshaping your personality. You should not allow anyone to force a new version of yourself, since real care means learning to appreciate you as you are. Those who understand your flaws but still stand beside you offer the kind of bond that allows you to remain yourself. Do not let people confuse you or belittle you to make their wishes stronger; you know your worth, however loudly they criticise.

Pressure to transform usually signals that feelings are not as deep as they appear, and staying in such situations can lead to harm. Nevertheless, change is acceptable when it comes from your own desire, not from outside demands. Personal growth is meaningful only when it is chosen freely, while love should bring respectful treatment rather than constant requests to become someone else.

Living in a world that keeps pushing us to fit in makes it difficult to remember who we really are. Ralph Waldo Emerson once pointed out that staying true to ourselves, despite these pressures, is one of the most important achievements a person can reach. I share this view and believe that following our own path brings clearer purpose and stronger results over time.

Choosing to act as an individual helps us set goals that actually match our values. When we understand what we want from life, we can plan better, avoid unnecessary mistakes, and bring order to our steps, whether at work or in our personal lives. This kind of preparation allows us to face challenges with more confidence and to build something meaningful instead of simply reacting to circumstances.

Working with personal effort also affects the people around us. Others notice when someone is consistent and reliable, and this trust strengthens relationships at work and at home. At the same time, independence does not mean ignoring others. Treating people with respect, making careful choices, and staying positive create a healthier environment where everyone can benefit.

Relying on ourselves is especially useful because not all group members give their best. Some work only to get through the day, and this limits progress. When we commit ourselves to daily effort, we create a future that does not depend on luck or on others. Continuing steadily, even when tasks feel difficult, adds up to real growth.

In the end, being ourselves is not about standing alone, but about taking charge of our direction. Hard work, thoughtful decisions, and a clear sense of purpose lead to results we can see and feel. If we stay focused, treat difficulties as temporary, and refuse to give up, we build the kind of future that makes both ourselves and those around us proud.

I share Churchill’s view that success lies in moving from one setback to another without losing enthusiasm. What counts is not avoiding failure but refusing to let it extinguish the drive to keep trying, because effort itself holds more value than the outcome.

To begin with, no one can know everything, yet attempting things remains essential since learning rarely happens without action. At times, failure may feel discouraging, but losing all enthusiasm suggests a deeper problem, such as losing interest or wasting time instead of using it to improve. When I sense repeated setbacks, I prefer to channel that energy into focus and growth, aiming to turn losses into steps toward winning and raising my own standards.

Moreover, while many people wish to become better, others accept staying at the same level because improving demands effort. Choosing to rise often involves wanting a brighter future, whether for family or personal independence. Remaining stuck after failure can project weakness and suggest contentment with little progress, whereas ambition encourages us to seek more than we currently possess.

Finally, avoiding the cycle of failure requires seizing opportunities, since the world tends to reward those who think carefully and avoid careless errors. As humans, mistakes are inevitable, but they can be corrected if we strengthen ourselves and hold onto motivations that keep us moving.

In conclusion, staying where we are is a choice, yet life gains meaning only when we dare to try. Even a single attempt can reveal possibilities that passivity will never offer.

I support Emerson’s view that staying true to oneself in a world that keeps pushing us to change is a major achievement, mainly because it brings success, authenticity, and control over one’s life.

To begin with, success matters greatly to society because we depend on remarkable individuals to move us forward. Philanthropists help cut poverty, inventors create tools such as cars, the internet, and computers that we now rely on every day, and human progress builds safer surroundings where people can enjoy longer and healthier lives. These advances show that personal achievement can benefit everyone.

In addition, being yourself is a real accomplishment because it allows you to become the person you actually want to be. When you stop pretending, you show others your true nature and build honest relationships. Living according to your own values also gives life a stronger sense of meaning instead of simply following what society expects.

Finally, taking charge of your life is important because it lets you make your own choices and shape your future. Deciding for yourself not only brings personal satisfaction but also helps you lead a more balanced and healthy life. Although some argue that following instructions is easier or more useful, creating your own success, staying authentic, and directing your life are key to human progress and to each person’s ability to choose a path that fits their goals.

All of these points lead to a meaningful achievement, since life is not a single story and each person has a different one. Staying yourself in a world that often conditions us to accept ready-made lives remains a significant accomplishment for anyone who refuses to simply follow the script given to them.

In my experience I do not disagree that Emerson’s notion that mastery prevents growth holds truth.

First, all people encounter mastery, and that condition hinders them from advancing in pursuits they once attempted. For instance, if you perform your own job and serve as a manager, you may observe that the products you sell are declining, and your performance suffers. Naturally, you will be compelled to attempt selling other products, yet you anticipate that this shift will occur and foresee feeling inadequate, deeming yourself unfit to continue in your role because you are distressed to see your position weaken rather than strengthen.

Second, mastery resembles being attached to a method while a friend argues that your approach is flawed. After your friend insists that you are mistaken, you recognize the error, but you remain constrained by mastery, leaving you no alternative but to avoid retrying. People are often reluctant to attempt what they have already mastered. For example, a teenager in school who receives a poor grade feels discouraged and may refuse to retake the test because of that mastery.

Third, fearing to retry something you care about, assuming it will unfold as it did initially, can limit progress. However, when you attempt it again, you gain greater awareness because you strive to avoid repeating earlier errors, and you must remain vigilant to prevent the same outcome, given your increased experience. We all can repeat actions; the key is to trust yourself.

Thus, you will notice that you advance regardless of difficulty or frequency of disappointment; you must remain optimistic and cautious when mastery is already present.

In conclusion, you should never abandon what you attempt, regardless of how often or how circumstances shift. Even when mastery seems to take hold, you always possess another opportunity to begin and trust that you can succeed, for that conviction is all you need to start again.

In my view, I accept the idea that feeling fully skilled can block further growth.

One reason is that many people reach a point where they think they know enough, and this stops them from improving in areas that matter to them. For instance, someone running a shop may notice that sales are falling, yet instead of looking for new strategies or products, they stick to old habits. This resistance often leads to frustration and a loss of confidence, making it harder to move forward when results do not improve.

Another reason is that being convinced of our own correctness can shut down helpful feedback. When a friend points out a mistake and we finally accept it, the sense of having already mastered the task can discourage further effort. In school, a student who does poorly on a test might avoid retaking it because the feeling of familiarity with the subject makes failure feel heavier, not lighter.

A third reason involves fear that trying again will repeat the same outcome. However, returning to a challenge usually brings more experience and a clearer sense of what to avoid. Paying closer attention and adjusting methods makes it possible to break old patterns. Anyone can repeat an action many times; what matters is believing that growth comes from persistence rather than from staying in comfortable routines.

In the end, giving up should not be an option, no matter how many setbacks occur. Even when something feels mastered, there is always another chance to begin again. Trust in one’s ability to improve, along with a positive outlook, is often the key to moving forward.

Some argue that a positive outlook is the main door to a successful life. I partly agree, though I also see limits to this idea. To begin with, optimism can push people toward achievement. Many accomplished individuals have turned belief in themselves into real progress. For instance, Michael Jordan was removed from his high school varsity team, yet his steady confidence and hard work allowed him to improve and eventually reach the top of his sport.

Another example comes from music, where Da Baby faced repeated doubt about his future. By remaining grounded and hopeful, he continued to move forward, and today he stands among the most popular rappers, with numerous gold and platinum records and a large following. His story shows how keeping a constructive mindset can help someone find their own route to success.

On the other hand, a positive attitude is not always the key. In situations such as war, people often cannot afford to feel calm or hopeful because they must focus on survival and vigilance. In such moments, a serious and cautious approach may be far more useful than optimism.

In conclusion, while positivity often supports success, there are also times when a realistic or even guarded outlook serves people better. Success, therefore, does not depend on one fixed state of mind.

Should people make their own decisions, or should they follow others—experts and authorities—regarding life’s experience. However, from what I contemplate, if you are alone, emerging without warning and lacking any experience, it is preferable because you obtain your own experiences, and no one disturbs your plans. You make your own decisions and follow your own rules. Conversely, if you have someone at your side who possesses greater experience, they will correct and irritate you by interfering persistently. Some individuals consider it better to follow another person’s decisions, yet others believe independence is superior, since you must formulate your own choices and adhere to your own principles; it resembles having a family—no one dictates what you do with your family. You need not imitate others; their guidance may be flawed while yours is sound, and independence is preferable because you establish your own family through your decisions and regulations.

To begin, solitude is superior because you accumulate experiences through mistakes.

You make your own decisions, but when you choose incorrectly and encounter failure, you gain deeper experiences from that error. As you learn from the misstep, you become more accountable. With significant experience derived from failure, you grow stronger and more confident in your conduct, which feels rewarding and cultivates greater responsibility through accumulated insight. Observers recognize this progress and place trust in you, understanding that you will become accomplished in the future; they comprehend you more fully because you are alone, uninfluenced by someone with greater experience. You elevate yourself and your choices.

Another consideration is that you must uphold the regulations you establish. When you devise your own rules, no one will challenge them provided others wish to remain in your company. Yet if you rely on someone more experienced, you must obey their standards, which you may resist. When you create and honor your own rules, you anticipate outcomes; however, adhering to another’s directives requires caution, since consequences remain uncertain. Thus, it is preferable to forge decisions and rules of your own, for you recognize their value relative to your aims; by doing so, you cultivate resilience and insight.

Finally, independence ensures no one will irritate you; you execute everything personally rather than relying on others’ assistance. You will achieve all feasible outcomes through your own effort, and within your vocation, organization, or academic setting, you become authoritative regarding your undertakings. You need not depend on others’ judgment; should you adopt their perspective and it aligns with their preferences, they will interfere—a situation undesirable because it compels you to proceed along paths you did not select. They will insist on their approach, yet you wish to chart your own course; therefore, pursue your own experiences and guidelines.

To conclude, individuals should make their own decisions and avoid those with greater experience or institutional affiliations. You must begin from nothing and progress through the process, acquiring insight from errors encountered during your efforts. As you accumulate experience, you become stronger and advance in areas you understand; observers will believe in you and expect that you will succeed. Conversely, you must devise your own rules, remain systematic in their design, and avoid imitating others. Create your own standards, understand their implications, and recognize whether outcomes will be favorable or adverse; if you follow another’s rules, results remain unknown. Establish your own regulations to develop distinction and expertise. Moreover, solitude prevents interference in your undertakings; you direct yourself, and others, witnessing your independence, will respect and follow your leadership. Ultimately, you now recognize that autonomy is optimal; you will not inherit others’ regulations or borrow their experiences, and solitude shields you from irritation—owing to these reasons, you should remain alone and begin anew.

Some believe it is wiser to follow other people’s choices, but others feel that being independent is better because you must create your own decisions and rules. That is why being alone helps you build your own life through your choices and standards.

To begin with, independence is better because you gain experience through mistakes. When you decide something and it turns out poorly, you gain valuable lessons from that error. Learning from failure makes you more careful and responsible. This growth gives you strength and confidence, and others begin to trust you more. They see hope in your progress because you act alone, without depending on someone with more experience.

Another point is that you should live by the rules you create. When you set your own standards, others will either respect them or choose not to be close to you. In contrast, following someone else’s experience often forces you to obey their rules, which can feel limiting. Making your own choices and rules helps you understand the possible outcomes, while borrowing someone else’s path creates uncertainty. Therefore, creating your own direction makes you stronger and wiser.

We get further when we stay active and refuse to stand still. By taking regular action, we move closer to the aims we carry in our minds and build habits that keep us going. Thomas Jefferson showed this by filling his years with work, most famously writing the Declaration of Independence, instead of spending time relaxing with friends. When we begin to shape our lives, we set targets each year, and every new year we try to reach them because checking progress always leads to fresh effort. This cycle does not end, since people who keep moving rarely allow themselves to simply stop.

Some individuals waste chances and leave their plans unfinished, yet inside most people there is a drive that will not let them stand still. Over time we see new phones, shoes and televisions, and behind each one stands a person who worked steadily to improve an idea. Generation after generation, our world keeps changing because people refuse to pause and choose instead to keep producing. When we act, we do so for a reason; it is impressive how we can keep giving effort without letting go. Others notice when someone does nothing, and inaction often feels like wasted time for everyone involved.

Life usually follows a clear path: we go to school, study, and then look for work that fits us. Each step depends on doing rather than waiting, so that we can reach goals, grow and gain knowledge. On this journey, there are always people who encourage us to move ahead, even when we feel like resting. For instance, during summer break it is easy to spend days playing games, eating freely and ignoring chores while parents work. If the dishwasher is full and the house is messy, they will likely be unhappy and ask you to switch off the screen, wash dishes and perhaps find a job. This is the moment when doing something starts turning into real progress instead of lost time. In the end, we achieve more when we stay busy, and even when we do not notice, each day brings its own small accomplishment.

People commonly make this choice in their teens, and it is among the hardest, because it asks them to leave old habits behind and push forward without looking back.

We often create a picture of someone the moment we meet, and that picture tends to stay. Because it is the earliest version of us that others see, it becomes the one they keep. Once people form this view, they usually hold it firmly, and shifting it takes time and consistent effort.

These early moments matter because they shape how people remember us later. If we appear unfriendly or upset during a first meeting, others may decide that is simply who we are. Even if we are normally cheerful, that single encounter can stick in their minds and influence how they treat us in the future. It becomes hard to show our true character once a label has settled.

What people believe about us depends heavily on that initial meeting. If we give a poor impression and later try to be kind, they may doubt us. They might assume we are pretending rather than changing, and continue to treat us with suspicion. Trust, once damaged at the start, is not rebuilt quickly.

At the same time, the way we act early on often returns to us in the same form. Others tend to respond to us as we first responded to them, which makes it even harder to rewrite their opinion. People do not usually change their minds easily after forming an impression, and they look for proof that matches what they already believe.

However, change is not impossible. With steady effort and honest actions, someone can reshape how others see them. Sometimes this happens without words, as daily behavior slowly proves the first impression wrong. A negative view can soften, and a positive one can fade if actions do not match it. Though first impressions are difficult to shift, they can still change when given enough time and evidence.

Yes, schools should run a single after-school homework club if they want to raise student achievement. Many young people struggle with assignments and need steady guidance. When teachers remain after lessons to support those students, the work becomes clearer and confusion drops. As a result, learners face tests with stronger understanding and earn better marks because they have practiced with help rather than guessing alone.

Some students, however, avoid staying after class, even when teachers offer extra time. This can frustrate staff who rearrange their evenings to help and then find no one in the room. Teachers already sacrifice personal time so that pupils can improve their results. In return, certain learners still delay or ignore tasks, which leads some instructors to stop giving extra chances and to warn that grades will fall if work is not completed. A single homework club would allow other teachers to leave and prepare for the next day without feeling pressured to stay.

In many cases, students who grasp material quickly finish assignments early and could support classmates in a club setting. Working together has benefits, yet when teachers let pupils cooperate freely, conversations often drift and little learning happens. When partners are not friends, collaboration sometimes works better, but many learners still dislike being helped by classmates. They prefer a teacher’s step-by-step guidance and worry that quick answers from friends may look like copying, especially if they cannot explain their work later.

Achievement would rise noticeably if schools created one club where teachers and volunteers assist those who find homework difficult. Some pupils skip tasks because they do not understand them or simply forget. Completing work at school removes many obstacles, and subjects that rarely assign homework become easier to manage when students use the time well. Even when teachers try to encourage effort, some learners accept low marks instead of trying, which limits their progress.

Pupils who finish early often like to work during class so they can avoid staying later. They may help others or ask a teacher for extra challenges. Some educators support this cooperation because asking questions and explaining ideas to each other deepens learning for everyone.

If schools contact parents and schedule a set time for homework, more students will finish early and feel less pressure at home. Many young people say they have no assignments, only to play and forget later. When teachers call parents to report missing work and poor grades, families can respond more quickly. Small rewards for consistent effort during the club would also lift spirits and show that progress matters.

Clubs in other schools have already shown that regular homework practice leads to stronger test results. Without this habit, revision feels harder when exams arrive. Some schools avoid such clubs because they assume all learners understand the work, or they trust claims like “I left it at home.” Meanwhile, volunteers who give up their time to help do not always receive appreciation. A clear, shared homework space would reduce these gaps and make support more reliable for everyone.

Technology has changed daily life, but in my view it has brought more harm than good because people struggle to manage it. Many have forgotten how rich life can be without screens and devices. There are plenty of valuable activities that do not require technology, such as playing outdoors with friends, borrowing books from libraries, and enjoying nature. These experiences help people feel calm and connected to the real world.

Some argue that teenagers should have no limits on phones or computers because they can learn useful things for their future. However, I believe young people need clear boundaries. Parents should check what their children are doing online to keep them safe. Unlimited access often leads to wasted time and contact with strangers, and speaking with others face to face is important for building trust and strong relationships. Meeting people online can be risky, since not everyone has good intentions.

Another concern is online shopping, which has become common on websites like Amazon or eBay. While these platforms are convenient, they also attract dishonest sellers who create fake pages to cheat buyers. Purchasing items without checking the safety of a website can lead to losing money and avoiding real-life activities, such as going out with family. This habit makes people more isolated and easier to deceive.

To reduce the influence of technology, parents can encourage children to have fun outside, meet friends in person, and stay active. Before playing or chatting with someone, it is wise to know who that person is, because some people may trick children into doing harmful things. Even playing video games or using social media without speaking should have limits until trust is established.

For these reasons, technology should not be freely available to young people. If parents decide to give phones or computers, strict rules and supervision are necessary. Technology makes it harder to finish tasks without constant contact with others, exposes people to scams, and causes children to lose important parts of their childhood. It is common for others to encourage smiles and fun activities so that happiness becomes the normal state, and many believe that people should aim to be content rather than angry or upset.

Bad moods can appear for simple reasons, such as a rough morning or harsh words from family over misunderstandings. Despite these triggers, many people still try to keep a positive attitude and wonder why others become angry without clear cause. Choosing kindness and patience often helps improve the atmosphere for everyone.

When someone feels down or faces mistreatment, support can make a real difference. Offering comfort and friendship to those who are bullied can lift their spirits and remind them that they are valued. It is important to be honest and open with people who have earned trust, while staying cautious around those who act insincere. Asking teachers or trusted adults for help is wise when problems become too difficult to handle alone.

Life should be guided by the goal of staying hopeful and treating others gently. Making good choices, working diligently at school, and avoiding bad habits help create a calmer mind. Negative comments from others should not define a person; believing in oneself and continuing to try builds real strength. Surrounding oneself with sincere people and focusing on personal growth can lead to steadier happiness and a more rewarding everyday life.

Although some people argue that praise is what builds students’ self-esteem, especially before tests or when they need to pass, it is more reasonable to believe that self-esteem should grow from achievement. Learners put real effort into their studies, look for ways to keep their energy high, and work steadily to reach strong results.

Students show this effort by staying responsible for their tasks. When they miss class, they meet with teachers after school to catch up. They usually focus on studying first, knowing that good grades follow serious work, and they often prefer to use breaks to finish homework rather than relax.

To keep moving forward, learners also try to maintain their energy. Many start the day with breakfast and bring snacks so they can stay focused. They understand that confidence grows when they take learning seriously, and they ask teachers for help when concepts are difficult. By organizing materials each time assignments are given, they make their work clearer and more manageable.

In addition, students work continuously to reach their best performance. After school, they study at home, complete homework, and practice exercises whenever they have time. Some visit the library to find books that support what they are learning in class, knowing that steady effort helps them pass their courses.

Even though praise can feel encouraging in certain moments, self-esteem is stronger when it comes from real achievement. By working hard, keeping their energy steady, and studying consistently, students build confidence that lasts.

Confusion and fear stop them from speaking up, and they wrongly believe that making a mistake will ruin everything. This fear keeps them silent and slows their growth.

Third, lack of self-trust plays a major role. Many individuals doubt their own value and depend on others to act for them. They sometimes pass their responsibilities to someone else because they feel ashamed of doing things alone. This habit weakens their ability to manage their own lives and distorts how they express emotions.

In life, nothing is truly impossible, and progress comes through change. Time alters circumstances, relationships, and even feelings from one moment to the next. There is no need to hide what matters to us. We cannot become perfect by avoiding errors, and we will never reach a flawless future. However, by choosing the right path, trusting ourselves, and acting without fear of judgment, we can live more fully and honestly.

If the school day became two hours longer, it would create more problems than benefits, so this change should not happen. A longer day would leave students with very little time for anything else once classes end. Young people need moments to rest and to step away from academic work, and adding extra hours would make that balance harder to find.

When school lasts longer, students would struggle to take part in other activities. There would be less chance to join sports teams or attend club meetings. Practice sessions for hobbies and interests would also shrink or disappear. Over time, this would limit the ways students can explore skills and friendships beyond the classroom.

Tiredness would quickly become a serious issue. Many students would lose interest in school if they had to stay longer each day, and some might even skip classes more often. Sleepiness during lessons could affect how well they understand new topics, which would harm their progress instead of helping it.

A longer school day would also disturb everyday life. Family time would decrease, and students would have fewer chances to look after their own interests or simply relax. Without enough free hours, it becomes difficult to organise daily routines or deal with personal responsibilities. Stress would build up, making it harder to stay motivated and focused.

For these reasons, the school day should not be made longer. Giving students enough time to rest, spend time with family, and follow their interests helps them grow in a healthier and more balanced way.

Thomas Jefferson insists that people must never stand still and that life becomes powerful when a community unites to achieve shared goals. In his view, the colonies faced a clear choice: remain under British authority or act together to win true freedom. Yet surrender also meant condemning women and children to suffering, simply because men refused to stand for justice. Dying for freedom, however, meant dying as free people, not as property.

Through writings and newspapers, Jefferson helped Americans see that they no longer had to obey a distant king. They were a people with the right to choose their leaders and shape their future. Hello. Today I would like to discuss the difference between working as part of a team and working by yourself. First, let me ask you a question: which style do you prefer? I personally choose teamwork, and I will explain why.

Both approaches have strengths and weaknesses. I enjoy working with others because teammates can offer new ideas and different ways to solve problems, and the process can still be enjoyable. At the same time, group work has its challenges, since there is often someone who prefers to play around rather than contribute seriously. On the other hand, working alone gives you full control over how the task is done, without needing to consider different opinions. You can also finish faster and shape the result exactly as you wish. However, doing everything yourself can feel lonely, and it is harder to generate many ideas without input from others.

I believe teamwork is more helpful because several people can support a presentation or a project, which usually makes everyone feel more confident. Working in a group also improves speaking skills, self-trust, and sociability, and it offers chances to meet new friends. Working alone can become boring, and without someone to share thoughts with, progress may slow down.

Spending too much time alone can affect personality and how others see us. People might think we do not want to cooperate, and this isolation can lead to sadness if we feel rejected. By contrast, group work teaches respect, different ways of thinking, and how to cooperate. Many activities in life, such as sports, require teamwork, and learning this skill is important for success in society and future jobs. When we work with people we trust, friendship grows and gives us confidence that is hard to find in other ways.

Friendship remains important when we work together, because it helps us succeed in life, in our careers, and in everyday jobs. For example, if you run out of fuel on a highway, handling the problem alone could be risky and exhausting. With teamwork, several people can push the car, control traffic, and call for help. This shows how valuable cooperation can be during difficult moments.

Of course, working alone depends on personal preferences, and some people do prefer it. However, there are always situations that cannot be solved without others. Teamwork builds respect and strong friendships, and it helps people feel useful and appreciated in ways that are hard to achieve alone.

Winston Churchill, once the leader of Britain, taught that moving ahead means accepting setbacks and refusing to give up. Many people share his view that failure does not end our chances to do well in life. When plans go wrong or choices lead nowhere, it can feel as if everything has slipped away, yet these moments only show that a different path is needed. In my view, offering students the chance to attend classes online or through video calls is a positive step. This option is helpful for those who live far from school and might otherwise struggle to continue their education. It also creates clear and steady communication with teachers, which supports real learning.

One strong advantage is the simplicity and speed of joining lessons from home. Online study is also useful during harsh weather, such as heavy snow, when roads become icy and travel is unsafe. In these cases, studying from home prevents delays and keeps education moving.

If I needed to choose, I would take online or video classes because they feel easier to manage. Learning in this way does not seem difficult, and I would gain more free time for other activities and for work. This flexibility makes it possible to balance study with daily responsibilities.

At the same time, this method is not suitable for everyone. Some students lack a computer or reliable internet, which makes online learning hard for them. As a result, while many benefit, others may fall behind. Online classes can be a good choice, but only when students have the right conditions.

Another important point is cost. Free online schools should be free for all students, with no charges to create equal opportunities. Moreover, online lessons help students avoid missing material, since they can often begin or continue at convenient times. In my opinion, this approach is a useful and practical way to support education.

Some people argue that young students should decide on a profession early, while others believe this brings more risks than benefits. In my view, committing to a career at a young age can be useful in some cases, but it also carries clear disadvantages that must not be ignored.

On the positive side, younger students often see possibilities that adults no longer notice. Because they are less influenced by past failures, they tend to believe that obstacles can be overcome and that new paths can be created. This mindset can encourage them to explore options and take initiative before fear of disappointment sets in. In addition, early commitment may help young people gain practical experience and open doors that might remain closed if they wait too long.

However, there are strong reasons against making such decisions too soon. A young person’s understanding of the world is still limited, and what appears to be a good opportunity may not match reality. Early choices can create pressure, especially when unexpected problems appear, and may lead to frustration if results do not follow expectations. In many cases, students discover later that their interests or circumstances have changed, making earlier plans difficult to continue.

For example, a seventeen-year-old in high school might start working to help a single mother who cannot cover all the family’s needs. At first, the student may believe it is possible to keep studying while supporting the household. Yet, when daily responsibilities grow, it often becomes clear that continuing education is harder than expected. This situation shows how youthful optimism can clash with adult demands.

In general, young students can imagine new solutions and believe that everything is achievable, which may help them seize future opportunities. Nevertheless, real life often requires more than good intentions. Ultimately, young people are indeed the future, but progress depends less on age and more on the ability to adapt and make thoughtful choices. Society should not dismiss young ambitions, yet it should also recognize that readiness comes from experience, not just from youth itself.

I do not agree with Emerson’s claim that staying true to oneself in a world that keeps pushing us to change is the greatest achievement. While personal authenticity matters, reaching a high level of success usually depends on more than just individual will.

One main reason is that people rarely accomplish major goals alone. Schools, teachers, and mentors often provide guidance and skills that individuals need to improve. Trying to reach a high standard without learning from others can slow progress and limit results. Working with others helps us see different views, correct mistakes, and build stronger abilities.

Another important point is that group work prepares us for real life. Most tasks in society require cooperation, clear communication, and shared responsibility. By joining teams, people learn how to solve problems, manage challenges, and understand the world better. These experiences shape them into more capable individuals than isolation could.

Finally, becoming truly successful in any field usually requires deep study. Whether someone wants to be a scientist, artist, or leader, they must learn about their area, practice constantly, and compare their work with existing knowledge. This process often involves teachers, colleagues, and feedback from others.

In conclusion, although staying true to personal values is valuable, I believe that the greatest achievements come from combining personal effort with learning, teamwork, and study, not from isolation.
